children.title: Conical Domains
children.top_down_role: Search regions governed by cone geometry or conic sections.

knowledge_statements.title: Conical Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex search regions invariant under nonnegative scaling and addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). A conical domain is a nonempty convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), meaning that \[x,y\in K,\ \alpha,\beta\ge 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha x+\beta y\in K.\] Consequently, \(0\in K\), \(K+K\subseteq K\), and \(\lambda K\subseteq K\) for every \(\lambda\ge 0\). The cone may be closed or nonclosed and pointed or nonpointed; these are additional properties. Except for \(K=\{0\}\), a conical domain is unbounded and hence noncompact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conical domain is a nonempty subset of Euclidean space closed under nonnegative linear combinations. Every such domain other than the zero cone is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is conical exactly when \(\alpha x+\beta y\in K\) for all \(x,y\in K\) and all \(\alpha,\beta\ge 0\).

source_refs.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27

source_witnesses.locator: 1.9 Polyhedral Convex Sets p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Optimization Dichotomy on a Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundedness and optimality certificate for a linear objective over a cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex cone and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). If \(c\in K^*\), then \(\min_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle=0\), attained at \(x=0\). If \(c\notin K^*\), some \(d\in K\) satisfies \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\), and scaling gives \(\inf_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear minimization over a cone has value zero exactly for a dual-cone coefficient; otherwise it is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\in K^*\iff\min_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle=0\), while \(c\notin K^*\) implies an infimum of \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Optimization Dichotomy on a Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical structural objects associated with a convex conical domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its dual cone is \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\), and its lineality space is \(\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\). The cone is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\). The dual cone is always closed and convex, even when \(K\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone contains vectors nonnegative on the cone; lineality is K intersect -K, and pointedness means zero lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\), \(\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\), and \(K\) is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cone, Lineality, and Pointedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of a convex cone's closure from its dual inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K\). Consequently, \(K=K^{**}\) exactly when \(K\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The double dual of a convex cone is its closure; a convex cone equals its double dual exactly when closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bipolar Representation of Cone Closure

children.title: Convex Star-Shaped Domain Pair
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for compact domains not naturally represented by boxes or polyhedra.

children.title: General Convex Domains
children.top_down_role: Convex search regions lacking a more specialized box, polyhedral, or conic representation.

knowledge_statements.title: General Convex Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex search domains without a required polyhedral or box representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). A nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a general convex domain if \[x,y\in C,\ t\in[0,1]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1-t)x+ty\in C.\] Thus every line segment joining two feasible points remains feasible. No finite inequality representation, boundedness, closedness, or full dimensionality is implied by convexity alone. If \(C\) is also closed and bounded, then it is compact, so every continuous objective \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) attains a global minimum on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general convex domain contains every line segment joining two of its points. Convexity alone does not imply a finite inequality representation, closedness, boundedness, or full dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is convex exactly when \((1-t)x+ty\in C\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and all \(t\in[0,1]\).

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Partition Methods on General Convex and Star Sets p. 119

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Partition Methods on General Convex and Star Sets p. 119

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Under Intersections and Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-independent stability properties of convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An arbitrary intersection of convex sets is convex. If \(C\) is convex and \(A(x)=Mx+b\) is affine, then \(A(C)\) is convex; if \(K\) is convex in the codomain, then \(A^{-1}(K)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity is preserved by arbitrary intersections, affine images, and affine inverse images.
assumptions_latex: All sets and affine maps have compatible finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{C_i\}_i\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\bigcap_iC_i\text{ convex};\quad C,K\text{ convex}\Rightarrow A(C),A^{-1}(K)\text{ convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Intersections and Affine Maps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-mixture formulation of convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex if and only if every finite convex combination \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\), where \(x_i\in C\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), belongs to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is convex exactly when it contains every finite convex combination of its points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is convex}\iff\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\in C\text{ for every finite convex combination}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Convex-Combination Closure

children.title: Star-Shaped Domains
children.top_down_role: Search regions organized around visibility from one or more kernel points.

knowledge_statements.title: Star-Shaped Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domains visible by line segments from at least one feasible center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is star-shaped if there exists a point \(c\in S\) such that \[[c,x]=\{(1-t)c+tx:t\in[0,1]\}\subseteq S\qquad\text{for every }x\in S.\] Any such \(c\) is a star center, and the set of all star centers is the kernel of \(S\). Every nonempty convex set is star-shaped, with every point as a star center, but a star-shaped domain need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is star-shaped when one feasible center can be joined to every feasible point by a segment lying entirely in the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is star-shaped exactly when some \(c\in S\) satisfies \([c,x]\subseteq S\) for every \(x\in S\).

notation.meaning: closed segment from the center to a point

source_refs.locator: 2.6.5 General Star-Shaped Sets p. 129

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6.5 General Star-Shaped Sets p. 129

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictness of the convex-to-star-shaped implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The planar cross \(S=([-2,2]\times[-1,1])\cup([-1,1]\times[-2,2])\) is star-shaped about the origin but is not convex: \((2,1),(1,2)\in S\), whereas their midpoint \((3/2,3/2)\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of perpendicular overlapping rectangles is star-shaped but not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is star-shaped and nonconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Star-Shaped Need Not Be Convex

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological consequence of visibility from a star center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S\) is star-shaped about \(c\), then \(H(x,t)=(1-t)x+tc\) maps \(S\times[0,1]\) continuously into \(S\) and deforms the identity to the constant map at \(c\). Hence \(S\) is path-connected and contractible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Straight-line motion to a star center contracts a star-shaped set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is path-connected and contractible}.
knowledge_statements.title: Contraction to a Star Center

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure of the set of all star centers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(\ker S=\{c\in S:[c,x]\subseteq S\ \forall x\in S\}\). The kernel is convex, possibly empty; \(S\) is star-shaped exactly when \(\ker S\ne\varnothing\), and \(S\) is convex exactly when \(\ker S=S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The star kernel is convex, is nonempty exactly for star-shaped sets, and equals the set exactly for convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker S\text{ is convex};\quad S\text{ star-shaped}\iff\ker S\ne\varnothing;\quad S\text{ convex}\iff\ker S=S.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of the Star Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of star-shaped domain geometry relative to a specified kernel point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subset X\) is star-shaped at \(x_0\in S\) if \[(\forall x\in S)\quad [x,x_0]=\{tx+(1-t)x_0:t\in[0,1]\}\subset S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is star-shaped at x0 when the entire segment joining x0 to every point in the set remains in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall x\in S)\ \{tx+(1-t)x_0:t\in[0,1]\}\subset S

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Domain Geometry
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for lower-dimensional continuous search domains.

children.title: Intrinsic Manifold Domains
children.top_down_role: Search domains treated through their intrinsic lower-dimensional geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent coordinate representations of optimization on an intrinsically specified smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a smooth \(d\)-manifold, \(f:M\to\mathbb R\), and \((U,\varphi)\) a chart. On \(U\), the problem is represented by \(\min_{z\in\varphi(U)}(f\circ\varphi^{-1})(z)\). For an overlapping compatible chart \((V,\psi)\), \[f\circ\varphi^{-1}=(f\circ\psi^{-1})\circ(\psi\circ\varphi^{-1})\quad\text{on }\varphi(U\cap V),\] so feasible points and objective values are independent of the selected chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local chart formulations of an intrinsic manifold problem are equivalent under smooth transition maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ\varphi^{-1}=(f\circ\psi^{-1})\circ(\psi\circ\varphi^{-1})\) on \(\varphi(U\cap V)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Chartwise Representation of Intrinsic Optimization
Intrinsic Manifold Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization domains specified intrinsically by charts rather than ambient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An intrinsic manifold domain is a smooth \(d\)-dimensional manifold \(M\) used directly as the feasible space of an optimization problem \(\min_{x\in M}f(x)\). The manifold is specified by an atlas of compatible charts \(\varphi_alpha:U_\alpha\to\mathbb{R}^d\), and feasibility is membership in \(M\), not satisfaction of an ambient-space equation. When a Riemannian metric \(g\) is supplied, distances, gradients, geodesics, and local search steps are defined intrinsically by \((M,g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intrinsic manifold domain is a smooth manifold treated as the feasible space in its own coordinates, optionally with a Riemannian metric defining optimization geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in M}f(x)\) is an optimization problem whose feasible geometry is defined intrinsically on \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the intrinsic-manifold formulation or its optimization-geometric claims. The chart expression also uses `\varphi_alpha` instead of the declared `\varphi_\alpha`. An authoritative differential-geometry or manifold-optimization source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Embedded Surface Domains
children.top_down_role: Search domains represented as surfaces embedded in an ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Failure Invalidates the Expected Surface Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the regular-level-set conclusion at a singular equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), the zero set is \(S=\{(0,0)\}\), but \(Dh(0,0)=0\). Thus the codimension-one regular-level-set conclusion and the formula \(T_{(0,0)}S=\ker Dh(0,0)=\mathbb R^2\) do not apply; the singleton is instead a zero-dimensional embedded manifold with tangent space \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singular zero set of x squared plus y squared is a point, not a regular one-dimensional surface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}Dh(0,0)<1\text{ and the regular codimension-one conclusion fails}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Failure Invalidates the Expected Surface Dimension

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent and Normal Spaces of a Regular Embedded Surface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient differential structure induced by a regular equality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0\le d<n\), let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n-d}\) be continuously differentiable, and suppose \(S=h^{-1}(0)\) with \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=n-d\) for every \(x\in S\). Then \(T_xS=\ker Dh(x)\), \(N_xS=\operatorname{range}Dh(x)^\top\), and \(\mathbb R^n=T_xS\oplus N_xS\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular equality-defined surface, tangent directions form the Jacobian nullspace and normal directions form its transposed range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_xS=\ker Dh(x),\quad N_xS=\operatorname{range}Dh(x)^\top,\quad\mathbb R^n=T_xS\oplus N_xS.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent and Normal Spaces of a Regular Embedded Surface
Embedded Surface Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-dimensional feasible surfaces represented inside a Euclidean ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{n-d}\) be continuously differentiable. An embedded surface domain is a set \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h(x)=0\}\] such that the Jacobian \(Dh(x)\) has rank \(n-d\) at every \(x\in S\). By this regularity condition, \(S\) is a \(d\)-dimensional embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and its tangent space is \(T_xS=\ker Dh(x)\). Optimization is performed over \(S\) while retaining the ambient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedded surface domain is a regular equality-constrained subset of Euclidean space whose full-rank constraint Jacobian gives a lower-dimensional smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=h^{-1}(0)\) is a \(d\)-dimensional embedded submanifold with \(T_xS=\ker Dh(x)\).

notation.meaning: constraint Jacobian at a feasible point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regular-level-set claim and tangent-space formula require an authoritative source with a specific theorem or section locator. The record should also state the integer range for d relative to n before promotion to candidate review.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Stationarity on an Embedded Surface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed optimization condition over a regular surface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x^*\) locally minimizes differentiable \(f\) over a regular equality-defined surface \(S\), then \(P_{T_{x^*}S}\nabla f(x^*)=0\), equivalently \(\nabla f(x^*)+Dh(x^*)^\top\lambda=0\) for a unique equality multiplier \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth constrained local optimum, the objective gradient is normal to the surface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{T_{x^*}S}\nabla f(x^*)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Stationarity on an Embedded Surface

intermediate_metadata.reason: The leaf inventory covers regular equality-defined embedded surfaces, the admissible dimension range including zero-dimensional surfaces, tangent and normal spaces, and rank-failure behavior. The proposed first-order stationarity record was deferred to equality-constrained or manifold optimization; intrinsic geometry and polynomial-specific structure were excluded as adjacent scopes.

children.title: Nonconvex Connectivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for separated components and nonconvex feasible geometry.

children.title: Connected Nonconvex Domains
children.top_down_role: Connected search regions whose segment geometry is nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Nonconvex Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected feasible regions that fail the line-segment criterion for convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is connected and nonconvex if it cannot be written as \(D=U\cup V\), where \(U\) and \(V\) are disjoint nonempty subsets open in the relative topology of \(D\), and if there exist \(x,y\in D\) and \(t\in(0,1)\) such that \((1-t)x+ty\notin D\). Thus the feasible region has one connected component but does not contain every segment between feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connected nonconvex domain has one topological component but omits at least one point from a segment joining two feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is connected and there exist \(x,y\in D\), \(t\in(0,1)\) with \((1-t)x+ty\notin D\).

notation.meaning: candidate separation in the relative topology

source_refs.locator: 4. General Nonconvex Problems p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: 4. General Nonconvex Problems p. 33

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on interpreting the connected-domain classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The topologist's sine curve \[D=\{(x,\sin(1/x)):0<x\le1\}\cup(\{0\}\times[-1,1])\subset\mathbb R^2\] is connected and nonconvex but not path-connected. Thus connectedness alone does not guarantee a feasible continuous path between every pair of points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connected nonconvex domain need not be path-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is connected and nonconvex but not path-connected.
knowledge_statements.title: Connected Need Not Be Path-Connected

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical hull consequence of nonconvex domain geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and nonconvex, then \(D\subsetneq\operatorname{conv}D\). Thus replacing \(D\) by its convex hull necessarily introduces points not in the original connected nonconvex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a nonempty nonconvex domain strictly enlarges the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\subsetneq\operatorname{conv}D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convex-Hull Enlargement

children.title: Disconnected Domains
children.top_down_role: Search regions split across separated feasible components.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible regions possessing at least two distinct topological components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). A nonempty domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is disconnected if there exist disjoint nonempty subsets \(U,V\subseteq D\), each open in the relative topology of \(D\), such that \(D=U\cup V\). Equivalently, \(D\) has at least two connected components. Every disconnected domain is nonconvex because every nonempty convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is path-connected and therefore connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disconnected domain admits a separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets. Equivalently, it has at least two connected components, and it cannot be convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is disconnected exactly when \(D=U\cup V\) for disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets \(U,V\subseteq D\).

notation.meaning: sets forming a separation of the domain

source_refs.locator: 4. General Nonconvex Problems p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: 4. General Nonconvex Problems p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component Separation Need Not Have Positive Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between topological disconnection and metric separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The domain \[D=\{(x,0):x\ge0\}\cup\{(x,1/x):x>0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\] has two disjoint connected components whose mutual distance is zero. Thus disconnection alone does not imply a positive Euclidean gap. Two disjoint nonempty compact subsets, by contrast, have positive distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disconnected components may approach arbitrarily closely; positive metric separation requires additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is disconnected and the distance between its two components is zero.

notation.meaning: infimum Euclidean distance between two sets

knowledge_statements.title: Component Separation Need Not Have Positive Distance

children.title: Disconnected Nonconvex Components
children.top_down_role: Search regions combining component separation with nonconvex within-component geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Nonconvex Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected domains whose individual connected components are themselves nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) have connected components \(\{D_j\}_{j\in J}\), where \(|J|\ge 2\). The domain has disconnected nonconvex components when every \(D_j\) is nonconvex; explicitly, for each \(j\in J\) there exist \(x_j,y_j\in D_j\) and \(t_j\in(0,1)\) such that \((1-t_j)x_j+t_jy_j\notin D_j\). This class combines disconnection of the domain with nonconvexity inside every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain has disconnected nonconvex components when it has at least two connected components and every component itself violates the line-segment criterion for convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\{D_j\}_{j\in J}\) is the family of connected components of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|J|\ge 2\) and every connected component \(D_j\) is nonconvex.

notation.meaning: a connected component of the domain

source_refs.locator: 4. General Nonconvex Problems p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: 4. General Nonconvex Problems p. 33

children.title: Noncompact Domains
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for truncation, recession, and escape behavior on unbounded search regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean search regions that fail compactness, including the closed unbounded regime associated with recession and escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. By the Heine--Borel characterization, \(D\) is noncompact exactly when it is not both closed and bounded; equivalently, \(D\) is not closed or is unbounded. In the important special case where \(D\) is closed, it is noncompact exactly when it is unbounded. On a closed unbounded domain, a continuous objective need not attain its infimum, and a minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subseteq D\) may satisfy \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\). Compact truncations \(D\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x\rVert\le R\}\) therefore require a separate argument controlling escape as \(R\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty Euclidean domain is noncompact when it is not both closed and bounded. For a closed domain this is equivalent to unboundedness, and minimizing sequences may then escape to infinity without attaining the infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is noncompact exactly when it is not closed or is unbounded; if \(D\) is closed, noncompactness is equivalent to unboundedness.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 General Minimization Problem p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 General Minimization Problem p. 5

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of attainment for a continuous objective on a closed noncompact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(D=\mathbb R\), the continuous function \(f(x)=e^{-x}\) satisfies \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=0\), but \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\in D\). Thus the infimum is unattained and the minimizing sequence \(x_k=k\) escapes to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function exp(-x) on the real line has infimum zero but no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^{-x}=0\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}e^{-x}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Unattained Infimum at Infinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value convergence for expanding radial truncations of a closed domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(f:D\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and set \(D_R=D\cap\{x:\|x\|\le R\}\). For every sufficiently large \(R\) with \(D_R\ne\varnothing\), define \(v_R=\inf_{x\in D_R}f(x)\). Then each \(D_R\) is compact, \(v_R\) is nonincreasing, and \(\lim_{R\to\infty}v_R=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\). This value convergence does not imply that truncation minimizers have a bounded accumulation subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infima over expanding compact truncations decrease to the full-domain infimum, although minimizers may escape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_R\downarrow\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\) as \(R\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Compact-Truncation Values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition preventing minimizing sequences from escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed. If \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is lower semicontinuous and coercive on \(D\), meaning \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\in D\) and \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\), then every sublevel set of \(f\) is compact and \(f\) attains its infimum on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity and coercivity on a closed domain guarantee a global minimizer despite noncompactness.
assumptions_latex: \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is lower semicontinuous and coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Attainment on Closed Domains

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Concave, DC, quadratic, minimax, multiplicative, Lipschitz, and fractional chapters

children.title: General Continuous Nonconvex Nonlinear Programs

children.title: Nonconvex Objectives with Convex Constraints
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for objective-driven nonconvexity over convex feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Objectives with Convex Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimization whose nonconvexity arises solely from the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). The problem \[\inf_{x\in C} f(x)\] is a nonconvex-objective problem with convex constraints when \(f\) is not convex on \(C\); equivalently, there exist \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) such that \(f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)>\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\). Constraint functions may be used provided their common feasible set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a nonconvex function over a nonempty convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) belongs to the nonconvex-objective, convex-feasible-set class.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Feasibility Does Not Make Local Minima Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-driven local-to-global failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[-2,2]\), define \[f(x)=\min\{(x+1)^2,(x-1)^2+\tfrac12\}.\] The continuous function \(f\) is nonconvex. The point \(x=1\) is a strict local minimizer with value \(1/2\), while \(x=-1\) is globally minimizing with value \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex objective can have a strict nonglobal local minimum even on an interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\) is a strict local minimizer but not a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Feasibility Does Not Make Local Minima Global

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value representation on a compact convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(\operatorname{conv}_C f\) be its convex envelope on \(C\). Then \[\min_{x\in C}\operatorname{conv}_C f(x)=\min_{x\in C}f(x).\] An envelope minimizer need not minimize \(f\), so value equality alone does not recover a primal optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope has the same minimum value as the original objective but may introduce spurious minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_C\operatorname{conv}_C f=\min_Cf\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Envelope Value Equivalence

children.title: Convex Objectives with Nonconvex Constraints
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for feasible-set-driven nonconvexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Objectives with Nonconvex Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimization whose nonconvexity arises from the feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and let \(F\subseteq D\) be nonempty and nonconvex. The problem \[\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\] is a convex-objective problem with nonconvex constraints. If \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(g_i:D\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(F=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), the defining feature remains the nonconvexity of \(F\), irrespective of which constraint functions produce it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a convex objective over a nonempty, nonconvex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) belongs to the convex-objective, nonconvex-feasible-set class.

notation.meaning: constraint function in an optional representation of the feasible set

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Objectives Can Have Nonglobal Feasible Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global failure caused solely by nonconvex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(D=[0,2]\), let \(f(x)=x\) and \(F=\{0,2\}=\{x\in D:x(2-x)\le0\}\). The objective is affine, while \(F\) is nonconvex. Relative to \(F\), \(x=2\) is an isolated local minimizer but is not global because \(f(0)<f(2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even an affine objective can have a nonglobal local minimizer on a nonconvex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2\) is locally minimizing on \(F\) but does not globally minimize \(f\) over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Objectives Can Have Nonglobal Feasible Local Minima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of convexifying a nonconvex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(f\) be convex on \(\operatorname{conv}F\). Then \[\inf_{x\in\operatorname{conv}F}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x).\] Equality holds for every affine \(f\), but can fail for convex nonlinear objectives: for \(F=\{0,2\}\) and \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\), the respective values are \(0\) and \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying the feasible set gives a lower bound, exact for affine objectives but potentially strict for nonlinear convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\operatorname{conv}F}f\le\inf_Ff\), with equality for affine \(f\) but not for every convex \(f\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Relaxation Boundary

children.title: Fully Nonconvex Nonlinear Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for models with nonconvex objectives and feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Nonconvex Nonlinear Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear minimization with both objective-driven and feasible-set-driven nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \(g_i:D\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define the nonempty feasible set \[F=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}.\] The nonlinear program \[\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\] is fully nonconvex when \(f\) is nonconvex on \(D\) and \(F\) is nonconvex. Thus both the objective and the feasible region depart from convex-program structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully nonconvex nonlinear program has both a nonconvex objective and a nonconvex feasible region.
assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is nonempty and nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) is a fully nonconvex nonlinear program.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous Nonconvexity Permits Nonglobal Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example exhibiting both sources of nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[-2,2]\), \(F=\{-1,1\}\), and \(f(x)=-x^2+x\). The objective and feasible set are nonconvex. Both feasible points are isolated local minimizers relative to \(F\), but only \(-1\) is globally minimizing because \(f(-1)=-2<f(1)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With both a nonconvex objective and feasible set, a feasible local minimizer can be nonglobal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\) is locally minimizing on \(F\), while \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)=\{-1\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Nonconvexity Permits Nonglobal Local Minima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of derivative-based conditions in the fully nonconvex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fully nonconvex nonlinear program, feasibility together with stationarity, KKT conditions, or local minimality does not by itself certify global optimality. A global certificate requires additional structure, such as a valid global lower bound matching the candidate value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local necessary conditions do not certify global optimality in the fully nonconvex class.
assumptions_latex: Both the objective and feasible region may be nonconvex.
No generalized-convexity or exact global-relaxation assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{stationarity or local minimality}\not\Longrightarrow\text{global optimality}\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Generic Local Optimality Certificate

children.title: Generalized-Convexity Tractability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separates genuinely global regimes from classes in which local information retains global force.

children.title: Level-Set Generalized-Convexity Pair
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for level-set generalized-convexity regimes.

children.title: Quasiconvex Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized through convex lower-level geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-space reduction when exact convex sublevel-feasibility tests are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\). Suppose \(L\le v^*\le U\), the level \(U\) is feasible, and feasibility of \(C\cap\{x:f(x)\le t\}\) can be decided exactly. Testing \(t=(L+U)/2\) and replacing \(U\) by \(t\) when feasible and \(L\) by \(t\) otherwise preserves \(L_k\le v^*\le U_k\) and gives \(U_k-L_k=2^{-k}(U-L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconvex minimization can be solved in value space by bisection over convex sublevel-feasibility problems.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and \(f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge\left\lceil\log_2\frac{U-L}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\implies U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Bisection Through Convex Sublevel Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable quasiconvex functions on open convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is quasiconvex if and only if \[f(y)\le f(x)\implies \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\le0\qquad(x,y\in D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable quasiconvexity is equivalent to a gradient inequality toward every point having no larger value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff[f(y)\le f(x)\Rightarrow\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\le0].
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Characterization of Differentiable Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of quasiconvex and convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x^3\) on \(\mathbb R\) is quasiconvex because it is nondecreasing, but it is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The increasing cubic is quasiconvex but not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=x^3\text{ is quasiconvex on }\mathbb R\text{ but not convex there}.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Does Not Imply Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-minimum consequences intrinsic to quasiconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is quasiconvex on a convex set \(C\), every strict local minimizer is a global minimizer. If \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex, meaning \(f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for distinct \(x,y\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), then \(f\) has at most one global minimizer on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict local minima of quasiconvex functions are global, and strict quasiconvexity implies uniqueness when a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ strict local minimum}\Rightarrow x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_C f;\quad f\text{ strictly quasiconvex}\Rightarrow|\operatorname*{argmin}_C f|\le1.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Minima and Strict Quasiconvexity
Quasiconvex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set definition of quasiconvex minimization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex if every sublevel set \(\{x\in D:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is convex for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Equivalently, \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\] for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). A quasiconvex model minimizes such an \(f\) over a convex feasible subset of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex model minimizes a function whose sublevel sets are convex over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconvex exactly when all its sublevel sets are convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quasiconvexity definition and model interpretation are standard and internally consistent, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Quasiconcave Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized through convex upper-level geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction to nested convex feasibility problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\sup_{x\in C}f(x)\) and \(S_\alpha=\{x\in C:f(x)\ge\alpha\}\). For quasiconcave \(f\), every \(S_\alpha\) is convex and \(S_\beta\subseteq S_\alpha\) when \(\beta>\alpha\). If exact feasibility of every \(S_\alpha\) is available and finite bounds \(L\le M\le U\) are known, bisection produces a bracket of width at most \(\varepsilon\) after \(\lceil\log_2((U-L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When superlevel feasibility is exactly tractable, bisection computes the quasiconcave maximum value to prescribed accuracy.
assumptions_latex: Each superlevel feasibility problem is exactly decidable.
Finite initial bounds \(L\le M\le U\) are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\ge\lceil\log_2((U-L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\Rightarrow U_N-L_N\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.title: Superlevel Feasibility and Value Bisection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonstrict Local Maxima Need Not Be Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for ordinary quasiconcavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[0,2]\), define \(f(x)=0\) for \(0\le x\le1\) and \(f(x)=x-1\) for \(1<x\le2\). This nondecreasing function is quasiconcave. Every point of \((0,1)\) is a nonstrict local maximizer, but the unique global maximizer is \(x=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary quasiconcavity does not make every nonstrict local maximum global.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the stated nondecreasing piecewise-linear function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Points in \((0,1)\) are locally maximizing, while \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{C}f=\{2\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonstrict Local Maxima Need Not Be Global

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Maximizer Sets and Strict Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of attained maximizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be quasiconcave. If the maximum value \(M\) is attained, then \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}f(x)=\{x\in C:f(x)\ge M\}\] is convex. If \(f\) is strictly quasiconcave, an attained maximizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximizers of a quasiconcave function form a convex set; strict quasiconcavity gives uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex and is a singleton under strict quasiconcavity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Maximizer Sets and Strict Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global consequence of quasiconcavity, contrasted with nonstrict local maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be quasiconcave. Every strict local maximizer of \(f\) relative to \(C\) is a global maximizer of \(f\) over \(C\). Ordinary nonstrict local maximizers need not be global.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconcavity makes strict local maxima global, but does not give the same guarantee for nonstrict local maxima.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is a strict local maximizer relative to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x^*)\ge f(y)\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Local Maxima Are Global

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Under Monotone Transformations and Pointwise Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic constructions preserving quasiconcavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex. If \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is quasiconcave and \(\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is nondecreasing, then \(\phi\circ f\) is quasiconcave. If \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) are quasiconcave on \(C\), then \(h(x)=\min_{1\le k\le r}f_k(x)\) is quasiconcave and \[\{x:h(x)\ge\alpha\}=\bigcap_{k=1}^r\{x:f_k(x)\ge\alpha\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nondecreasing scalar transformations and finite pointwise minima preserve quasiconcavity.
assumptions_latex: The stated functions are real-valued and quasiconcave on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f\) and \(\min_k f_k\) are quasiconcave on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Monotone Transformations and Pointwise Minima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative characterization on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is quasiconcave on \(D\) if and only if, for every \(x,y\in D\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function is quasiconcave exactly when every direction toward a point of no smaller value has nonnegative directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is quasiconcave}\iff\bigl[f(y)\ge f(x)\Rightarrow\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\ge0\bigr].
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Characterization of Differentiable Quasiconcavity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict segment-inequality variant of quasiconcavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is strictly quasiconcave if, for every distinct \(x,y\in C\) and every \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)>\min\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconcavity requires every proper interior point of a segment between distinct points to exceed the smaller endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\ne y,\ 0<\lambda<1\Longrightarrow f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)>\min\{f(x),f(y)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Quasiconcavity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion of concave maximization in quasiconcave maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every concave real-valued function on a convex domain is quasiconcave, and every strictly concave function is strictly quasiconcave. Neither converse holds; for example, \(f(x)=x^3\) is strictly quasiconcave on \(\mathbb R\), because it is strictly increasing, but it is not concave on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concavity implies quasiconcavity, while monotone functions show that quasiconcavity is strictly broader.
assumptions_latex: The function is concave, or strictly concave for the strict conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ concave}\Longrightarrow f\text{ quasiconcave}.
knowledge_statements.title: Concavity Implies Quasiconcavity
Quasiconcave Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set definition of quasiconcave maximization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconcave if every superlevel set \(\{x\in D:f(x)\geq\alpha\}\) is convex for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Equivalently, \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\geq\min\{f(x),f(y)\}\] for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). A quasiconcave model maximizes such an \(f\) over a convex feasible subset of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconcave model maximizes a function whose superlevel sets are convex over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconcave exactly when all its superlevel sets are convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quasiconcavity definition and maximization interpretation are standard and internally consistent, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sign conversion between quasiconcave maximization and quasiconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real-valued function \(f\) on a convex set \(C\), \(f\) is quasiconcave if and only if \(-f\) is quasiconvex. Moreover, \(\sup_{x\in C}f(x)=-\inf_{x\in C}[-f(x)]\), with identical optimizer sets after exchanging \(\operatorname*{argmax}\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating the objective converts quasiconcave maximization exactly into quasiconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is quasiconcave}\iff -f\text{ is quasiconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign Duality with Quasiconvex Minimization

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns convex superlevel geometry, maximizer structure, strict-local optimality, closure rules, feasibility bisection, and the differentiable first-order characterization. Quasiconvex lower-level theory and the symmetric sign-duality statement are excluded to the sibling pair and represented by a cross-index. The foundational definition remains missing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic compact-domain attainment theorem proposed for this leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact. If \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is upper semicontinuous, then \(f\) attains its maximum on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-semicontinuous function attains its maximum on a nonempty compact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}f(x)\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment under Upper Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns convex superlevel geometry, maximizer-set structure, strict quasiconcavity, strict-local globality, closure rules, differentiable characterization, and threshold-feasibility search. Quasiconvex lower-level theory is excluded to the sibling, and generic compact-domain attainment is deferred because it does not use quasiconcavity. Expansion remains necessary because the ordinary definition is still deferred.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasiconcave minimization over a compact convex subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty compact convex set and let \(f\) be quasiconcave on \(X\). Then the minimum of \(f\) over \(X\) is attained at an extreme point of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of a quasiconcave function over a nonempty compact convex set is attained at an extreme point of that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in\operatorname{ext}(X):\quad f(x^*)=\min_{x\in X}f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-Inequality Certificate on a Convex Feasible Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained first-order global certificate for pseudoconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of an open convex domain \(D\), and let differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be pseudoconvex. If \(x^*\in C\) satisfies \[\nabla f(x^*)^{\mathsf T}(y-x^*)\ge0\quad\text{for every }y\in C,\] then \(x^*\) globally minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first-order variational inequality is a global optimality certificate for pseudoconvex minimization over a convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and pseudoconvex on the open convex domain \(D\).
The displayed variational inequality holds at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Certificate on a Convex Feasible Set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between level-set and derivative-based generalized convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x^3\) on \(\mathbb R\) is strictly increasing and hence quasiconvex. It is not pseudoconvex: \(f'(0)=0\), but \(0\) is not a global minimizer; equivalently, \(f(-1)<f(0)\) while \(f'(0)(-1-0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function x cubed is quasiconvex but not pseudoconvex because it has a nonglobal stationary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconvex but not pseudoconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Does Not Imply Pseudoconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Placement within level-set generalized convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every differentiable pseudoconvex function on an open convex domain is quasiconvex. The converse fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable pseudoconvex functions are quasiconvex, but quasiconvexity is strictly weaker.
assumptions_latex: The domain is open and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every lower-level set of \(f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoconvexity Implies Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental unconstrained optimality property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and pseudoconvex. If \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\), then \(x^*\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every stationary point of a differentiable pseudoconvex function is globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoconvex Stationarity Is Globally Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Minima of Pseudoconvex Programs Are Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global property for pseudoconvex minimization over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of an open convex set \(D\), and let differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be pseudoconvex. Every local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\) is a global minimizer over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudoconvexity rules out nonglobal local minima on convex feasible sets.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Minima of Pseudoconvex Programs Are Global

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Sufficiency with Quasiconvex Inequality Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global constrained certificate for a pseudoconvex objective and differentiable quasiconvex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and pseudoconvex, and let each differentiable \(g_i:D\to\mathbb R\) be quasiconvex. If \(x^*\) is feasible and multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\) satisfy \[\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0,\] then \(x^*\) globally minimizes \(f\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT conditions are globally sufficient for a pseudoconvex objective with differentiable quasiconvex inequality constraints.
assumptions_latex: Every \(g_i\) is differentiable and quasiconvex on \(D\).
Feasibility, stationarity, multiplier nonnegativity, and complementarity hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sufficiency with Quasiconvex Inequality Constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict derivative-based variant of differentiable pseudoconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:D	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable. The function is strictly pseudoconvex if, for all distinct \(x,y\in D\), \[f(y)\le f(x)\Longrightarrow 
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)<0.\] Equivalently, \(
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\ge0\) implies \(f(y)>f(x)\) whenever \(x
e y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict pseudoconvexity makes every direction toward a distinct point of no greater value a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)\le f(x),\ x\ne y\Longrightarrow\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Pseudoconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion of differentiable convex objectives in the pseudoconvex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex, then \(f\) is pseudoconvex on \(D\). The converse fails: \(f(x)=x+x^3\) is pseudoconvex on \(\mathbb R\), because \(f'(x)=1+3x^2>0\), but it is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every differentiable convex function is pseudoconvex, while a strictly increasing nonconvex function disproves the converse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is pseudoconvex on }D.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable Convexity Implies Pseudoconvexity
Pseudoconvex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable generalized-convex minimization based on a first-order implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. The function \(f\) is pseudoconvex on \(D\) if, for every \(x,y\in D\), \[\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\geq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(y)\geq f(x).\] Equivalently, \(f(y)<f(x)\) implies \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)<0\). A pseudoconvex model minimizes such a function over a convex subset of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudoconvexity makes every direction toward a lower value a strict descent direction at the current point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\geq0\) implies \(f(y)\geq f(x)\) for all \(x,y\in D\).

notation.meaning: gradient of the objective at the current point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The differentiable pseudoconvexity implication and its contrapositive are consistent, but the record has no authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Invex Models
children.top_down_role: Models whose generalized path structure places them in an invex regime.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global certificate for differentiable inequality-constrained invex programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Suppose \(D\) is invex and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are differentiable and invex with respect to the same map \(\eta\). If a feasible \(x^*\) and multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\) satisfy \[\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0,\] then \(x^*\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT conditions are globally sufficient when the objective and constraints share the same invexity map.
assumptions_latex: The domain, objective, and all inequality functions use one common invexity map.
\(x^*\) is feasible and the displayed stationarity, nonnegativity, and complementarity conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Map Invex KKT Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit differentiable nonconvex invex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x+x^3\) on \(\mathbb R\) and define \[\eta(y,x)=\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{f'(x)}=\frac{y+y^3-x-x^3}{1+3x^2}.\] Since \(f'(x)>0\), this map is defined everywhere and \(f(y)-f(x)=f'(x)\eta(y,x)\), so \(f\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\). Yet \(f''(x)=6x\) changes sign, so \(f\) is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The increasing cubic-plus-linear function is invex for an explicit map but is not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\) but is not convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Invexity Strictly Extends Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is the Straight-Displacement Special Case
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between differentiable convexity and invexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex, then the inequality \[f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\] holds with \(\eta(y,x)=y-x\). Thus differentiable convexity is the straight-displacement invex special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable convex functions are invex for the ordinary displacement map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies the invex inequality with \(\eta(y,x)=y-x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is the Straight-Displacement Special Case

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary Invex Points Are Global Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental unconstrained invex optimality result under an explicit eta convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be invex with respect to \(\eta\), and suppose differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \[f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\quad(x,y\in D).\] If \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\), then \(f(y)\ge f(x^*)\) for every \(y\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every stationary point of an invex function is globally minimizing.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and satisfies the displayed invex inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Invex Points Are Global Minima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak and KKT-based strong duality for a differentiable common-map invex inequality program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le0\}\), consider the Wolfe dual \[\max_{u\in D,\lambda\ge0}\ f(u)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(u)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \nabla f(u)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(u)=0.\] If \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are differentiable and invex with respect to one common map \(\eta\), every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \((u,\lambda)\) satisfy \(f(x)\ge f(u)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(u)\). If an optimal primal point admits KKT multipliers, its KKT pair is dual optimal and the values coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common invexity map gives weak Wolfe duality, while an optimal KKT pair gives strong duality and dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: The domain and all model functions use the same invexity map \(\eta\).
For strong duality, an optimal primal point with KKT multipliers exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^*\le p^*\); an optimal primal KKT pair satisfies \(d^*=p^*\) and attains the dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Map Invex Wolfe Duality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of invex functions sharing one displacement map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_r:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and invex with respect to the same map \(\eta\), and let \(a_k\ge0\). Then \(F=\sum_{k=1}^r a_kf_k\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\): \[F(y)-F(x)\ge \nabla F(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\qquad(x,y\in D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative linear combination of differentiable functions sharing one invexity map remains invex for that map.
assumptions_latex: \(f_k\) is differentiable and invex with respect to the same \(\eta\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=1}^r a_kf_k\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\).

notation.meaning: common invex displacement based at x

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Map Nonnegative Combination Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Local Minima of Invex Functions Are Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global result obtained from first-order stationarity on an open invex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and invex with respect to \(\eta\), and let differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \[f(y)-f(x)\ge \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\qquad(x,y\in D).\] Every local minimizer \(x^*\in D\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open invex domain, every local minimum of a differentiable invex function is global.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is open and invex with respect to \(\eta\).
\(f\) is differentiable and invex with respect to \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Local Minima of Invex Functions Are Global

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-fixed definition of differentiable invex models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\eta:D\times D\to\mathbb R^n\). The domain is invex with respect to \(\eta\) when \(x+t\eta(y,x)\in D\) for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). A differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is invex with respect to this same map when \(f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\) for all \(x,y\in D\). Here the second argument \(x\) is the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invexity replaces the straight displacement from x to y in the convex gradient inequality by a specified feasible displacement map.
assumptions_latex: The argument order of \(\eta(y,x)\) is fixed with \(x\) as base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x+t\eta(y,x)\in D,\qquad f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x).

notation.meaning: Invex displacement based at \(x\) and directed toward the comparison point \(y\).

review_flags: The eta argument convention is stated explicitly because conventions vary.
knowledge_statements.title: Invex Domain and Invex Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Invexity Gives a Unique Stationary Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict variant of stationary-point global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be invex with respect to \(\eta\), and let differentiable \(f:D	o\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(y)-f(x)>
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\) whenever \(x
e y\). If \(
abla f(x^*)=0\), then \(f(y)>f(x^*)\) for every \(y
e x^*\). Hence \(x^*\) is the unique global minimizer and no other stationary point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every stationary point of a strictly invex function is its unique global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The strict invex inequality holds for distinct points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)=\{x^*\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Invexity Gives a Unique Stationary Minimizer
Invex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable generalized-convex models defined relative to an invexity map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\eta:D\times D\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(x+t\eta(y,x)\in D\) for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). A differentiable function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\) if \[f(y)-f(x)\geq\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\] for every \(x,y\in D\). An invex model minimizes such a function on an \(\eta\)-invex feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invexity replaces straight-line displacements in the convex gradient inequality by a specified invexity map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)-f(x)\geq\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\) for every \(x,y\in D\).

notation.meaning: invex displacement from the base point

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Concave Minimization: Theory, Applications and Algorithms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines concave minimization over an explicitly represented closed convex set, its set-difference lifting, its quasiconcave extension, and the polyhedral specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be closed and convex, with each \(g_i\) convex, and let \(f\) be concave. Concave minimization is \[\min\{f(x):x\in D\}.\] It is equivalently \[\min\{t:(x,t)\in G\setminus H\},\qquad G=D\times\mathbb R,\quad H=\{(x,t):f(x)>t\},\] where \(H\) is convex. Requiring only that \(f\) be quasiconcave gives quasiconcave minimization; if \(D\) is polyhedral, the concave problem is linearly constrained concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concave minimization minimizes a concave objective over a closed convex set described by convex inequalities. It admits an equivalent lifted set-difference formulation. Quasiconcave minimization relaxes concavity to quasiconcavity, and a polyhedral feasible set yields the linearly constrained subclass.
assumptions_latex: D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ is closed and convex}
f\text{ is concave; for the extension, }f\text{ is quasiconcave}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in D}f(x)=\min\{t:(x,t)\in(D\times\mathbb R)\setminus\{(x,t):f(x)>t\}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global optimal solutions, unboundedness, and convex-maximization reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for problem (P) and the sign-reversal representation connecting convex maximization with concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) denote the global minimum value of problem \((P)\) over its feasible set \(D\). A point \(x^*\in D\) satisfying \(f(x^*)=v\) is a global optimal solution (global minimum), and \(X^*=\{x\in D:f(x)=v\}\) denotes the set of all such solutions. If \(v=-\infty\), then \((P)\) is unbounded. If \(g\) is convex and \(Y\) is convex, then maximizing \(g\) over \(Y\) is equivalent to minimizing the concave function \(-g\) over \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symbol v denotes the global minimum value of (P), and X* is the set of feasible points attaining it. The problem is called unbounded when v is minus infinity. Maximizing a convex function over a convex set is equivalently formulated as minimizing its concave negative over the same set.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is convex on the convex set }Y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X^*=\{x\in D:f(x)=v\},\qquad v=-\infty\Rightarrow (P)\text{ is unbounded},\qquad \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{y\in Y}g(y)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in Y}(-g(y)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Alone Does Not Ensure Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for concave minimization on a general convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=x\). Then \(C\) is nonempty and convex and \(f\) is affine, hence concave, but \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0\] is not attained in \(C\). Therefore convexity of the feasible set and concavity of the objective alone do not guarantee a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave objective on a nonclosed convex set can have a finite but unattained infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0\), but \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A global minimizer of a concave function minimizes its convex envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way minimizer inclusion for concave minimization over a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a convex domain, let \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave, and let \(F\) be the convex envelope of \(f\) over \(S\). Then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S} f(x)\subseteq \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S} F(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every global minimizer of a concave function on a convex domain is also a global minimizer of its convex envelope on that domain; the converse is not asserted.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is the convex envelope of }f\text{ over }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}F(x).

children.title: Separable Concave Minimization
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for coordinate-separable concave objectives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of independent minimization on a coupled convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^2:x_1+x_2=1\}\) and \(\phi_1(u)=\phi_2(u)=-u^2\). Then \[\min_{x\in C}\bigl(\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\bigr)=-1,\] whereas \[\min_{u\in[0,1]}\phi_1(u)+\min_{u\in[0,1]}\phi_2(u)=-2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear coupling constraint can invalidate independent coordinate minimization despite objective separability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\sum_j\phi_j(x_j)=-1>-2=\sum_j\min_{u\in[0,1]}\phi_j(u)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Can Prevent Coordinatewise Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise additive concave objectives on a common convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. If each \(\phi_j\) is concave on the projection of \(C\) onto coordinate \(j\), then a separable concave-minimization problem has the form \[\inf_{x\in C}\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j).\] Separability means that each summand depends on only one decision coordinate; it does not require the feasible set to be a Cartesian product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable concave-minimization problem minimizes a sum of univariate concave coordinate functions; feasibility may still couple the coordinates.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_j\) is concave on the relevant coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective \(x\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)\) is concave and additively separable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Additively Separable Concave Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Decomposition on Cartesian Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent coordinate minimization when feasibility contains no cross-coordinate coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\prod_{j=1}^n C_j\), where every \(C_j\) is nonempty, and suppose each scalar infimum is finite. Then \[\inf_{x\in C}\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)=\sum_{j=1}^n\inf_{u\in C_j}\phi_j(u).\] If every scalar infimum is attained, the global minimizer set equals \[\prod_{j=1}^n\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C_j}\phi_j(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Cartesian feasible set, an additively separable objective decomposes exactly into independent coordinate problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint infimum is the sum of the coordinate infima, with the stated product formula under attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Decomposition on Cartesian Feasible Sets
Separable Concave Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave minimization with an additive coordinatewise objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and for each \(j=1,\ldots,n\), let \(\phi_j\) be concave on the projection of \(C\) onto coordinate \(j\). A separable concave minimization problem is \[\inf_{x\in C}\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j).\] The objective is concave because it is a sum of concave coordinate functions, while separability means that no summand depends on more than one decision coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a sum of univariate concave functions, minimized over a convex feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_j\) is concave on the relevant coordinate domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)\) is a separable concave objective on \(C\).

children.title: Canonical DC Programs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit DC objective and inequality form on a convex base domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. A canonical DC program is displayed as \[\inf_{x\in D}\bigl(g_0(x)-h_0(x)\bigr)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where every \(g_i\) and \(h_i\), including the index \(i=0\), is convex on \(D\). The selected decompositions are part of the displayed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical DC program explicitly writes its objective and each nonlinear inequality as a difference of two convex functions on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective and all displayed nonlinear inequalities are in explicit difference-of-convex form.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Difference-of-Convex Program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation dependence of canonical DC models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f=g-h\) on \(D\), where \(g\) and \(h\) are convex, then for every convex function \(q\) on \(D\), \[f=(g+q)-(h+q).\] Hence a DC function generally has many convex-difference decompositions, even though each chosen decomposition represents the same function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same convex function to both components produces another valid DC decomposition, so the representation is not unique.
assumptions_latex: \(g,h,q\) are convex on the common convex domain \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=(g+q)-(h+q)\) is another valid DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness of DC Decompositions

Equalities, when present, require an explicitly equivalent DC constraint representation. The displayed decompositions are part of the model representation and need not be unique.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective and constraint functions admit the displayed DC representations \(g_i-h_i\).
