children.title: Reverse-Convex Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for convex base regions restricted by reverse-convex constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex base optimization restricted by convex-function superlevel constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be convex on \(C\). A reverse-convex program has the form \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\geq0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Each constraint retains a superlevel set of a convex function, equivalently excluding the convex strict sublevel set \(\{x\in C:g_i(x)<0\}\); the resulting feasible region is generally nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex program minimizes a convex objective over a convex base set after imposing convex-function superlevel constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible region is \(C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)\geq0\}\), equivalently the convex base with finitely many convex strict sublevel sets excluded.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex Program
Reverse-Convex Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex base models restricted by superlevel constraints of convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and let \(g_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. A reverse-convex program has the form \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\geq0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Each reverse-convex constraint retains a superlevel set of a convex function, equivalently excluding the convex open set \(\{x\in C:g_i(x)<0\}\); its feasible set is generally nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex program adds convex-function superlevel constraints to a convex base problem, generally producing a nonconvex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible region is \(C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)\geq0\}\), which is generally nonconvex.

children.title: Programs with Separated Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for models with isolated or low-dimensional nonconvex components.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(G_i:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{F(x,y):G_i(x,y)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ (x,y)\in X\times Y\}\) has nonconvexity confined to the \(y\)-block.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a two-block formulation in which all failure of joint convexity is isolated in one block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A program has separated nonconvexity if it can be written as \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}\ F(x,y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad G_i(x,y)\le 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where, for each fixed \(y\in Y\), the functions \(x\mapsto F(x,y)\) and \(x\mapsto G_i(x,y)\) are convex on \(X\). Thus every fixed-\(y\) subproblem is convex, while nonconvex dependence may occur through \(y\) or through interactions between \(x\) and \(y\). The nonconvexity is low-dimensional when \(k=\dim Y\) is small relative to \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A program has separated nonconvexity when fixing a designated, often low-dimensional variable block leaves a convex optimization problem in all remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Programs with Separated Nonconvexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-block formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the navigation container, but no citation is supplied for the exact term or its proposed scope. An authoritative source is needed to distinguish this class from biconvex, partially convex, and low-dimensional nonconvex formulations.

children.title: Noncanonical DC Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for DC-representable models requiring additional transformation.

assumptions_latex: The original objective and constraint functions admit finite convex-difference representations on \(C\) after an equivalent reformulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reformulated problem is a DC program equivalent to the original problem on \(C\).

notation.meaning: convex components of the reformulated objective
convex components of the reformulated constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats noncanonicality as DC representability obtained only after an equivalent transformation or lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A noncanonical DC program is an optimization problem not initially displayed in convex-difference form but equivalent, possibly after introducing auxiliary variables and constraints, to \[\inf_{z\in C}\ \bigl(g_0(z)-h_0(z)\bigr)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(z)-h_i(z)\le 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where every \(g_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\), including the index \(i=0\), is convex. Equivalence means that feasible solutions correspond under the reformulation and have identical objective values, so their global optimal values agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noncanonical DC program becomes a difference-of-convex program only after an equivalent algebraic reformulation or lifting with auxiliary variables.

children.title: Single-Constraint Quadratic Optimization
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for the classical one-quadratic-constraint regime.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set defined by the single quadratic inequality is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{f_0(x):x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ f_1(x)\le 0\}\) has one quadratic objective and exactly one quadratic inequality constraint.

notation.meaning: space of real symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the inequality-constrained one-quadratic-constraint model, including indefinite objective or constraint matrices; equality-constrained variants are distinct formulations.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-constraint quadratic optimization problem has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_1(x)\le 0,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb{S}^n\) for \(i\in\{0,1\}\). No positive-semidefiniteness assumption is imposed in the general class. A trust-region problem is the subcase in which, for some \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\rho\ge 0\), the single constraint is \(\lVert Ax-d\rVert_2^2\le\rho^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a quadratic function subject to exactly one quadratic inequality. Indefinite matrices are allowed, and trust-region problems are an important subcase.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Constraint Quadratic Optimization

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact matrix certificate for the Euclidean-ball trust-region subcase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:\|x\|_2\le\Delta\}\) with \(\Delta>0\). A feasible \(x^*\) is globally optimal if and only if there exists \(\lambda^*\ge0\) such that \[(Q+\lambda^*I)x^*=-c,\qquad Q+\lambda^*I\succeq0,\qquad\lambda^*(\|x^*\|_2-\Delta)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region point is globally optimal exactly when a nonnegative multiplier gives stationarity, complementarity, and a positive-semidefinite shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ optimal}\iff\exists\lambda^*\ge0\text{ satisfying shifted-PSD stationarity and complementarity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Global Optimality Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Semidefinite Solution in the Regular One-Constraint Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tractability consequence of the S-lemma for rational regular instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational data, strict feasibility, and finite optimal value, the S-lemma converts lower-bound testing for a one-quadratic-constraint problem into a semidefinite feasibility condition involving one scalar multiplier. Standard semidefinite optimization algorithms therefore compute the optimal value to prescribed accuracy in time polynomial in the input size and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), subject to the usual quantitative regularity assumptions for bit-complexity guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular one-quadratic-constraint problems admit polynomial-time approximate solution through their exact semidefinite dual characterization.
assumptions_latex: Strict feasibility and finite optimal value hold.
The quantitative regularity required by the chosen SDP bit-complexity model holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\widehat v-v^*|\le\varepsilon\text{ is computable by an exact-duality SDP in polynomial time under the stated regularity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Time Semidefinite Solution in the Regular One-Constraint Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Lagrangian Dual Under Strict Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong duality for a finite-valued one-quadratic-constraint problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v^*=\inf\{f_0(x):f_1(x)\le0\}\), assume strict feasibility and \(v^*>-\infty\). Then \[v^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(f_0(x)+\lambda f_1(x)\bigr).\] Equivalently, \(\gamma\le v^*\) is certified by some \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \(f_0(x)-\gamma+\lambda f_1(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible one-quadratic-constraint problem with finite value has no Lagrangian duality gap, and a scalar multiplier certifies lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_x(f_0(x)+\lambda f_1(x)).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Lagrangian Dual Under Strict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Feasibility Is Essential to the Basic S-Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity boundary for the scalar-multiplier equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without a point satisfying \(f_1(x)<0\), the implication \(f_1(x)\le0\Rightarrow f_0(x)\ge0\) need not admit \(\lambda\ge0\) with \(f_0+\lambda f_1\ge0\) globally. For \(f_1(x)=x^2\) and \(f_0(x)=x\), the implication holds on the feasible set \(\{0\}\), but \(x+\lambda x^2\) is negative for some \(x\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic S-lemma can fail without strict feasibility even when the quadratic implication is true.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{quadratic implication without strict feasibility}\not\Rightarrow\text{scalar S-lemma certificate}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Feasibility Is Essential to the Basic S-Lemma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact implication certificate for one quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0,f_1\) be real quadratic functions and suppose there exists \(\bar x\) with \(f_1(\bar x)<0\). Then \[f_1(x)\le0\Rightarrow f_0(x)\ge0\quad\text{for all }x\] if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \[f_0(x)+\lambda f_1(x)\ge0\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility, nonnegativity of one quadratic over a quadratic sublevel set is equivalent to a scalar nonnegative-multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [f_1\le0\Rightarrow f_0\ge0]\iff\exists\lambda\ge0:\ f_0+\lambda f_1\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R^n.

children.title: Linearly Constrained Quadratic Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linearly constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax\le b,\] where \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Its feasible region \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is polyhedral. The program is convex when \(Q\succeq0\); it is a nonconvex quadratic program when \(Q\not\succeq0\), including the concave case \(Q\preceq0\) and the indefinite case in which \(Q\) has eigenvalues of both signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly constrained quadratic program minimizes a quadratic objective over a polyhedron and is nonconvex when its quadratic matrix is not positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearly Constrained Quadratic Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-Hardness Inherited from Box Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity of the general polyhedral class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact nonconvex linearly constrained quadratic minimization is NP-hard, because finite boxes are polyhedra and concave box-quadratic minimization is an NP-hard subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearly constrained class is NP-hard because it contains NP-hard box-constrained quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{nonconvex linearly constrained QP minimization is NP-hard}.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness Inherited from Box Quadratic Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Relative to the Feasible Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correction of the full-space Hessian test for lower-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) is convex on a convex polyhedron \(P\) if \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd\ge0\) for every direction \(d\) parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\). Thus \(Q\not\succeq0\) does not by itself imply nonconvexity on a lower-dimensional feasible polyhedron; when \(P\) is full-dimensional, convexity on \(P\) is equivalent to \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic convexity must be tested along feasible affine-hull directions; global indefiniteness can be irrelevant on a lower-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q|_P\text{ convex}\iff d^{\mathsf T}Qd\ge0\text{ for all }d\in\operatorname{lin}(P-P).

notation.meaning: direction space parallel to the affine hull of P

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Relative to the Feasible Affine Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient unboundedness certificates for noncompact polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), \(x\in P\), and \(d\ne0\) satisfy \(Ad\le0\). If \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\), or if \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd=0\) and \((Qx+c)^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(q(x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative quadratic recession curvature, or zero curvature with negative linear slope, certifies unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\ \lor\ [d^{\mathsf T}Qd=0\land(Qx+c)^{\mathsf T}d<0]\Rightarrow\inf_Pq=-\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Direction Unboundedness Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave Quadratic Minimum on a Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point reduction for bounded polyhedral feasible regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) is a nonempty polytope and \(q\) is concave on \(P\), then \[\min_{x\in P}q(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)}q(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave quadratic minimized over a polytope has an optimal extreme point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{P}q\cap\operatorname{ext}(P)\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Concave Quadratic Minimum on a Polytope

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation complexity parameterized by negative eigenvalues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and complexity of an approximation algorithm for problem (1) when its quadratic matrix is indefinite and its feasible region is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose D is indefinite, the feasible region of (1) is compact, and t is the number of negative eigenvalues of D. Then there exists an algorithm that finds an \epsilon-approximate solution of (1) in O\!\left(\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right)^t\ell\right) steps, where \ell denotes the time required to solve a convex quadratic program of the same size as (1).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact indefinite quadratic problem has an approximation algorithm whose bound grows exponentially with the number of negative eigenvalues and includes the cost of solving a same-size convex quadratic program.
assumptions_latex: t\text{ is the number of negative eigenvalues of }D.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_\epsilon=O\!\left(\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right)^t\ell\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave reduction preserving the minimum value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded reduction for the linearly constrained quadratic-program construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(t\), define \(\varphi_t(x)=\min\{F(x,y)\mid y\in M(t)\}\). Then \(\varphi_t\) is concave, \(\varphi_t(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in M(t)\), and \[\min_{x\in M(t)}\varphi_t(x)=\min_{x\in M(t)}f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing F(x,y) over y in M(t) produces a concave function of x that underestimates f on M(t) and has the same minimum value there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi_t\text{ is concave},\quad \varphi_t(x)\leq f(x)\ \forall x\in M(t),\quad \min_{x\in M(t)}\varphi_t(x)=\min_{x\in M(t)}f(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-scale-invariant approximate solution for quadratic optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative objective-gap definition of an approximate feasible solution to quadratic problem (1), together with its stated invariance property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x^\star be an optimum of (1). A feasible point x' is an \epsilon-approximate solution if there exists another feasible point x^\# such that Q(x')-Q(x^\star)\le\epsilon\left[Q(x^\#)-Q(x^\star)\right]. This definition is insensitive to translations or dilations of the objective function Q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is epsilon-approximate if its gap from the optimum is no more than epsilon times the gap of another feasible point. The definition is unchanged by translating or dilating the objective.
assumptions_latex: x^\star\text{ is an optimum of problem (1).}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'\text{ is }\epsilon\text{-approximate}\iff\exists x^\#\text{ feasible}:\ Q(x')-Q(x^\star)\le\epsilon\left[Q(x^\#)-Q(x^\star)\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A box-constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad \ell_i\le x_i\le u_i,\quad i=1,\ldots,n,\] where \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\) and all bounds are finite with \(\ell_i\le u_i\). The feasible set is the hyperrectangle \([\ell,u]\). The problem is a nonconvex quadratic program precisely when the objective is not convex on this box, in particular whenever a feasible direction of the box has negative quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a quadratic function over finite componentwise bounds, forming a hyperrectangle; negative curvature along feasible directions makes the problem nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained Quadratic Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-Hardness of Concave Box Quadratic Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity already present in the concave subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact minimization of a concave quadratic over a finite box is NP-hard. In particular, a weighted Max-Cut instance can be represented as minimizing the negative of its convex quadratic cut objective over \([0,1]^n\); vertex attainment makes the continuous box optimum equal to the binary optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the concave box-quadratic subfamily is NP-hard, despite always having an optimal vertex.
assumptions_latex: Input coefficients and bounds are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{concave box-QP minimization is NP-hard}.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness of Concave Box Quadratic Minimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary local optimality conditions and the convex sufficiency boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x^*\) locally minimizes differentiable \(q\) on \([\ell,u]\), then \[\ell_i<x_i^*<u_i\Rightarrow
abla_iq(x^*)=0,\quad x_i^*=\ell_i<u_i\Rightarrow
abla_iq(x^*)\ge0,\quad x_i^*=u_i>\ell_i\Rightarrow
abla_iq(x^*)\le0.\] These conditions are sufficient for global optimality when \(q\) is convex on the box, in particular when \(Q\succeq0\), but not in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box local minimizer satisfies coordinatewise gradient-sign conditions; these certify global optimality in the convex subclass only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\nabla q(x^*)+N_{[\ell,u]}(x^*).

notation.meaning: normal cone of the box at x*

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise First-Order Box Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Box Stationarity Is Not Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of first-order certification in the nonconvex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([-1,1]\), \(q(x)=-x^2\) has the stationary point \(x=0\), but \(q(0)=0\) while the global minimum is \(-1\), attained at \(x=\pm1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior stationary point of a nonconvex box quadratic need not be globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla q(0)=0\quad\text{but}\quad0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{[-1,1]}q.
knowledge_statements.title: Box Stationarity Is Not Global Optimality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave Quadratic Minimum Occurs at a Box Vertex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point structure of the concave subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(Q\preceq0\), and let \([\ell,u]\) be a nonempty finite box. Then \[\min_{x\in[\ell,u]}q(x)=\min_{v\in V}q(v),\qquad V=\{v:v_i\in\{\ell_i,u_i\}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave quadratic minimized on a box has an optimal box vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in[\ell,u]}q(x)=\min_{v\in V}q(v).
knowledge_statements.title: Concave Quadratic Minimum Occurs at a Box Vertex

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb{S}^n\) for every \(i=0,\ldots,m\). The QCQP is convex when \(Q_i\succeq0\) for all indices; otherwise the objective or at least one constraint can introduce nonconvexity. Linear inequalities are included by taking the corresponding \(Q_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP has a quadratic objective and finitely many quadratic inequalities; it is generally nonconvex when an objective or constraint matrix is not positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity inherited from linearly constrained quadratic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact nonconvex QCQP minimization is NP-hard because affine inequalities are QCQP constraints with zero quadratic part, so the class contains NP-hard box-constrained and linearly constrained quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General nonconvex QCQP is NP-hard even when its quadratic constraints specialize to affine bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{general nonconvex QCQP minimization is NP-hard}.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness of General QCQP

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Sufficiency in the Convex QCQP Subclass
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality certificate at the convex boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and that some \(\bar x\) satisfies \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every constraint. A feasible \(x^*\) is globally optimal if and only if there exist \(\lambda_i\ge0\) such that \[\nabla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla f_i(x^*)=0,\qquad\lambda_i f_i(x^*)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex QCQP satisfying Slater's condition, KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_i\succeq0\) for the objective and every constraint quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ globally optimal}\iff\exists\lambda\ge0\text{ satisfying KKT}.
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sufficiency in the Convex QCQP Subclass

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation of a QCQP before relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(y=(1,x)\) and \(M_i=\begin{bmatrix}r_i&q_i^{\mathsf T}\\q_i&Q_i\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(f_i(x)=\langle M_i,Y\rangle\) with \(Y=yy^{\mathsf T}\). Hence the QCQP is exactly \[\min\ \langle M_0,Y\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\langle M_i,Y\rangle\le0,\ Y_{00}=1,\ Y\succeq0,\ \operatorname{rank}Y=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP has an exact linear matrix formulation over a positive-semidefinite rank-one lift.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP uses the quadratic functions in the accepted definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{QCQP}\equiv\text{PSD lifted formulation with }Y_{00}=1\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}Y=1.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Rank-One Matrix Formulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct relaxation fact whose canonical home is the dedicated semidefinite-relaxation node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dropping \(\operatorname{rank}Y=1\) from the homogeneous lift gives a semidefinite lower bound that need not be exact for a multi-constraint nonconvex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The claim is mathematically correct but is deferred locally because inexactness of the Shor relaxation is method-owned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_{\mathrm{SDP}}\le v_{\mathrm{QCQP}},\quad\text{with possible strict inequality}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Relaxation Claim Proposed by Builder

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A multiplier-and-minimizer certificate for strong Lagrangian duality in problem (10.80) with \(X=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\). Suppose there exist \(\bar y\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(L(x,\bar y):=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\bar y_i g_i(x)\) is convex, \(\bar x\) minimizes \(L(\cdot,\bar y)\), and \(g_i(\bar x)\leq0\) and \(\bar y_i g_i(\bar x)=0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then strong duality holds: \(\psi_X^*=f_X^{\natural}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong duality holds when a nonnegative multiplier makes the Lagrangian convex and that Lagrangian has a feasible minimizer satisfying complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: L(x,\bar y)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\bar y_i g_i(x)\text{ is convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi_X^*=f_X^{\natural}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional two-block form with affine and bilinear expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear program has objective and constraint functions of the form \[\phi_i(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}B_i y+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i^{\mathsf T}y+c_i,\qquad i=0,\ldots,m,\] with \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), \(B_i\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(c_i\in\mathbb R\). Each \(\phi_i\) is affine in either block when the other is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear program contains pairwise products between two variable blocks and is affine in either block separately.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients have the displayed real dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonaffine cross-block term is bilinear and every fixed-block expression is affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indefinite Joint Curvature of a Nonzero Bilinear Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-curvature boundary for a pure cross-block term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}By\), \[\nabla^2q=\begin{bmatrix}0&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}.\] If \(B\ne0\), this matrix has positive and negative eigenvalues. Thus \(q\) is separately affine but neither jointly convex nor jointly concave on a full-dimensional open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero bilinear form has indefinite joint curvature despite separate affinity.
assumptions_latex: The joint domain contains a full-dimensional open convex subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}By\) is separately affine and jointly neither convex nor concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Joint Curvature of a Nonzero Bilinear Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure bilinear objective over a Cartesian product of compact polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are nonempty compact polytopes, then both \(\min_{x\in P,y\in Q}x^{\mathsf T}By\) and \(\max_{x\in P,y\in Q}x^{\mathsf T}By\) are attained at some \((v,w)\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\times\operatorname{vert}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure bilinear objective over a product of compact polytopes has an optimal vertex pair.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is exactly \(P\times Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each extremum has an optimizer in \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\times\operatorname{vert}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Pair Attainment over Product Polytopes

children.title: Biconvex Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for two-block conditional convexity.

assumptions_latex: All objective and constraint functions are real-valued on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixing either variable block produces a convex optimization problem in the other block.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses separate convexity of the objective and all inequality functions on a Cartesian product domain.

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190
Part I. Biconvex and Bilinear Problems

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A biconvex program has the form \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}\ f(x,y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x,y)\le0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex, and each of \(f\) and \(g_i\) is convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(y\in Y\) and convex in \(y\) for every fixed \(x\in X\). Joint convexity is not required. Consequently, fixing either block yields a convex optimization subproblem in the remaining block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biconvex program is convex in either of two variable blocks when the other block is fixed, though it need not be jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Biconvex Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190
Part I. Biconvex and Bilinear Problems

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic block-coordinate method for two-block biconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From a feasible \((x^k,y^k)\), choose \(x^{k+1}\) as a global minimizer of the feasible \(x\)-section with \(y=y^k\), then choose \(y^{k+1}\) as a global minimizer of the feasible \(y\)-section with \(x=x^{k+1}\). Then \[f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\leq f(x^{k+1},y^k)\leq f(x^k,y^k).\] If these values are bounded below, the objective-value sequence converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact alternating minimization produces nonincreasing objective values; a lower bound ensures convergence of the values, not necessarily of the iterates or to a global optimum.
assumptions_latex: Both block subproblems are feasible and attain global minima at every iteration.
Objective-value convergence additionally requires a finite lower bound along the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\leq f(x^k,y^k)\), and boundedness below implies convergence of \(f(x^k,y^k)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Alternating Convex Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise Optimality Is Not Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for alternating minimization and blockwise certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,y)=(xy-1)^2\) on \([-1,1]^2\), \(f\) is convex in each block separately. The point \((0,0)\) is coordinatewise globally minimizing because \(f(x,0)=f(0,y)=1\) for all \(x,y\), but it is not globally minimizing because \(f(1,1)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinatewise minimum of a biconvex objective can be strictly suboptimal globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is coordinatewise minimizing but not globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Optimality Is Not Global Optimality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Sections of a Biconvex Feasible Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sectionwise geometry induced by biconvex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:g_i(x,y)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(X,Y\) are convex and every \(g_i\) is separately convex. Then \(S_y=\{x:(x,y)\in S\}\) and \(S^x=\{y:(x,y)\in S\}\) are convex for every fixed opposite block, although \(S\) need not be jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every one-block feasible section is convex, but the full feasible set need not be convex.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is convex in either block with the other fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_y\) and \(S^x\) are convex for all fixed blocks.

notation.meaning: Feasible sections in the two blocks

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Sections of a Biconvex Feasible Set

children.title: Convex–Concave Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for opposing curvature across blocks or components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global certificate under the minimizer–maximizer convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point exactly when \[f(x^*,y)\leq f(x^*,y^*)\leq f(x,y^*)\qquad\forall x\in X,\ \forall y\in Y.\] It then certifies optimality for both orders and equality of their values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two global saddle inequalities certify minimax and maximin optimality.
assumptions_latex: The minimizer controls \(x\) and the maximizer controls \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities are necessary and sufficient for a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Inequality Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Without Concavity in the Maximizing Block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature boundary for minimax equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=Y=[0,1]\) and \(f(x,y)=(x-y)^2\), \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)=\tfrac14>0=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y).\] Here \(f\) is convex rather than concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping maximizing-block concavity can create a strict minimax gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x\max_y f>\max_y\min_x f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Concavity in the Maximizing Block

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained two-block saddle convention; constrained variants require separately specified feasible correspondences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex–concave minimax program is \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}f(x,y),\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex sets, \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) is convex for every fixed \(y\), and \(y\mapsto f(x,y)\) is concave for every fixed \(x\). This definition alone does not assert minimax equality or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex–concave minimax program is convex in the minimizing block and concave in the maximizing block.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is real-valued and has the stated blockwise curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizing and maximizing blocks have opposing curvature roles.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Minimax Program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuous compact form of the minimax theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be nonempty compact convex sets and let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Then \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y),\] and a saddle point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity, compact convex domains, and opposing block curvature imply minimax equality and saddle-point attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_X\max_Y f=\max_Y\min_X f\), with an attained saddle point.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Convex–Concave Minimax Equality

assumptions_latex: The objective and constraint functions have the stated blockwise curvature on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is convex in the minimizing block and concave in the opposing block.

notation.meaning: convex and concave variable blocks, respectively

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the two-block minimax sense: convex in the minimizing block and concave in the maximizing block.

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex-concave program in the two-block minimax sense has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\ \sup_{y\in Y}\ f(x,y),\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex, \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every fixed \(y\in Y\), and \(y\mapsto f(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every fixed \(x\in X\). In constrained variants, admissible functions preserve convex feasible sections for the minimizing block and concave-compatible sections for the maximizing block. Joint convexity of \(f\) is neither required nor generally meaningful across the opposing roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the minimax sense, a convex-concave program has an objective convex in the minimizing variables and concave in the maximizing variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unconstrained convex-concave minimax formula is coherent, but the immutable container describes opposing curvature across blocks or components and does not itself fix the minimax convention. The sentence about concave-compatible feasible sections is not a precise mathematical condition. The cited source must be inspected to determine the intended convention before selecting a reliable replacement.

children.title: Multilinear Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for higher-order products over multiple blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algorithm for an unconstrained multiaffine objective on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multiaffine objective in \(n\) scalar variables on a box, evaluation at all \(2^n\) vertices is exact. If one evaluation costs \(T_p\), exhaustive enumeration takes \(O(2^nT_p)\) time and can use \(O(n)\) working memory beyond the incumbent and input storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box-vertex enumeration is exact but exponential in the number of scalar variables.
assumptions_latex: The only feasible-set restriction is the box.
Objective values admit exact or certified comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact optimization is possible in \(O(2^nT_p)\) time.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Vertex Enumeration Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-Box Vertex Reduction Fails under Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the box vertex theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,1]^2\) with the additional constraint \(x+y=1\), the bilinear objective \(xy\) has maximum \(1/4\) at \((1/2,1/2)\), which is not a vertex of the ambient box. Thus coupled constraints invalidate unrestricted ambient-box vertex reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled constraints can force a multilinear optimum away from all ambient-box vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ambient-box vertex enumeration is not generally exact for coupled constrained models.

notation.meaning: Bilinear special case used for the boundary example

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Box Vertex Reduction Fails under Coupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple-block programs whose defining expressions are affine in each block separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multilinear program over \(X_1\times\cdots\times X_k\) has objective and constraint functions that are multiaffine: fixing all blocks except \(x^{(j)}\) leaves an affine function of \(x^{(j)}\). In finite dimensions such expressions are finite sums of constant, affine, and cross-block multilinear terms. Degree-two cross-block terms are bilinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilinear program is affine in each variable block separately but may contain products spanning several blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_j}\) is nonempty for every block.
All defining expressions are finite multiaffine expressions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every defining expression is affine in each block with the other blocks fixed.

notation.meaning: The j-th variable block and domain

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Attainment of Multiaffine Functions on Boxes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical box-domain extremum theorem for a multiaffine objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{j=1}^n[\ell_j,u_j]\) be a nonempty compact box and let \(p:B\to\mathbb R\) be affine in each scalar coordinate with the others fixed. Then \[\min_Bp=\min_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(B)}p(v),\qquad \max_Bp=\max_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(B)}p(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiaffine function on a compact box attains both extrema at box vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is affine in every scalar coordinate separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both extrema are attained at vertices of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Attainment of Multiaffine Functions on Boxes

children.title: Power-Product Program Family
children.top_down_role: Power-product models extending the convex geometric-programming regime.

children.title: Convexifiable Posynomial Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for the convex geometric-programming boundary.

assumptions_latex: The objective and inequality functions are posynomials, while equality constraints are monomial equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The logarithmic change \(x_j=e^{y_j}\) converts the geometric program into a convex optimization problem.

notation.meaning: positive monomial coefficients and real exponent vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the standard logarithmic convexification of posynomial-form geometric programs on the positive orthant.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every posynomial be \(p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{a_{kj}}\), with \(c_k>0\), and let every monomial have one such term. Under \(x_j=e^{y_j}\), a constraint \(p(x)\le1\) is equivalent to \[\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\exp\!\left(a_k^{\mathsf T}y+\log c_k\right)\right)\le0,\] which is convex in \(y\). A monomial equality becomes affine after taking logarithms. Applying the same logarithm to a positive posynomial objective yields an equivalent convex objective because the logarithm is strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-variable geometric programs with posynomial inequalities and monomial equalities become convex after taking logarithms of variables and the positive objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexifiable Posynomial Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

children.title: General Signomial Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for nonconvex signomial models.

assumptions_latex: The domain is the strictly positive orthant \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\).
Each signomial is a finite sum of generalized monomials with real coefficients and real exponents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Allowing coefficients of either sign yields the general signomial-program class, which is not generally convex after logarithmic substitution.

notation.meaning: nonzero real coefficients and real exponent vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses generalized real exponents on positive variables and permits mixed coefficient signs.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A signomial on the positive orthant is a function \[s(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{a_{kj}},\] where \(c_k\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\) and \(a_{kj}\in\mathbb{R}\). A general signomial program minimizes one signomial subject to finitely many signomial inequalities and equalities over \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\). Unlike a posynomial, a signomial may have coefficients of both signs. After \(x_j=e^{y_j}\), it becomes a signed sum of exponentials, so the logarithmic transformation does not in general produce a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general signomial program uses finite sums of real-power monomials with coefficients of either sign on positive variables and is generally nonconvex after logarithmic substitution.
knowledge_statements.title: General Signomial Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

children.title: Domain-Sensitive Power Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for power models whose validity depends on sign and domain restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Points Can Destroy Finiteness or Real-Valuedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary zero and sign failures for real power atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The atom \(x^{-1}\) is not finite at \(x=0\), and the real atom \(x^{1/2}\) is undefined for \(x<0\). Thus a nominal constraint such as \(-1\le x\le1\) does not itself provide a valid common domain for either expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero can be singular for negative powers, while negative values can be invalid for fractional powers.
assumptions_latex: Power atoms are interpreted as finite, single-valued real functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\notin\operatorname{dom}(x^{-1})\) and \(( -\infty,0)\cap\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbb R}(x^{1/2})=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Points Can Destroy Finiteness or Real-Valuedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power Identities Depend on the Admitted Real Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of formal exponent laws when negative bases and principal real roots are mixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nonnegative principal square root, take \(x=-1\). Then \[(x^2)^{1/2}=1\neq-1=x^{2(1/2)}.\] Hence \((x^a)^b=x^{ab}\) is not valid on arbitrary real domains without compatible base restrictions and branch conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent-composition identities can fail on negative bases, so reformulations must preserve the declared real domain and branch.
assumptions_latex: The outer exponent \(1/2\) denotes the nonnegative real square root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^2)^{1/2}\ne x\), so unrestricted use of \((x^a)^b=x^{ab}\) is invalid.
knowledge_statements.title: Power Identities Depend on the Admitted Real Domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for algebraic substitutions involving power atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two power-model formulations have expression maps \(F\) and \(\widetilde F\), feasible effective domains \(E\) and \(\widetilde E\), and a change of variables \(T\). They are optimization-equivalent if \(T:E\to\widetilde E\) is bijective and \(F(x)=\widetilde F(T(x))\) for every \(x\in E\). Formal equality away from excluded zeros, signs, or branches is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-model reformulation is valid only when it preserves values and the complete feasible effective domain.
assumptions_latex: Every power atom has a declared finite, single-valued real domain.
The proposed transformation and its inverse are defined on the respective feasible effective domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T:E\leftrightarrow\widetilde E\text{ bijective and value-preserving}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\inf_{x\in E}F(x)=\inf_{z\in\widetilde E}\widetilde F(z).

notation.meaning: feasible effective domains of the two formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Preserving Reformulation Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Real Domains of Scalar Power Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent-by-exponent domain classification under a declared standard real-power convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=p/q\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}\) be in lowest terms with \(q>0\), and define \(x^{p/q}\) using the real \(q\)-th root. If \(q\) is odd, its finite real domain is \(\mathbb R\) for \(p>0\) and \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) for \(p<0\). If \(q\) is even, its domain is \([0,\infty)\) for \(p>0\) and \((0,\infty)\) for \(p<0\). This includes nonzero integers as \(q=1\). For irrational \(a\), the canonical definition \(x^a=\exp(a\log x)\) has domain \((0,\infty)\); when \(a>0\), it has the continuous finite extension \(0^a=0\). The value of \(0^0\) is convention-dependent and must be declared explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced-rational denominator parity, exponent sign, and the treatment of zero determine the finite real domain of a scalar power.
assumptions_latex: Rational exponents are reduced to \(p/q\) with \(q>0\).
Even roots use the nonnegative real branch.
Irrational powers use \(\exp(a\log x)\) on positive bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}_{\mathbb R}(x^{p/q})=\begin{cases}\mathbb R,&q\text{ odd},\ p>0,\\\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},&q\text{ odd},\ p<0,\\[0,\infty),&q\text{ even},\ p>0,\\(0,\infty),&q\text{ even},\ p<0.\end{cases}

notation.meaning: nonzero rational exponent in lowest terms with positive denominator

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Real Domains of Scalar Power Atoms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective Domain Is the Common Atom Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-level construction from the declared domains of constituent power atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a finite optimization model on a declared set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) contains power occurrences \(h_k(x)^{a_k}\) with declared finite, single-valued real domains \(D_k\), then its effective domain is \[E=X\cap\bigcap_k\{x:h_k(x)\in D_k\}.\] Every objective value, constraint value, equivalence claim, and feasibility statement for the model is restricted to \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The valid model domain is the intersection of the declared search set with every power atom's real domain.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many power occurrences appear.
Each occurrence has a declared finite, single-valued real domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E=X\cap\bigcap_k h_k^{-1}(D_k).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the complete power model

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domain Is the Common Atom Domain

assumptions_latex: Every power atom is assigned a real exponent and an explicit real-valued domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D=\{x\in X:x_j\in D_{a}\text{ for every occurring atom }x_j^{a}\}\).

notation.meaning: Largest prescribed real domain on which the power atom is single-valued and finite
Effective domain of the complete model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued power models with explicit sign, zero, and exponent-dependent domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain-sensitive power model is an optimization problem whose expressions contain atoms \(x_j^a\), with each atom interpreted only on a specified set \(D_a\subseteq\mathbb R\) where it is real, single-valued, and finite. For \(a\in\mathbb Z\), one may take \(D_a=\mathbb R\), excluding zero when \(a<0\). For nonintegral rational or irrational powers, the chosen real branch and sign restrictions must be stated explicitly; the universally valid convention \(D_a=(0,\infty)\) is always admissible. The feasible set is intersected with all such atom domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power model is domain-sensitive when every real power carries explicit sign and zero restrictions, and feasibility includes the common domain of all power atoms.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Sensitive Power Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the domain-sensitive power-model container and is mathematically plausible, but no source supports the exponent-dependent real-domain conventions or the treatment of branches and sign restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Domain Curvature of a Real Power Atom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential and curvature classification on the strictly positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\mathbb R\), the atom \(p_a(x)=x^a=\exp(a\log x)\) on \((0,\infty)\) satisfies \(p_a'(x)=ax^{a-1}\) and \(p_a''(x)=a(a-1)x^{a-2}\), yielding the usual exponent-based monotonicity and curvature classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the positive domain, a real power has an unambiguous derivative and exponent-based curvature classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_a''\ge0\text{ for }a\le0\text{ or }a\ge1,\qquad p_a''\le0\text{ for }0\le a\le1.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Domain Curvature of a Real Power Atom

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns sign, zero, branch, effective-domain, and domain-preserving-reformulation issues. Its exponent-by-exponent domain convention remains unresolved. The proposed positive-domain curvature claim is sound but deferred as misplaced: positive-domain atom properties, posynomial convexification, and general signomial structure belong to adjacent scopes.

children.title: Ratio-Product Program Family
children.top_down_role: Composite models organized through ratios or products of component functions.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Multiplicative Programming Problems and Fractional Programming

children.title: Single-Ratio Fractional Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for one-ratio continuous models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X} f(x)/g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minimization form with one everywhere-positive denominator.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-ratio fractional program has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)},\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the feasible set and \(g(x)>0\) throughout \(X\). Positivity makes the quotient finite whenever \(f\) and \(g\) are finite and fixes the direction of inequalities after multiplication by \(g(x)\). A maximization problem with the same single quotient is included by replacing \(f\) with \(-f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-ratio fractional program optimizes one quotient of a numerator by a denominator that remains strictly positive over the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Ratio Fractional Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-subproblem method for an attained continuous single-ratio minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_k\in\arg\min_{x\in X}(f(x)-\lambda_k g(x))\) and set \(\lambda_{k+1}=f(x_k)/g(x_k)\). Under the stated compactness and continuity assumptions, \(\lambda_1\ge v^*\); unless equality terminates the method, \((\lambda_k)_{k\ge1}\) decreases to \(v^*\). A zero residual \(f(x_k)-\lambda_k g(x_k)=0\) certifies that \(x_k\) is globally ratio-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dinkelbach's method solves exact subtractive subproblems and converges monotonically to the optimal ratio after its first update.
assumptions_latex: Every parametric subproblem is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_k\to v^*,\qquad \phi(\lambda_k)=0\Longleftrightarrow \lambda_k=v^*.

notation.meaning: global minimizer of the current subtractive subproblem

knowledge_statements.title: Dinkelbach Iteration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bound for convex sublevel feasibility bisection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\ell\le v^*\le u\), decide at each midpoint \(\alpha\) whether \(f(x)-\alpha g(x)\le0\) is feasible on \(X\). Feasibility replaces \(u\) by \(\alpha\); infeasibility replaces \(\ell\) by \(\alpha\). After \(k\) exact tests the bracket width is \((u-\ell)2^{-k}\), so width at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact sublevel-feasibility bisection halves the value bracket at every test.
assumptions_latex: A finite valid bracket \([\ell,u]\) is known.
Every feasibility test is decided correctly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge\left\lceil\log_2\frac{u-\ell}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\Longrightarrow u_k-\ell_k\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Bisection Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-feasibility structure for a standard single-ratio subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is convex, \(f\) is convex and nonnegative on \(X\), and \(g\) is positive and concave on \(X\), then \(f/g\) is quasiconvex. For \(\alpha\ge0\), \[\{x\in X:f(x)/g(x)\le\alpha\}=\{x\in X:f(x)-\alpha g(x)\le0\},\] a convex set; negative sublevels are empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative convex numerator divided by a positive concave denominator is quasiconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is concave and strictly positive on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f/g\text{ is quasiconvex on }X.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Fractional Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniform ratio transformations at zeros or sign changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g\) vanishes at a feasible point, the quotient may be undefined or unbounded nearby. If \(g\) changes sign, multiplication by \(g(x)\) does not preserve a uniform inequality direction. The subtractive sublevel equivalence and positive-perspective reformulations therefore require restriction to sign-definite regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Denominator zeros or sign changes invalidate the standard positive-denominator equivalences.
assumptions_latex: The feasible domain contains a zero of \(g\) or points at which \(g\) has opposite signs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{f/g\le\alpha\}=\{f-\alpha g\le0\}\text{ need not hold globally}.
knowledge_statements.title: Denominator-Sign Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear reformulation when the original polyhedron is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{(c^Tx+c_0)/(d^Tx+d_0):Ax\le b\}\), assume the polyhedron is nonempty and bounded and \(d^Tx+d_0>0\) throughout it. With \(t=(d^Tx+d_0)^{-1}\) and \(y=tx\), the problem is equivalent to \[\min c^Ty+c_0t\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ay\le bt,\ d^Ty+d_0t=1,\ t\ge0.\] Boundedness excludes transformed feasible points with \(t=0\), and optimizers recover by \(x=y/t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Charnes–Cooper converts a bounded positive-denominator linear-fractional problem into an equivalent linear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(P_{CC}),\qquad x=y/t.
knowledge_statements.title: Charnes–Cooper Linear-Fractional Reformulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric characterization of a positive-denominator single-ratio minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)/g(x)\) and \(\phi(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}(f(x)-\lambda g(x))\). If \(g>0\) on \(X\), then \(\phi(\lambda)\ge0\) for \(\lambda\le v^*\) and \(\phi(\lambda)<0\) for \(\lambda>v^*\). If the ratio minimum is attained, then \(\phi(v^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal ratio is the threshold where the subtractive value function changes from nonnegative to negative; attainment makes it a zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^*=\sup\{\lambda:\phi(\lambda)\ge0\},\qquad \phi(v^*)=0\text{ under attainment}.
knowledge_statements.title: Subtractive Value Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a constrained continuous optimization problem with one ratio objective and a denominator of constant positive sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g,h_1,\ldots,h_m:C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(S=\{x\in C:h_k(x)\leq0,\ k=1,\ldots,m\}\), and suppose \(g(x)>0\) for every \(x\in C\). Then \(\sup\{f(x)/g(x):x\in S\}\) is called a single-ratio fractional program. If \(g(x)<0\) throughout \(C\), replacing \((f,g)\) by \((-f,-g)\) yields an equivalent ratio with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing one ratio over a constrained set is a single-ratio fractional program when its denominator is positive throughout the domain. A denominator that is negative throughout can be normalized by negating both numerator and denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in S}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\text{ is a single-ratio fractional program.}

children.title: Multi-Ratio Program Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for extrema, sums, and systems of ratios.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records two scalar formulations using multiple ratios and their stated relationship to the corresponding multi-objective fractional problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i(x)=f_i(x)/g_i(x)\) with \(g_i(x)>0\) for \(x\in S\). Two multi-ratio formulations are \(\sup_{x\in S}\min_{1\leq i\leq p}q_i(x)\) and \(\sup_{x\in S}\sum_{i=1}^p q_i(x)\). The first is sometimes called a generalized fractional program. Both are related to the multi-objective fractional problem \(\max\{(q_1(x),\ldots,q_p(x)):x\in S\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive denominators, several ratios can be combined by maximizing their minimum or their sum. The max-min formulation is sometimes called a generalized fractional program, and both formulations are related to the vector-valued multi-objective fractional problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in S}\min_i q_i(x)\text{ and }\sup_{x\in S}\sum_i q_i(x)\text{ are multi-ratio formulations; the former is sometimes called a generalized fractional program.}

children.title: Extremal-Ratio Programs
children.top_down_role: Fractional programs aggregating component ratios through an extremal operator.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i,g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) with \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I} f_i(x)/g_i(x)\), or dually \(v^*=\sup_{x\in X}\min_{i\in I} f_i(x)/g_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite worst-ratio minimization and best-guaranteed-ratio maximization.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extremal-ratio program aggregates finitely many well-defined ratios by an extremum. Its minimax form is \[\inf_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)},\] and its maximin form is \[\sup_{x\in X}\min_{i\in I}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}.\] Every denominator satisfies \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\). Thus each indexed quotient is defined on the common feasible domain, while the extremal operator selects the worst or best component at each feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extremal-ratio program minimizes the largest, or maximizes the smallest, member of a finite family of positive-denominator ratios.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremal-Ratio Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold Bisection for Convex Fractional Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasiconvex method for nonnegative-threshold worst-ratio minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X\) is convex, each \(f_i\) is convex, and each \(g_i\) is positive and concave on \(X\). For fixed \(t\geq0\), the system \(f_i(x)-t g_i(x)\leq0\) is convex and its feasibility is monotone in \(t\). If \(0\leq L\leq v^*\leq U\), bisection returns a value bracket of width at most \(\varepsilon\) after \(\lceil\log_2((U-L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) convex-feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard convex-fractional assumptions and a nonnegative value bracket, worst-ratio minimization admits threshold bisection.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i\) is convex and every \(g_i\) is positive and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(\lceil\log_2((U-L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) convex-feasibility tests produce an \(\varepsilon\)-wide value bracket.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Bisection for Convex Fractional Components

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph and hypograph representations for the two seed variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\), then \[\inf_{x\in X}\max_i\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}=\inf_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ f_i(x)-t g_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\},\] and \[\sup_{x\in X}\min_i\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}=\sup_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ f_i(x)-t g_i(x)\geq0\ \forall i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One common threshold gives exact epigraph and hypograph formulations of worst- and best-component ratio objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i(x)>0\) for every \(x\in X\) and every index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The threshold inequalities are equivalent to \(t\geq\max_i f_i/g_i\) and \(t\leq\min_i f_i/g_i\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Reformulations of Extremal Ratios

children.title: Sum-of-Ratios Programs
children.top_down_role: Fractional programs whose objective combines several ratio terms additively.

notation.meaning: Numerator and denominator of ratio i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted finite sum; fixed real weights can be absorbed into the numerators.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sum-of-ratios program has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)},\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the index set is finite, and every denominator obeys \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\). The numerators, denominators, and feasible set may be nonconvex. A weighted objective \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f_i(x)/g_i(x)\) is included by absorbing each fixed real weight \(w_i\) into its numerator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum-of-ratios program optimizes a finite sum of quotient terms whose denominators are positive throughout the common feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Ratios Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating sums of ratios from independent single-ratio problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), take \(r_1(x)=x\) and \(r_2(x)=1-x\), both representable with denominator one. Then \[\min_{x\in X}(r_1(x)+r_2(x))=1,\qquad \min_Xr_1+\min_Xr_2=0.\] Thus a shared decision generally prevents separate optimization of the ratio terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing each ratio independently and summing the results generally gives the wrong value.
assumptions_latex: All component ratios share the same decision vector and feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_X\sum_i r_i\) need not equal \(\sum_i\min_Xr_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Decisions Prevent Componentwise Decoupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lift for minimization of a finite sum of positive-denominator ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\), then \[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}=\inf_{x\in X,t\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m t_i:f_i(x)-t_i g_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\right\}.\] Whenever the lifted optimum is attained, an optimal solution satisfies \(t_i=f_i(x)/g_i(x)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One epigraph variable per component gives an exact lifted sum-of-ratios model.
assumptions_latex: Every denominator is strictly positive on the common feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and lifted infima agree, with componentwise equality at any attained lifted optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Componentwise Epigraph Lift

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a multi-ratio fractional program seeking the supremum of an additive collection of ratios over a convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, and suppose the displayed ratios are well-defined on \(S\). The multi-ratio fractional program is
\[
\sup\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}:x\in S\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous sum-of-ratios program seeks the supremum of the sum of p ratios f_i(x)/g_i(x) over a convex feasible region S in R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}:x\in S\right\}

children.title: Multiple-Ratio Systems
children.top_down_role: Models containing several coupled ratio objectives or constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) specifies admissible simultaneous ratio values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible exactly when }x\in X\text{ and }R(x)\in Y\).

notation.meaning: Admissible set for simultaneous ratio values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued ratio systems before choosing a sum or extremal scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiple-ratio system is specified by the vector mapping \[R(x)=\left(\frac{f_1(x)}{g_1(x)},\ldots,\frac{f_m(x)}{g_m(x)}\right),\qquad x\in X,\] with \(g_i(x)>0\) for every \(i\) and \(x\in X\). Feasibility imposes a joint condition \(R(x)\in Y\), where \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\); equivalently, it may impose finitely many predicates \(\Phi_k(R(x),x)\leq0\). An objective may depend on \(x\) and the entire vector \(R(x)\), without requiring a sum or extremal scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-ratio system constrains or optimizes the vector of several positive-denominator ratios jointly, without prescribing a particular scalar aggregation.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Ratio Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed vector-ratio formulation is coherent, but the exact boundary of the class, including arbitrary joint predicates and objectives depending on the entire ratio vector, is not supported by a source and is not sufficiently canonical to validate without one.

children.title: Multiplicative Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for products of structured factors.

assumptions_latex: Each factor \(h_i:X\to\mathbb R\) is finite on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}\prod_{i=1}^{m}h_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products of structured factors with an explicitly stated common domain.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiplicative program optimizes an objective containing a finite product of factor functions, in the canonical form \[\inf_{x\in X}H(x),\qquad H(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}h_i(x).\] The feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) lies in the common domain of all factors. Factor signs and possible zeros are part of the model specification; positivity is required only when a logarithmic representation is invoked. Product constraints, such as \(\prod_{i=1}^{m}h_i(x)\leq c\), belong to the same class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative program optimizes or constrains a finite product of structured factors defined on a common feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative Convex Factors Need Not Have a Convex Product
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary distinguishing convex factors from log-convex factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), \(h_1(x)=x^2\) and \(h_2(x)=(1-x)^2\) are nonnegative and convex, but \(H(x)=x^2(1-x)^2\) is not convex because \(H(0)=H(1)=0\) while \(H(1/2)=1/16\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even two nonnegative convex factors can have a nonconvex product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonnegativity and convexity of all factors do not imply convexity of their product.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Convex Factors Need Not Have a Convex Product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical curvature-preserving subclass of multiplicative programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex and let \(h_i:X\to(0,\infty)\) be log-convex for \(i=1,,m\). Then \(H=\prod_i h_i\) is log-convex and therefore convex on \(X\), with \(\log H=\sum_i\log h_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product of positive log-convex factors is log-convex and convex.
assumptions_latex: Every factor is strictly positive and log-convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\prod_i h_i\) is log-convex, hence convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Products of Positive Log-Convex Factors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic factorization of a finite product into binary product equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m h_i(x)\), introduce \(z_1=h_1(x)\) and \(z_j=z_{j-1}h_j(x)\) for \(j=2,\ldots,m\). The exact lifted system satisfies \(z_m=H(x)\), and its projection onto \((x,z_m)\) is the graph of \(H\). Replacing a product equality by an outer relaxation generally yields only a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite product has an exact chain lift using binary product equations.
assumptions_latex: Every factor is finite on the common domain.
All binary product equations are imposed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted system projects exactly to \(z_m=\prod_i h_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Recursive Product Lift

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-product characterization of a quadratic function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-and-inertia characterization of quadratic functions representable as products of two affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=c^Tx+\tfrac12x^TQx with Q=Q^T, and define \widetilde Q=\begin{bmatrix}Q&c\\c^T&0\end{bmatrix}. Then f can be decomposed into a product of two affine functions if and only if (i) \operatorname{rank}(\widetilde Q)-1\leq\operatorname{rank}(Q)\leq2 and (ii), when \operatorname{rank}(Q)=2, Q has one negative and one positive eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic function factors into two affine functions exactly when the stated augmented-matrix rank condition holds and a rank-two quadratic matrix has one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a product of two affine functions}\iff\left(\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde Q)-1\leq\operatorname{rank}(Q)\leq2\right)\land\left(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=2\Rightarrow Q\text{ has one negative and one positive eigenvalue}\right).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and continuity of the finite minimax aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\). If every \(f_i\) is convex on a convex set \(X\), then \(F\) is convex on \(X\). If every \(f_i\) is continuous on \(X\), then \(F\) is continuous on \(X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment theorem for a finite maximum of continuous pseudoconcave component functions on a polytope; g-vertex is understood in the active-set sense defined in the source context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a nonempty polytope, let I be finite, and define g(x)=\max_{i\in I}f_i(x), where each f_i is continuous and pseudoconcave on X. Then the minimum value of g over X is attained at a g\text{-vertex}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^\star\in X:\ x^\star\text{ is a }g\text{-vertex and }g(x^\star)=\min_{x\in X}g(x).
