knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-index minimization of a pointwise supremum.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A semi-infinite minimax program has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{t\in T}f(x,t),\] where the decision vector \(x\) is finite-dimensional and \(T\) is an infinite index set. Its epigraph form is \[\inf_{x,\tau}\{\tau:x\in X,\ f(x,t)\leq\tau\text{ for every }t\in T\}.\] When the supremum is not attained, \(\sup\) rather than \(\max\) is essential; the epigraph equivalence still holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semi-infinite minimax program minimizes a supremum over an infinite index set, equivalently imposing one epigraph inequality for every index.
knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Infinite Minimax Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-restriction method with exact worst-index separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(T_k\subset T\), globally solve \[L_k=\min_{x\in X}\max_{t\in T_k}f(x,t)\] and let \(x_k\) be an optimizer. Compute \(U_k=\sup_{t\in T}f(x_k,t)\). Then \(L_k\le v^*\le U_k\). Thus \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\) certifies that \(x_k\) is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal. If the gap is larger, an exact maximizer, when one exists, or a declared approximate maximizer may be added, with its separation error included in subsequent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange methods alternate finite minimax restrictions and worst-index separation; their lower–upper gap is a global value certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every finite restricted problem is solved globally.
The separation value is exact; any approximate separation error is explicitly included in the upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\le v^*\le U_k\), and \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow\phi(x_k)-v^*\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Restriction and Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Danskin-type certificate for compact-index convex minimax optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex semi-infinite minimax point is optimal exactly when active component gradients balance the feasible-set normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(T\) is compact.
Every component is convex and differentiable in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\phi(x)\iff0\in\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla_xf(x^*,t):t\in T(x^*)\}+N_C(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index First-Order Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonattained Suprema Defeat Exact Finite Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for exact discretization of an infinite index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0\}\), \(T=(0,1)\), and \(f(0,t)=t\). Then \(\sup_{t\in T}f(0,t)=1\), whereas \(\max_{t\in S}f(0,t)<1\) for every finite \(S\subset T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonattained supremum can make every finite index restriction strictly inexact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{t\in T}f(0,t)=1>\max_{t\in S}f(0,t)\) for every finite \(S\subset T\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Suprema Defeat Exact Finite Restriction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity of the supremum objective under compact continuous indexing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(T\) be compact metric spaces and let \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then \(\phi(x)=\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is continuous, every active set \(T(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is nonempty and compact, and \(\min_{x\in X}\phi(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint continuity on compact decision and index sets makes the worst-case objective continuous and ensures attainment of both extrema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\in C(X)\), \(T(x)\ne\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\phi(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Index Regularity and Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex semi-infinite minimax specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f(\cdot,t)\) is convex on \(C\) for every \(t\in T\), then \(\phi(x)=\sup_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is convex on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of an arbitrary family of convex functions is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi=\sup_{t\in T}f(\cdot,t)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Preservation by Suprema

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-valued dual representation for compact convex semi-infinite minimax programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, let \(T\) be compact Hausdorff, and let \(f:C\times T\to\mathbb R\) be continuous with \(f(\cdot,t)\) convex for every \(t\). Then \[\min_{x\in C}\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal P(T)}\min_{x\in C}\int_T f(x,t)\,d\mu(t),\] and the maximum over regular Borel probability measures is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact convex semi-infinite minimax has an attained probability-measure dual under continuity and convexity in the decision variable.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous and \(f(\cdot,t)\) is convex for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal P(T)}\min_{x\in C}\int_Tf(x,t)\,d\mu(t)\), with an optimal \(\mu\).

notation.meaning: regular Borel probability measures on the index space
measure-valued multiplier for the infinite constraint family

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Measure Minimax Dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient convergence conditions for nested finite restrictions of a compact continuous semi-infinite minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(T\) be compact metric spaces, let \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let finite sets \(T_k\subseteq T_{k+1}\) have dense union in \(T\). Define \(\phi_k(x)=\max_{t\in T_k}f(x,t)\), \(\phi(x)=\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)\), and \(L_k=\min_X\phi_k\). Then \(\phi_k\uparrow\phi\) uniformly and \(L_k\uparrow v^*=\min_X\phi\). If \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_X\phi_k\) and \(U_k=\phi(x_k)\), then \(0\le U_k-L_k\le\|\phi-\phi_k\|_\infty\to0\), and every cluster point of \((x_k)\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested finite restrictions with dense index union close the certified minimax gap and have only globally optimal cluster points.
assumptions_latex: The finite restrictions are nested with dense union, and each restricted problem is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_k\to\phi\) uniformly, \(L_k\uparrow v^*\), \(U_k-L_k\to0\), and every cluster point of \((x_k)\) minimizes \(\phi\).

notation.meaning: restricted lower bound and feasible upper bound

review_flags: No universal iteration bound follows without quantitative regularity and a specified index-selection rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Finite Restrictions Converge Uniformly

children.title: Maximin Programs
children.top_down_role: Global models organized around maximizing a pointwise minimum.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) and \(\inf_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is finite for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{t\in T}f(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization of the worst indexed value, without asserting minimax equality.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximin program has the form \[\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{t\in T}f(x,t),\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(T\) are nonempty. For each decision \(x\), the inner infimum is its worst indexed value, and the outer problem selects the decision with the largest such guarantee. If \(T=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(f_i(x)=f(x,i)\), the inner value is \(\min_{i=1,\ldots,m}f_i(x)\). This definition alone does not assert equality with the reversed quantity \(\inf_{t\in T}\sup_{x\in X}f(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximin program chooses a decision maximizing its worst indexed payoff; no equality with the reversed minimax order is implied.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximin Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Gap After Reversing the Extremal Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of maximin–minimax equality without additional assumptions or mixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-by-two payoff table has a strict maximin–minimax gap.
assumptions_latex: The payoff is one on matching indices and zero otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_x\inf_t f(x,t)=0<1=\inf_t\sup_x f(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Gap After Reversing the Extremal Order

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity of a Finite Worst-Payoff Aggregate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-optimization specialization of finite maximin programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) be concave. Then \[G(x)=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\] is concave on \(X\). Consequently, maximizing \(G\) over \(X\) has a convex hypograph formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite pointwise minimum of concave payoffs is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=\min_i f_i\) is concave on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Concavity of a Finite Worst-Payoff Aggregate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relation between maximin and reversed minimax values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every real-valued function \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) on nonempty sets, \[\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{t\in T}f(x,t)\leq\inf_{t\in T}\sup_{x\in X}f(x,t),\] whenever the two sides are well-defined as extended-real values. Equality requires additional structural assumptions and is not part of the maximin definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximin value never exceeds the reversed minimax value, but equality is not automatic.
assumptions_latex: The displayed extended-real values are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_x\inf_t f(x,t)\leq\inf_t\sup_x f(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Maximin–Minimax Inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted formulation for finitely many payoff components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(f_i(x)=f(x,i)\), then \[\sup_{x\in X}\min_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)=\sup_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ t\leq f_i(x)\text{ for every }i\}.\] Under attainment, an optimal decision \(x^*\) corresponds to \(t^*=\min_i f_i(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximin problem has an exact hypograph formulation using one guaranteed-payoff variable bounded by every component.
assumptions_latex: \(T=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is finite and every \(f_i\) is real-valued on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise-minimum and hypograph formulations have the same supremum, with the stated correspondence when the optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maximin Hypograph Formulation

children.title: Nested Extremal Aggregates
children.top_down_role: Models containing layered minimum or maximum aggregation across component families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{i\in I}\inf_{j\in J_i}f_{ij}(x)\).

notation.meaning: Inner index set associated with i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative alternating supremum-infimum aggregate inside an outer optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nested extremal-aggregate program places two or more ordered extremal operators inside its objective or constraints. A representative form is \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{i\in I}\inf_{j\in J_i}f_{ij}(x).\] The ordering is part of the model: the inner value \(\inf_{j\in J_i}f_{ij}(x)\) is formed separately for each \(i\), after which the outer supremum is taken. Interchanging the two operators generally defines a different function and a different optimization problem unless additional interchange conditions are established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested extremal program optimizes an ordered composition of minima, maxima, infima, or suprema; changing their order generally changes the model.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Extremal Aggregates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Increasing and Locally Difference-of-Monotonic Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local order-structure definitions on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f is locally increasing (respectively, locally dm) on \mathbb{R}_+^n if, for every x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n, there exists a box [a,b] containing x in its interior such that f is increasing (respectively, dm) on [a,b].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is locally increasing, respectively locally difference-of-monotonic, when every point of the nonnegative orthant is interior to a box on which the corresponding property holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\;\exists [a,b]\ni x\text{ with }x\in\operatorname{int}[a,b]\text{ such that }f\text{ is increasing (respectively dm) on }[a,b].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-monotonicity and constancy along lineality fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of monotonicity relative to a closed convex cone and its consequence on fibers parallel to the cone's lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) a closed convex cone, and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is \(K\)-monotonic on \(X\) if \[x,x'\in X,\quad x'-x\in K\implies f(x')\ge f(x).\] Equivalently, for each \(x\in X\) and \(u\in K\), the map \(\theta\mapsto f(x+\theta u)\) is nondecreasing over the feasible nonnegative parameters \(\{\theta\ge0:x+\theta u\in X\}\). If \(L=K\cap(-K)\) and \(Q\) satisfies \(\ker Q=L\), then \[x,x'\in X,\quad Qx=Qx'\implies f(x)=f(x').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is K-monotonic on X when movement between feasible points in a K-direction cannot decrease its value. It is consequently constant on every fiber whose directions lie in the lineality space of K.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'-x\in K\implies f(x')\ge f(x),\qquad Qx=Qx'\implies f(x)=f(x')

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization for quasiconcave functions through closure of pointwise upper-level sets under addition of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\operatorname{rec}X\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be quasiconcave. Then \(f\) is \(K\)-monotonic on \(X\) if and only if, for every \(x^0\in X\), with \(\gamma=f(x^0)\), \[x^0+K\subseteq X(\gamma):=\{x\in X:f(x)\ge\gamma\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconcave function is K-monotonic exactly when adding any vector from K to a point leaves the result in the upper level set determined by that point's value.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\operatorname{rec}X\text{ is a closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }K\text{-monotonic on }X\iff \forall x^0\in X,\ x^0+K\subseteq\{x\in X:f(x)\ge f(x^0)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone Monotonicity and the Rank Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines monotonicity relative to a closed convex cone, the associated rank property, and invariance along the cone's lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone. The function \(f\) is monotonic on \(\Omega\) with respect to \(M\) if \(f(x+u)\geq f(x)\) for all \(x\in\Omega\) and \(u\in M\). If, in addition, \(M\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(\Omega)\) and \(\dim M^*=k\), then \(f\) has the rank-\(k\) property on \(\Omega\). For the lineality space \(L=M\cap(-M)\), one has \(\dim L=n-k\) and \(f(x+u)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in\Omega\) and \(u\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is monotonic with respect to a closed convex cone when movement in any cone direction cannot decrease its value. When the cone lies in the recession cone of the domain and its dual has dimension k, this is called the rank-k property. The function is then constant along the cone's lineality directions, whose dimension is n-k.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
M\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(\Omega)\text{ and }\dim M^*=k\text{ for the rank-property conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim L=n-k\quad\text{and}\quad f(x+u)=f(x)\quad\forall x\in\Omega,\ \forall u\in L,\qquad L=M\cap(-M).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization obtained by quotienting out the lineality space of the ordering cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\operatorname{rec}X\) be a closed convex cone with lineality space \(L\), and let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) have rank \(r\) and satisfy \(\ker Q=L\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When K lies in the recession cone of X, a function is K-monotonic exactly when it factors through a linear map whose kernel is the lineality space of K, and the induced function is monotonic with respect to the projected cone Q(K).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical deterministic method for a compact normal/conormal monotonic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compact normal \(G\subseteq[\ell,u]\), closed conormal \(H\subseteq[\ell,u]\), and continuous componentwise nondecreasing \(f\), outer polyblock approximation maintains a polyblock \(P_k\supseteq G\). A selected proper vertex \(v^k\in H\) gives the upper bound \(f(v^k)\); its radial projection \(p^k\) onto the upper boundary of \(G\) gives a feasible incumbent when \(p^k\in H\). Replacing \(v^k\) by the standard coordinate cut vertices preserves an outer cover. With exact projections and standard exhaustive proper-vertex selection, incumbent bounds increase to and vertex bounds decrease to \(\max_{G\cap H}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer polyblock approximation successively cuts an outer cover of the normal set and obtains convergent bounds, using the conormal set to test relevant vertices and projected incumbents.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is nonempty, compact, and normal relative to \([\ell,u]\).
\(H\) is closed and conormal relative to \([\ell,u]\), and \(G\cap H\ne\varnothing\).
Radial projections are exact and proper vertices are selected exhaustively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_k\le v^*\le U_k,\qquad L_k\uparrow v^*,\quad U_k\downarrow v^*.

notation.meaning: incumbent lower and vertex upper bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Outer Polyblock Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional bounds used by order-based partition methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is componentwise nondecreasing and \([a,b]\subseteq[\ell,u]\), then \(f(a)\le f(x)\le f(b)\) for every \(x\in[a,b]\). Thus \(f(b)\) is a regional upper bound for maximization, and every feasible \(x\in[a,b]\) supplies the lower bound \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower and upper corners bound an increasing objective throughout a box.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Monotonic Program and Increasing Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the displayed canonical monotonic model, componentwise monotonicity, and closure under pointwise minimum and maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical monotonic optimization problem is \[\max\{f(x):g(x)\le 0\le h(x),\ x\in\mathbb R_+^n\},\] where \(f,g,h\) are increasing on \(\mathbb R_+^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical monotonic program maximizes an increasing function on the nonnegative orthant subject to inequalities involving increasing functions. Increasing means nondecreasing under componentwise order, and pointwise minima and maxima preserve this property.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposition Is Nonunique and Does Not Imply Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of the difference representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\varphi=g-h\) with componentwise nondecreasing \(g,h\), then \(\varphi=(g+r)-(h+r)\) for every componentwise nondecreasing \(r\), so the decomposition is nonunique. Moreover, on \([0,1]\), \(g(x)=x\) and \(h(x)=x^2\) are nondecreasing while \(g(x)-h(x)=x-x^2\) is not monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Difference-of-monotonic decompositions are nonunique, and the represented difference need not itself be monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{difference-of-monotonic representability}\not\Rightarrow\text{monotonicity of the represented function}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Functions Admit Difference-of-Monotonic Representations on Boxes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient construction demonstrating the breadth of the representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=[\ell,u]\) and let \(\varphi\) be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(B\). If \(M_i\ge\max_{x\in B}\{-\partial_i\varphi(x),0\}\), then \[g(x)=\varphi(x)+\sum_{i=1}^nM_ix_i,\qquad h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^nM_ix_i\] are componentwise nondecreasing on \(B\) and \(\varphi=g-h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable function on a compact box has a difference-of-monotonic decomposition obtained by adding a sufficiently steep increasing linear function.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi=g-h\quad\text{with }g,h\text{ componentwise nondecreasing on }B.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Functions Admit Difference-of-Monotonic Representations on Boxes

assumptions_latex: Every displayed component function is finite and componentwise nondecreasing on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf\{g_0(x)-h_0(x):x\in B,\ g_k(x)-h_k(x)\leq0,\ k=1,\ldots,p\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit difference representation on a componentwise ordered box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A difference-of-monotonic program admits the representation \[\inf_{x\in B}\ g_0(x)-h_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_k(x)-h_k(x)\leq0,\quad k=1,\ldots,p,\] where \(B=[\ell,u]\) and every \(g_k,h_k:B\to\mathbb R\) is componentwise nondecreasing. The representation, rather than monotonicity of each difference, defines the class. Opposing monotone components may create a nonmonotone objective and nonnormal feasible regions, so both components must be retained in any order-based reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A difference-of-monotonic program expresses each objective or constraint function as one componentwise increasing function minus another on an ordered box.

knowledge_statements.title: Models with Hidden Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted canonical form exposing componentwise order structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem has hidden monotonicity on a box \(B=[\ell,u]\subset\mathbb R^n\) if it admits an objective-preserving reformulation \(\max\{\Phi(z):z\in G\cap H\}\), possibly after introducing auxiliary variables, such that \(\Phi\) is componentwise nondecreasing, \(G\subseteq B\) is normal, and \(H\subseteq B\) is conormal. Normality means \(z\in G\) and \(\ell\leq w\leq z\) imply \(w\in G\); conormality means \(z\in H\) and \(z\leq w\leq u\) imply \(w\in H\). Equivalence requires equality of optimal values and projection of every lifted feasible point to an original feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hidden monotonicity exists when an equivalent reformulation exposes an increasing objective over intersecting downward- and upward-closed sets in an ordered box.
assumptions_latex: All inequalities between vectors are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(P)=\max\{\Phi(z):z\in G\cap H\}\) with \(\Phi\) increasing, \(G\) normal, and \(H\) conormal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic equivalence conditions, not a validated characterization of the ambiguously defined hidden-monotonicity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) maximize \(f(x)\) over \(X\), and let \(L\) maximize \(\Phi(z)\) over \(Z\) with projection \(\pi:Z\to X\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimizer Equivalence for a Hidden-Monotonicity Reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded statement using the source-defined problems (11.47)–(11.48) and objects \(\varphi\), \(\Phi\), \(R\), and \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Operation Libraries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive primitive library for factorable nonlinear expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). An elementary-operation library \(\mathcal L\) is a specified collection of constants, coordinate projections, and finite-arity functions with declared domains. The factorable expressions generated by \(\mathcal L\) are defined recursively: every constant and projection \(x\mapsto x_i\) is factorable, and if \(e_1,\ldots,e_k\) are factorable and \(\varphi\in\mathcal L\) is defined at \((e_1(x),\ldots,e_k(x))\) for every \(x\in D\), then \(x\mapsto\varphi(e_1(x),\ldots,e_k(x))\) is factorable. Typical libraries contain arithmetic operations and selected univariate elementary functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primitive library generates factorable expressions recursively from variables, constants, and domain-valid compositions of its supported operations.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive in \(\mathcal L\) has a declared arity and domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F(\mathcal L,D)\) is the smallest expression class closed under domain-valid composition by primitives in \(\mathcal L\).

notation.meaning: Factorable expressions generated on the domain.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary semantic boundary for recursively generated factorable expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Membership of an inner expression in \(\mathcal F(\mathcal L,D)\) does not by itself make composition with every supported primitive valid. If \(D=[-1,1]\), \(e(x)=x\), and the real logarithm belongs to \(\mathcal L\) with domain \((0,\infty)\), then \(e\in\mathcal F(\mathcal L,D)\) but \(\log\circ e\notin\mathcal F(\mathcal L,D)\), because \(e(D)\) is not contained in the logarithm's domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supported primitive can be composed only when all possible inner values lie in its declared domain; logarithm of a sign-changing expression is a counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\mapsto\log x\notin\mathcal F(\mathcal L,[-1,1]).

notation.meaning: Declared real domain of the logarithm primitive.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact expression-graph lifting through intermediate variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a factorable expression \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) have an acyclic expression graph whose noninput nodes are ordered topologically. Assign a variable \(z_j\) to each noninput node and impose \(z_j=\varphi_j(v_{j1},\ldots,v_{jk_j})\), where every argument \(v_{jr}\) is an original variable, a constant, or an earlier auxiliary variable. If \(z_m\) represents the root, then the graph formulation \(z_m=f(x)\) is exact: for each \(x\in D\), forward evaluation gives a unique auxiliary vector satisfying all node equations, and every satisfying auxiliary vector has \(z_m=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression graph is represented exactly by one auxiliary variable and defining equation per operation node, evaluated in topological order.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite, acyclic, and domain-valid on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_m=f(x)\iff \exists z_{1:m-1}\;\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}z_j=\varphi_j(v_{j1},\ldots,v_{jk_j})\).

notation.meaning: Auxiliary variable for expression-graph node j.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a finite acyclic expression graph has \(N\) noninput operation nodes and \(E\) incoming argument arcs, its full graph lift introduces \(N\) auxiliary variables and \(N\) defining primitive relations. Given an explicit topological ordering, the lift has \(O(N+E)\) incidence size and can be assembled in \(O(N+E)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full exact lift has one auxiliary and one relation per operation node and is assembled in linear graph time.

Nodes and argument arcs are explicitly encoded in topological order.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorable Constraint Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint systems generated by finite factorable expression graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a factorable constraint system is a finite family \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i\in I\) and \(h_j(x)=0\) for \(j\in J\), where every \(f_i\) and \(h_j\) is generated by a fixed elementary-operation library. Replacing every noninput expression-graph node by an auxiliary variable and its defining equation produces an extended feasible set \(\widehat F\). The original feasible set is exactly its projection: \(F=\{x\in D:\exists z\text{ such that }(x,z)\in\widehat F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorable constraint system uses finitely many library-generated expressions and has an exact auxiliary-variable graph formulation whose projection is the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_x(\widehat F)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of factorable equalities to an inequality-only factorable system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\in\mathcal F(\mathcal L,D)\) and \(-h\in\mathcal F(\mathcal L,D)\), then \(h(x)=0\) is equivalent on \(D\) to \(h(x)\le0\) and \(-h(x)\le0\). Consequently, when the generated expression class is closed under negation, every finite mixed factorable constraint system has an equivalent inequality-only factorable representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When negation is supported, each factorable equality can be replaced exactly by its two signed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h(x)=0\iff h(x)\le0\ \wedge\ -h(x)\le0.

notation.meaning: Expressions generated by the fixed primitive library on the domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Subexpression Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reuse of common expression-graph nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose expressions \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) contain identical occurrences of a subexpression \(s(x)\). A shared-subexpression representation forms the union directed acyclic graph and assigns one auxiliary variable \(z_s\) to the common node, with the single defining equation \(z_s=s(x)\); every parent expression uses that same variable. For each \(x\) in the common domain, graph evaluation determines one value of \(z_s\), so merging identical nodes preserves every root value and the projection of the extended formulation. If separate copies are retained, exact consistency requires equality of their auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical subexpressions may share one graph node and auxiliary variable without changing expression values or the projected feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The occurrences of \(s\) have identical operations, arguments, and domains.
The combined expression graph is finite and acyclic.

children.title: Composite DC Representations
children.top_down_role: DC representations built from nested or externally composed function structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient condition for recognizing a convex term in a composite DC representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_p)\) has convex components on \(C\), and \(G\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing on a convex set containing \(F(C)\). Then \(G\circ F\) is convex on \(C\). The analogous condition applies to \(H\circ K\). Convexity of both the inner components and outer function without the required monotonicity does not suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex coordinatewise-nondecreasing outer function preserves convexity under composition with convex components; convexity alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing on a convex set containing \(F(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\circ F\text{ is convex on }C.

notation.meaning: Scalar components of the inner mapping.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Monotone Convex Composition Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Alone Does Not Preserve Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex-composition recognition without a suitable monotonicity or range condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[-1,1]\), let \(F(x)=x^2\) and \(G(t)=(t-1)^2\). Both functions are convex on their respective domains, but \((G\circ F)(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) has second derivative \(12x^2-4\), which is negative near \(x=0\). Thus \(G\circ F\) is not convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex outer function composed with a convex inner function need not be convex when the outer function lacks the needed monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\circ F\text{ is not convex on }[-1,1].
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Alone Does Not Preserve Composition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite DC Representation with Explicit Outer Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested convex-minus-convex representation retaining explicit inner and outer maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) and \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), and let \(F:C\to U\), \(K:C\to V\), \(G:U\to\mathbb R\), and \(H:V\to\mathbb R\). An identity \(f=(G\circ F)-(H\circ K)\) is a composite DC representation on \(C\) when \(G\circ F\) and \(H\circ K\) are finite convex functions on \(C\). Convexity is required of the scalar composites, not separately of every inner or outer map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite DC representation is a difference of two finite convex composite functions, with the outer domains containing the corresponding inner ranges.
assumptions_latex: \(G\circ F\) and \(H\circ K\) are finite and convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=(G\circ F)-(H\circ K)\text{ is DC on }C.

notation.meaning: Declared domains containing the ranges of the inner maps.
Convex scalar composite terms retained without expansion.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite DC Representation with Explicit Outer Domains
Composite DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC decomposition whose convex terms retain nested composition structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A composite DC representation of \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is an identity \(f(x)=G(F(x))-H(K(x))\), where \(F:C\to\mathbb R^p\) and \(K:C\to\mathbb R^q\) may themselves be vector-valued compositions, while the scalar composites \(G\circ F\) and \(H\circ K\) are finite convex functions on \(C\). Thus the represented function is difference-of-convex on \(C\); the representation records the composite expression structure rather than requiring either composite term to be expanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite DC representation expresses a function as the difference of two convex composite functions while retaining their nested structure.
assumptions_latex: \(G\circ F\) and \(H\circ K\) are finite and convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=(G\circ F)-(H\circ K)\) is a DC function on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Outer functions producing convex composite terms.

children.title: Separable DC Representations
children.top_down_role: DC representations exposing variable-wise or block-wise separability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Does Not Imply Block Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between generic DC structure and additive block-separable structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\) is DC on \(\mathbb R^2\), since \(x_1x_2=((x_1+x_2)^2-(x_1-x_2)^2)/4\), but it cannot be written as \(u(x_1)+v(x_2)\) on any rectangle with nonempty interior. Hence it has no DC representation whose two convex terms are both separable across the singleton blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bilinear product is DC but not additively separable, so generic DC representability does not imply block-separable DC representability.
assumptions_latex: The chosen blocks are x_1\text{ and }x_2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is DC but has no singleton-block-separable DC representation on a nondegenerate rectangle}.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Does Not Imply Block Separability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC decomposition in which both convex terms separate across the same variable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), where each \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is convex. A block-separable DC representation is an identity \(f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^m(g_i(x_i)-h_i(x_i))\), where every \(g_i,h_i\) is finite and convex on \(C_i\). Equivalently, \(f=g-h\) with \(g(x)=c+\sum_i g_i(x_i)\) and \(h(x)=\sum_i h_i(x_i)\), both convex and block-separable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both convex terms in a block-separable DC representation decompose additively over the same variable blocks.
assumptions_latex: g_i,h_i:C_i\to\mathbb R\text{ are finite and convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=c+\sum_i(g_i(x_i)-h_i(x_i))=g(x)-h(x).

notation.meaning: Variable block in the product domain.
Convex positive and negative components for block i.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable DC Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Characterization of Separable DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a separable DC representation and DC representability of each additive block component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\) and every \(f_i\) has a DC decomposition \(f_i=g_i-h_i\) on \(C_i\), then collecting the components gives a block-separable DC representation of \(f\). Conversely, every block-separable DC representation makes \(f\) additively separable, with block functions \(f_i=g_i-h_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additively separable function has a block-separable DC representation exactly when its displayed block components are DC, up to redistribution of constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall i,\ f_i=g_i-h_i)\Longleftrightarrow f=c+\sum_i(g_i-h_i).
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Characterization of Separable DC Functions
Separable DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise or blockwise separable DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), where each \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is convex, and write \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\). A separable DC representation is an identity \(f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(g_i(x_i)-h_i(x_i)\bigr)\), where each \(g_i,h_i:C_i\to\mathbb R\) is finite and convex. Equivalently, \(g(x)=c+\sum_i g_i(x_i)\) and \(h(x)=\sum_i h_i(x_i)\) are convex on \(C\), and \(f=g-h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable DC representation decomposes a function into a sum of blockwise differences of finite convex functions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) and \(h_i\) is finite and convex on \(C_i\).

notation.meaning: Variable block in the product domain.
Convex component functions for block i.

children.title: Polynomial DC Representations
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for DC decompositions of polynomial expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic convexification of a polynomial on a compact convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Define \(\mu=\max_{x\in C}\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2p(x))\}\). For any \(\rho\geq\mu\), define \(g_\rho(x)=p(x)+(\rho/2)\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) and \(h_\rho(x)=(\rho/2)\lVert x\rVert_2^2\). Then \(g_\rho\) and \(h_\rho\) are convex on \(C\), and \(p=g_\rho-h_\rho\) is a DC representation on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real polynomial on a nonempty compact convex set admits a DC representation obtained by adding and subtracting a sufficiently large quadratic term.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(x)=g_\rho(x)-h_\rho(x)\) with \(g_\rho\) and \(h_\rho\) convex on \(C\) whenever \(\rho\geq\mu\).

notation.meaning: Maximum negative-curvature compensation required on C.
Convex terms in the quadratic DC representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Uniform Quadratic Convexification on Unbounded Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of the seed's constant-quadratic Hessian compensation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p(t)=-t^4\), the polynomial \(p(t)+(\rho/2)t^2\) has second derivative \(-12t^2+\rho\), which is negative for sufficiently large \(|t|\) for every finite \(\rho\ge0\). Thus the seed's constant-quadratic convexification need not extend from compact domains to \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed quadratic cannot always compensate polynomial negative curvature on an unbounded domain; minus the fourth power is a counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(t)+(\rho/2)t^2\text{ is not convex on }\mathbb R\text{ for any finite }\rho.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Uniform Quadratic Convexification on Unbounded Domains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global polynomial DC existence, distinct from constant-quadratic convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every polynomial \(p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), there exist polynomials \(g,h\) convex on \(\mathbb R^n\) such that \(p=g-h\). Thus compactness is required by the seed's uniform constant-quadratic construction, not by existence of every polynomial's global DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real multivariate polynomial is globally a difference of two convex polynomials, although a constant quadratic correction may fail globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists g,h\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\text{ convex on }\mathbb R^n\text{ with }p=g-h.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Convex-Polynomial Difference Decomposition

children.title: DC Feasible-Set Representation System
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for feasible sets induced by DC constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of Finite DC Inequality Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a finite conjunction or disjunction of DC inequalities by one DC inequality and then by one convex and one reverse-convex inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge 1\) and let \(g_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be DC functions on a common domain. The conjunctive system \(g_i(x)\le 0\) for every \(i\) is equivalent to \(\max_{1\le i\le m}g_i(x)\le 0\), whereas the disjunctive system \(g_i(x)\le 0\) for at least one \(i\) is equivalent to \(\min_{1\le i\le m}g_i(x)\le 0\). Each aggregate is DC. If the relevant aggregate has a decomposition \(g=p-q\) with \(p\) and \(q\) convex, then \(g(x)\le 0\) is equivalent to the existence of \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(p(x)-t\le 0\) and \(t-q(x)\le 0\). The first inequality is convex and the second is reverse convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite conjunction of DC inequalities is represented by their pointwise maximum, while a finite disjunction is represented by their pointwise minimum. Decomposing the resulting DC function as p−q and introducing a scalar t yields one convex inequality and one reverse-convex inequality.
assumptions_latex: g_i\text{ is DC on a common domain}\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^m g_i(x)\le0\right)\iff \max_i g_i(x)\le0,\qquad \left(\bigvee_{i=1}^m g_i(x)\le0\right)\iff \min_i g_i(x)\le0,\qquad g(x)\le0\iff\exists t\in\mathbb{R}:\ p(x)-t\le0,\ t-q(x)\le0

children.title: DC-Representable Sets
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions viewed through an overall DC set representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Representability Does Not Imply Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary boundary between DC describability and convexity of the represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=\mathbb R\), the inequality \(1-x^2\le0\) is DC because \(1-x^2=1-x^2\) is a difference of the convex functions \(1\) and \(x^2\). Its represented set is \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\), which is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single DC inequality can represent a nonconvex set; the complement of the open unit interval is an example.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:1-x^2\le0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\text{ is DC-representable and nonconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Representability Does Not Imply Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-set representation by finitely many finite-valued DC inequalities on a convex ambient domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A set \(S\subseteq C\) is finitely DC-representable relative to \(C\) if there are finite convex functions \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), such that \(S=\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}\). This property is relative to the ambient domain and does not imply that \(S\) is convex; for \(m=0\), the represented set is \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely DC-representable set is the intersection of finitely many DC inequality sublevel sets relative to a convex ambient domain.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}.
Each g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb R\text{ is finite and convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite DC-Representable Set
DC-Representable Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite feasible-set representation by DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A set \(S\subseteq C\) is DC-representable relative to \(C\) if there exist finitely many pairs of finite convex functions \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb R\) such that \(S=\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). The representation is relative to the chosen ambient domain and decomposition; it asserts finite DC describability, not convexity of \(S\). The case \(m=0\) represents \(S=C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is DC-representable when finitely many differences of convex functions describe it by inequalities on a convex ambient domain.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb R\) is finite and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\{x\in C:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0\}\).

children.title: DC Constraint Systems
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions represented through collections of DC constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntax and exact inequality-only normalization of finite DC constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a convex domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a finite DC constraint system consists of inequalities \(g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\) and equalities \(a_j(x)-b_j(x)=0\), where all component functions are finite and convex on \(C\). Each equality is equivalent to the two DC inequalities \(a_j-b_j\le0\) and \(b_j-a_j\le0\), so every mixed finite system has an exact inequality-only DC form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite DC constraint system uses differences of finite convex functions, and each equality can be normalized exactly to two signed DC inequalities.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}.
The inequality and equality index sets are finite.
All convex components are finite on C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_j-b_j=0\iff(a_j-b_j\le0)\wedge(b_j-a_j\le0).

notation.meaning: Finite convex component functions on the common ambient domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite DC Constraint System
DC Constraint Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inequality and equality systems built from convex differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a convex domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a DC constraint system consists of inequalities \(g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i\in I\) and equalities \(a_j(x)-b_j(x)=0\) for \(j\in J\), where all component functions are finite and convex on \(C\), and \(I,J\) are finite. Each equality is equivalently represented by the two DC inequalities \(a_j-b_j\leq0\) and \(b_j-a_j\leq0\). Hence every such system has an inequality-only DC representation with the same feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC constraint system uses finite convex differences in inequalities and equalities; each equality can be replaced exactly by two DC inequalities.
assumptions_latex: All component functions are finite and convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_j-b_j=0\iff (a_j-b_j\leq0)\wedge(b_j-a_j\leq0)\).

children.title: Quadratic-to-Bilinear Reformulation
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for exposing quadratic interactions as bilinear structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-to-Bilinear Reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variable-copy reformulation exposing quadratic products as bilinear terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) on \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), introduce a copy \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) and impose \(y=x\). Define \(\beta(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^nQ_{ij}x_i y_j+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\). Then \(q(x)=\beta(x,y)\) whenever \(y=x\). Consequently, replacing every occurrence of \(q(x)\) in an objective or constraint by \(\beta(x,y)\), together with the linear linking equations \(y=x\), gives an exact extended formulation whose projection onto \(x\) is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copying the variables and linking the copy by equality converts a quadratic expression exactly into a bilinear expression in two variable blocks.
assumptions_latex: The linking constraint \(y=x\) is imposed exactly.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp exactness boundary for variable-copy bilinearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bilinear replacement is generally not equivalent if the link \(y=x\) is relaxed or omitted. For \(q(x)=x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), replacing \(x^2\) by \(xy\) with independent \((x,y)\in[-1,1]^2\) changes the minimum from \(0\) to \(-1\), attained at \((x,y)=(1,-1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent copied variables turn exact bilinearization into a different problem; equality linking is essential.
assumptions_latex: The copied variable varies independently in \([-1,1]\).

children.title: Separable Curvature Reformulation
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for diagonal and separable curvature exposure.

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Curvature Reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal coordinates exposing quadratic curvature term by term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and let \(Q=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^{\mathsf T}\) be an orthogonal eigendecomposition. Under the invertible change of variables \(y=U^{\mathsf T}x\), the quadratic function \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) becomes \(q(Uy)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i y_i^2+(U^{\mathsf T}c)^{\mathsf T}y+d\). Thus all quadratic curvature is separable by coordinate; terms with positive, zero, and negative \(\lambda_i\) expose convex, affine, and concave directions respectively, without changing feasible points under the inverse map \(x=Uy\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonal eigenvector change of variables diagonalizes a symmetric quadratic, exposing its convex and concave curvature as separable univariate terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(Uy)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i y_i^2+(U^{\mathsf T}c)^{\mathsf T}y+d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Separability Does Not Imply Problem Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on what orthogonal diagonalization achieves for a constrained model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although an orthogonal eigenbasis makes a quadratic objective separable, it need not make the transformed feasible set a Cartesian product. For \(D=[-1,1]^2\) and an orthogonal matrix \(U\) that is not a signed coordinate permutation, \(U^{\mathsf T}D\) is a non-axis-aligned rotated square and cannot equal \(D_1\times D_2\) for intervals \(D_1,D_2\). Thus diagonal objective curvature alone does not decompose the optimization problem into independent scalar problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral rotation separates quadratic curvature but generally rotates and couples the constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is orthogonal and is not a signed coordinate permutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U^{\mathsf T}D\neq D_1\times D_2\text{ for all intervals }D_1,D_2.\)

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(D\).
There exists \(\rho\geq 0\) such that \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x))\geq-\rho\) for every \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional spectral convexification using a uniform lower Hessian-eigenvalue bound.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g(x)=f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) and \(h(x)=\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2\). Then
\[
f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\qquad(x\in D).
\]
Moreover, \(\nabla^2g(x)=\nabla^2f(x)+\rho I\succeq0\) and \(\nabla^2h(x)=\rho I\succeq0\) throughout \(D\). Thus the negative spectral curvature of \(f\) is transferred to the subtracted convex quadratic while the objective values and minimizers are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform lower bound on Hessian eigenvalues yields an exact difference-of-convex representation by adding and subtracting the same convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral DC Transformations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 Convex and Concave Functions p. 35

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least constant quadratic shift within the isotropic DC family on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, let \(f\in C^2(D)\), and set \(m:=\inf_{x\in D}\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))>-\infty\). Then \(g_\rho(x)=f(x)+\frac\rho2\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) is convex on \(D\) exactly when \(\rho\ge -m\). Under the restriction \(\rho\ge0\), the least admissible uniform shift is \(\rho_\star=\max\{0,-m\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex domain, the smallest nonnegative isotropic convexifying shift is the negative of the worst Hessian eigenvalue, truncated at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.

notation.meaning: infimum of the smallest Hessian eigenvalue over D

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Isotropic Curvature Shift

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Finite Uniform Shift Without a Curvature Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of isotropic spectral convexification on a domain with unbounded negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-x^4\) on \(D=\mathbb R\), \(f''(x)=-12x^2\) is unbounded below. For every finite \(\rho\ge0\), the shifted function \(g_\rho(x)=-x^4+\frac\rho2x^2\) has \(g_\rho''(x)=-12x^2+\rho<0\) for sufficiently large \(|x|\). Hence no finite uniform quadratic shift makes \(g_\rho\) convex on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When Hessian curvature is unbounded below, no finite isotropic quadratic shift need produce the seed's DC split.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall\rho<\infty)\quad f(x)+\tfrac\rho2x^2\text{ is not convex on }\mathbb R.\)
knowledge_statements.title: No Finite Uniform Shift Without a Curvature Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive–Negative Spectral Split of a Quadratic Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical anisotropic DC decomposition specialized to a symmetric quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^{\mathsf T}\) be symmetric, and define \(Q_+=U\operatorname{diag}(\max\{\lambda_i,0\})U^{\mathsf T}\) and \(Q_-=U\operatorname{diag}(\max\{-\lambda_i,0\})U^{\mathsf T}\). Then \(Q=Q_+-Q_-\) with \(Q_+,Q_-\succeq0\), so \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx=x^{\mathsf T}Q_+x-x^{\mathsf T}Q_-x\) is an exact difference of convex quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting positive and negative eigenvalues gives an exact anisotropic DC decomposition of every symmetric quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=Q_+-Q_-,\quad Q_+,Q_-\succeq0.\)

notation.meaning: magnitude of the negative spectral part of Q

knowledge_statements.title: Positive–Negative Spectral Split of a Quadratic Form

children.top_down_role: Reformulations separating a lower-dimensional nonconvex core from simpler subordinate problems.

children.title: Decomposition by Projection
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for isolating global variables through projection.

assumptions_latex: For each \(y\in P(X)\), the fiber infimum is interpreted in the extended-real sense and is attained when minimizers are asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original optimum equals the optimum of the projected value function, and an optimal projected point together with an optimal fiber solution recovers a global optimizer.

notation.meaning: Linear projection onto the global-variable space
Feasible fiber above a projected point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elimination by partial infimization is the standard exact projection identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact projection through fiberwise partial minimization; tractability of the subordinate fiber problems is separate.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y\in P(X)\), let \(X_y=\{x\in X:Px=y\}\) and \(v(y)=\inf_{x\in X_y}f(x)\). Then
\[
\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in P(X)}v(y).
\]
If \(y^*\) minimizes \(v\) and \(x^*\in X_{y^*}\) satisfies \(f(x^*)=v(y^*)\), then \(x^*\) globally minimizes \(f\) on \(X\). Conversely, every global minimizer \(x^*\) projects to a minimizer \(Px^*\) of \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization over each projection fiber converts the problem exactly into optimization of a value function over the projected variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition by Projection

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection decomposition on an ambient domain containing empty fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) contain \(P(X)\) and define \(\bar v(y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ Px=y\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Then \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\bar v(y)\). Thus empty fibers are represented exactly by \(+\infty\) and need not be removed from the outer domain beforehand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning plus infinity to empty fibers extends projection decomposition to an ambient outer domain without changing the optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\bar v(y).
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Projection Form

children.title: Parametric Reformulation
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for global search over parameterized subordinate problems.

assumptions_latex: For each \(y\in Y\), the subordinate feasible set \(Z(y)=\{z\in Z:G(y,z)\leq0\}\) is nonempty.
The subordinate minimum is attained whenever optimizer recovery is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global optimization of the joint problem is equivalent to global optimization of its parameter value function, followed by solution of one subordinate problem.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: partial minimization defines the exact parametric value-function reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nested reformulation with a low-dimensional outer parameter and subordinate inner optimization.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\inf\{F(y,z):y\in Y,\ z\in Z,\ G(y,z)\leq0\}.
\]
For \(y\in Y\), define \(Z(y)=\{z\in Z:G(y,z)\leq0\}\) and \(V(y)=\inf_{z\in Z(y)}F(y,z)\). Then the joint optimal value is \(\inf_{y\in Y}V(y)\). If \(y^*\) minimizes \(V\) and \(z^*\in Z(y^*)\) attains \(V(y^*)\), then \((y^*,z^*)\) is globally optimal for the joint problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating one variable block as a parameter produces an exact outer optimization of subordinate optimal values.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Reformulation

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nested reformulation allowing infeasible subordinate parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\in Y\), let \(Z(y)=\{z\in Z:G(y,z)\le0\}\) and define \(\bar V(y)=\inf_{z\in Z(y)}F(y,z)\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Then, without requiring every subordinate problem to be feasible, \(\inf\{F(y,z):y\in Y,\ z\in Z(y)\}=\inf_{y\in Y}\bar V(y)\). The effective outer domain is \(\{y\in Y:\bar V(y)<+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Giving an infeasible subordinate problem value plus infinity yields an exact outer value-function formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) and \(Z\) are the parameter and subordinate spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{F(y,z):y\in Y,\ z\in Z(y)\}=\inf_{y\in Y}\bar V(y).
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Parametric Reformulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive propagation of outer and subordinate absolute errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*=\inf_{y\in Y}\bar V(y)\in\mathbb R\). If \(\bar V(y_\varepsilon)\le p^*+\varepsilon\) and \(z_\delta\in Z(y_\varepsilon)\) satisfies \(F(y_\varepsilon,z_\delta)\le\bar V(y_\varepsilon)+\delta\), then \(F(y_\varepsilon,z_\delta)\le p^*+\varepsilon+\delta\). Consequently, choices with \(\varepsilon_j,\delta_j\to0\) generate a minimizing sequence for the joint problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-optimal parameter and delta-optimal subordinate solution are jointly epsilon-plus-delta optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(y_\varepsilon,z_\delta)-p^*\le\varepsilon+\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Nested Recovery

children.title: Partly Convex Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for models convex in one block and globally difficult in another.

knowledge_statements.title: Partly Convex Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise model convex in the subordinate variables for every fixed global-variable value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\). A problem
\[
\inf\{f(y,z):y\in Y,\ z\in Z,\ g_i(y,z)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,p)\}
\]
has a partly convex decomposition with global block \(y\) and convex block \(z\) if, for every fixed \(y\in Y\), the functions \(z\mapsto f(y,z)\) and \(z\mapsto g_i(y,z)\) are convex on \(Z\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\). Consequently, each fixed-\(y\) subordinate feasible set and optimization problem is convex, although the full problem need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partly convex model becomes a convex optimization problem in one block whenever the other, globally difficult block is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixing the global block \(y\) leaves a convex optimization problem in \(z\); nonconvexity may remain in the joint dependence or in the dependence on \(y\).

notation.meaning: Inequality constraint function indexed by i

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

source_witnesses.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent geometric formulation of convexity in the subordinate block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(y\in Y\), let \(f_y(z)=f(y,z)\) and \((g_i)_y(z)=g_i(y,z)\). The model is partly convex in \(z\) if and only if the epigraphs of these functions, relative to \(Z\), are convex for every \(y\) and \(i\). Under these conditions, \(F_y=\{z\in Z:g_i(y,z)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,p)\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partly convexity is equivalently fiberwise epigraph convexity, and every fixed-parameter feasible fiber is convex.
assumptions_latex: The fiber functions are real-valued on \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_y\) and every \((g_i)_y\) are convex on \(Z\) exactly when their relative epigraphs are convex; consequently \(F_y\) is convex.

notation.meaning: Epigraph of h relative to Z
Feasible subordinate fiber at fixed y

knowledge_statements.title: Fiberwise Epigraph Characterization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone-Coefficient LP Representation of the GPL Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A monotonicity regime in which the Lagrangian dual of the partly convex GPL model equals the dual of an endpoint-based LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(j\), suppose \(c_j(x),a_{1j}(x),\ldots,a_{mj}(x)\) are either all increasing on \([r,s]\) or all decreasing on \([r,s]\). Let \(J_+\) and \(J_-\) be the corresponding increasing and decreasing index sets. Then the Lagrangian dual of \((GPL)\) is the dual of the LP relaxation
\[\min_{x,y}\left\{\sum_{j\in J_+}c_j(r)y_j+\sum_{j\in J_-}c_j(s)y_j+\langle c^0,x\rangle\right\}\]
subject to
\[\sum_{j\in J_+}a_{ij}(r)y_j+\sum_{j\in J_-}a_{ij}(s)y_j+\langle B_i,x\rangle\le b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad y\ge0,\quad r\le x\le s.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each column's objective coefficient and constraint coefficients are jointly increasing or jointly decreasing on the box, the GPL Lagrangian dual equals the dual of the LP relaxation formed by evaluating increasing columns at r and decreasing columns at s.
assumptions_latex: \forall j,\ \{c_j,a_{1j},\ldots,a_{mj}\}\text{ are either all increasing on }[r,s]\text{ or all decreasing on }[r,s]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{LagDual}(GPL)=\operatorname{Dual}(LP_{\mathrm{endpoint}}).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convexity in one variable block for every fixed value of the other block; it requires neither joint convexity nor convexity in the second block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \((P)\): minimize \(f(z)\) subject to \(f^i(z)\le 0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(f,f^i:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R\) are continuous. The problem is called a partly convex program if there exists a splitting \(z=(x,\theta)\), with \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\theta\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(n+p=N\), such that, for every \(\theta\in\mathbb R^p\), the functions \(f(\cdot,\theta)\) and \(f^i(\cdot,\theta)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). This blockwise condition does not ensure global convexity: the feasible set can be nonconvex or disconnected, and a local minimum need not be global.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous inequality-constrained problem is partly convex if its variables can be split into x and theta so that, for every fixed theta, the objective and all constraint functions are convex in x. This does not make the full problem convex: its feasible set can be nonconvex or disconnected, and local minima need not be global.
assumptions_latex: f,f^i:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R\text{ are continuous},\quad i=1,\ldots,m
\forall\theta\in\mathbb R^p,\quad f(\cdot,\theta)\text{ and }f^i(\cdot,\theta)\text{ are convex on }\mathbb R^n,\quad i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (P)\text{ is a partly convex program. The definition does not imply that }Z=\{z\in\mathbb R^N:f^i(z)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ is convex or connected, or that every local minimum is global.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a global optimization model whose objective and constraints are convex in the y-block for each fixed x in the model domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A partly convex problem has the form
\[
\inf\{F(x,y)\mid G_i(x,y)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in C,\ y\in D\},
\]
where \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is compact and convex, \(D\subset\mathbb R^p\) is closed and convex, and \(F,G_i:C\times D\to\mathbb R\) are lower semicontinuous. For every fixed \(x\in C\), the functions \(F(x,\cdot)\) and \(G_i(x,\cdot)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are convex on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partly convex problem has a compact convex x-domain and a closed convex y-domain, lower-semicontinuous objective and constraints, and convex dependence on y for each fixed x.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is compact and convex}
D\subset\mathbb R^p\text{ is closed and convex}
F,G_i:C\times D\to\mathbb R\text{ are lower semicontinuous}
\forall x\in C,\quad F(x,\cdot),G_i(x,\cdot)\text{ are convex on }D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{F(x,y)\mid G_i(x,y)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in C,\ y\in D\}\text{ is a partly convex problem.}
