children.title: Coverage Discrepancy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage quality under differing dimension, sample-budget, or design conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cube-specific curse-of-dimensionality boundary for point designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(n\)-point design in \([0,1]^d\) has maximum-norm fill distance \(h_n\ge\tfrac12 n^{-1/d}\). Therefore coverage-only certification of a Lipschitz error of order \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(\varepsilon^{-d})\) sites in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any n-point cube design has fill distance at least one half n to the minus one over d.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Covering Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fill Distance, Dispersion, and Star Discrepancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes three standard design-quality statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D_n=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subset[0,1]^d\), define \(h_n=\sup_x\min_i\|x-u_i\|_\infty\), \(\operatorname{disp}(D_n)=\sup\{\lambda(B):B\text{ is an axis-parallel box},\ B\cap D_n=\varnothing\}\), and \(D_n^*=\sup_{a\in[0,1]^d}|n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf1_{[0,a)}(u_i)-\lambda([0,a))|\). These measure metric covering, largest empty-box volume, and anchored-box distributional error, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fill distance, dispersion, and star discrepancy measure metric covering, empty boxes, and anchored-box distributional error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three statistics encode distinct coverage information and require valid conversions before substitution.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill Distance, Dispersion, and Star Discrepancy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supplies valid cube-specific conversions among coverage statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(D_n\subset[0,1]^d\), with axis-parallel boxes and the maximum norm, \[h_n^d\le \operatorname{disp}(D_n)\le 2^dD_n^*.\] Consequently, \(h_n\le2(D_n^*)^{1/d}\), and either vanishing dispersion or vanishing star discrepancy implies vanishing fill distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the unit cube, fill distance is controlled through empty-box dispersion, which is in turn controlled by star discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_n^d\le\operatorname{disp}(D_n)\le2^dD_n^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Valid Discrepancy-to-Covering Comparisons

assumptions_latex: The domain is \(X=[0,1]^d\), equipped with the maximum norm.
The evaluation design after \(n\) samples is \(D_n\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic error certificate is \(0\le\min_{z\in D_n}f(z)-f^\star\le Lh_n\); thus any regime with \(h_n\to0\) is globally consistent.

notation.meaning: Volume of the largest empty axis-parallel box

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage measures as deterministic regimes controlling global-search error for Lipschitz objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_n\) be the first \(n\) evaluation sites. Its covering regime is described by \(h_n\), while its axis-parallel dispersion is the largest empty-box volume \(v_n\). A design is coverage-consistent when \(h_n\to0\); a rate \(h_n=O(a_n)\) defines an \(a_n\)-coverage regime. If \(x^\star\) minimizes \(f\), choose \(z_n\in D_n\) with \(\lVert z_n-x^\star\rVert_\infty\le h_n\). Lipschitz continuity then gives \(0\le\min_{z\in D_n}f(z)-f^\star\le Lh_n\). Consequently, coverage radius directly determines a worst-case optimization-error regime, whereas discrepancy or dispersion requires a geometric conversion before implying such a bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering radius directly bounds Lipschitz optimization error; discrepancy or empty-box volume affects optimization only after conversion to a covering guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Discrepancy Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The central mathematical claim is an explicit optimization-error certificate, so generic property is not the best exact kind; certificate is more appropriate. The relation between empty-box dispersion or discrepancy and covering radius is left unspecified, and the statement contains proof text.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rejected Builder claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proposed universal inequality \(\operatorname{disp}(D_n)\le(2h_n)^d\) is false: an empty axis-parallel box may be highly elongated, so its volume is not controlled by the \(d\)-th power of its shortest scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dispersion is not universally bounded by (2h) to the d; elongated empty boxes invalidate that direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Builder's claimed two-sided comparison between \(h_n^d\) and dispersion cannot be accepted.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Reverse Dispersion Bound

intermediate_metadata.reason: This regime leaf owns definitions, valid conversions, the deferred Lipschitz-error regime, and dimensional covering limits. The Builder's false reverse dispersion bound is deferred. Quasirandom construction, randomized maximin coverage, and stratified sampling are excluded as sibling method scopes.

children.title: Markovian Global Search
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for stochastic transition-based search families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Markov condition for a stochastic global-search state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state process \((X_n)\) is Markov with kernels \(K_n\) when, for every measurable \(A\), \[\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid X_0,\ldots,X_n)=K_n(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}\] Every archive, temperature, or adaptive parameter affecting the next transition must be included in \(X_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The current state must contain all transition-relevant information for the search to be Markov.
assumptions_latex: \((X_n)\) takes values in a measurable state space.
The conditional transition laws are represented by kernels \(K_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditional-law equality characterizes transition sufficiency of the declared Markov state.
knowledge_statements.title: Transition-State Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity Does Not Imply Global Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between equilibrium and best-so-far optimization convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Existence of, or convergence to, an invariant distribution \(\pi\) does not by itself imply that \(X_n\) or \(\min_{i\le n}f(X_i)\) approaches a global minimum. If \(\pi(A_\varepsilon)=0\) for \(A_\varepsilon=\{x:f(x)<f^\star+\varepsilon\}\), a stationary chain has probability zero of occupying \(A_\varepsilon\) at any fixed time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equilibrium convergence is not an optimization guarantee without continued access to near-optimal regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Invariant-distribution convergence alone is insufficient for global-search convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Does Not Imply Global Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Miss-probability bound under persistent conditional access to a measurable target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A be measurable and \tau_A=\inf\{n\ge1:X_n\in A\}. If, for n=0,\ldots,T-1, \Pr(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)\ge p_n almost surely on \{\tau_A>n\}, then \Pr(\tau_A>T)\le\prod_{n=0}^{T-1}(1-p_n)\le\exp(-\sum_{n=0}^{T-1}p_n).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional lower bounds on reaching a target set give product and exponential bounds on the probability of missing it through a finite horizon.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional lower bounds hold before the first hit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\tau_A>T)\le\prod_{n<T}(1-p_n)\le e^{-\sum_{n<T}p_n}.

notation.meaning: first positive-time visit to the target set
conditional lower bound on the next-step hit probability

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Conditional Hitting Bound

assumptions_latex: The feasible state space \(X\) is measurable and the objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is measurable.
For each incumbent level, the transition kernels assign uniformly persistent probability to every better sublevel set.
The algorithm records the best state visited.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the persistent-hitting condition, the recorded best value converges almost surely to \(f^\star=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Best objective value through time n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-homogeneous or inhomogeneous Markov transitions with best-so-far recording.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(X_0\in X\). Given \(X_n=x\), draw \(X_{n+1}\) from \(K_n(x,\cdot)\), evaluate \(f(X_{n+1})\), and update \(B_{n+1}=\min\{B_n,f(X_{n+1})\}\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(A_\varepsilon=\{x:f(x)<f^\star+\varepsilon\}\). A sufficient global-search condition is the existence of numbers \(p_{n,\varepsilon}\in[0,1]\) satisfying \(K_n(x,A_\varepsilon)\ge p_{n,\varepsilon}\) for all \(x\), with \(\sum_n p_{n,\varepsilon}=\infty\). Then the chain hits each \(A_\varepsilon\) almost surely, and the recorded values converge to \(f^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move through the domain using stochastic transition kernels and record the best state; persistent probability of hitting every near-optimal set ensures global convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General proposal-and-acceptance scheme for Markovian global search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General iterative scheme parameterized by an initial distribution, transition kernels, and acceptance probabilities; optional record dependence extends beyond the strict current-pair Markov property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sample $x_1\sim P_1$ on $A$, evaluate $y_1=f(x_1)$, and set $n=1$. At iteration $n$, repeatedly sample $z_n\sim Q_n(x_n,\cdot)$ until $z_n\in A$, evaluate $f(z_n)$, and set $x_{n+1}=z_n$ with probability $p_n$ and $x_{n+1}=x_n$ with probability $1-p_n$. Set $y_{n+1}=f(z_n)$ upon acceptance and $y_{n+1}=y_n$ otherwise, then stop or continue according to the stopping criterion. The kernel $Q_n$ may depend on $n$ and $x_n$, and $p_n$ may depend on $n,x_n,z_n,y_n,$ and $f(z_n)$. The scheme also permits dependence on $(x_{on},y_{on})$; nontrivial such dependence is not Markovian with respect to $(x_n,y_n)$ alone. Particular choices of $P_1,Q_n,$ and $p_n$ yield particular global random-search algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample an initial feasible point. At each iteration, draw proposals from a state-dependent transition distribution until a feasible proposal is obtained, evaluate it, and accept it with a prescribed probability; otherwise retain the current point. Update the stored objective value consistently and repeat until stopping. The initial, proposal, and acceptance distributions determine the particular method. Optional use of the incumbent record lies outside strict dependence on the current point-value pair alone.
assumptions_latex: P_1\text{ is a probability distribution on }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}=\begin{cases}z_n,&\text{with probability }p_n,\\x_n,&\text{with probability }1-p_n.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Markovian dependence in global random search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes current-state and record-state definitions from rules that use both states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_1,f(x_1),\ldots,x_n,f(x_n))$ be the conditional distribution used to generate $x_{n+1}$. The algorithm is Markovian in the current-state sense when, for every $n\ge 1$, this distribution equals $P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_n,f(x_n))$. Alternatively, with $y_{on}=\min_{i\le n}f(x_i)$ and $f(x_{on})=y_{on}$, a record-state Markovian rule satisfies $P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_1,f(x_1),\ldots,x_n,f(x_n))=P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_{on},y_{on})$. A rule that depends nontrivially on both $(x_n,y_n)$ and $(x_{on},y_{on})$ is not Markovian with respect to the current pair alone, although its structure is closely related.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global random search is current-state Markovian if its next-point distribution depends on the search history only through the current point and objective value. A record-state alternative depends only on the best point and value observed so far. Nontrivial simultaneous use of the current and record pairs falls outside the strict current-pair definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_1,f(x_1),\ldots,x_n,f(x_n))=P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_n,f(x_n))

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state barrier example showing failure under summable uphill acceptance probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the path graph \(a-b-c\), with proposals moving to adjacent vertices, \(f(a)=0\), \(f(b)=H>0\), \(f(c)=-1\), and \(X_0=a\). If \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\exp(-H/T_n)<\infty\), then \(\Pr(X_n=a\text{ for every }n)>0\). Thus simulated annealing can remain forever at the nonglobal local minimum \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the probabilities of crossing a necessary energy barrier are summable, simulated annealing can remain in a nonglobal well with positive probability.
assumptions_latex: The proposal graph is the path \(a-b-c\), with positive adjacent-edge proposals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(X_n=a\text{ for all }n)>0.\)

notation.meaning: energy barrier separating the initial well from the global minimum

knowledge_statements.title: Premature-Cooling Trap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state symmetric-proposal Metropolis kernel underlying simulated annealing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite, let \(Q(x,y)=Q(y,x)\) be an irreducible proposal kernel, and fix \(T>0\). For \(y\ne x\), set \(P_T(x,y)=Q(x,y)\min\{1,\exp(-(f(y)-f(x))/T)\}\), with the diagonal chosen to make \(P_T\) stochastic. Then \(P_T\) is reversible with respect to \(\pi_T(x)=Z_T^{-1}\exp(-f(x)/T)\). Consequently \(\pi_T\) is its unique stationary distribution and \(\pi_T(X^\star)\to1\) as \(T\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed temperature, finite-state Metropolis search with a symmetric irreducible proposal has a Gibbs stationary law that concentrates on global minimizers as temperature vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_T(x)\propto e^{-f(x)/T}\) is the unique stationary distribution and \(\pi_T(X^\star)\to1\) as \(T\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Temperature Gibbs Reversibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state symmetric Metropolis annealing with a barrier-depth cooling threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite and let the symmetric proposal kernel induce a connected graph. Define \(H(\gamma)=\max_{z\in\gamma}f(z)\), \(H(x,A)=\min_{\gamma:x\leadsto A}H(\gamma)\), and \(\Gamma^\star=\max_{x\notin X^\star}(H(x,X^\star)-f(x))\). For the time-inhomogeneous Metropolis chain with \(T_n=c/\log(n+n_0)\), if \(c>\Gamma^\star\) and \(n_0>1\), then \(\Pr(X_n\in X^\star)\to1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite connected landscape, logarithmic cooling slower than the deepest nonglobal energy barrier yields convergence in probability to the global-minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: The symmetric proposal kernel is irreducible and assigns positive probability to every graph edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(X_n\in X^\star)=1.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-State Logarithmic Cooling Theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state annealing iteration allowing asymmetric proposals; symmetric Metropolis annealing is the special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite, let \(T_n>0\), and let \(Q\) be an irreducible proposal kernel with mutual support: \(Q(x,y)>0\iff Q(y,x)>0\). Given \(X_n=x\), draw \(Y_n\sim Q(x,\cdot)\) and, when \(Q(x,Y_n)>0\), accept \(Y_n=y\) with probability \[\alpha_n(x,y)=\min\left\{1,\exp\left(-\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{T_n}\right)\frac{Q(y,x)}{Q(x,y)}\right\};\] otherwise retain \(x\). Record a least-objective incumbent among visited states. For symmetric \(Q\), the proposal ratio cancels. This definition makes no convergence claim for an arbitrary cooling schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-state simulated annealing uses temperature-dependent Metropolis-Hastings moves and records the best visited state.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is irreducible and has mutual support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rule defines finite-state simulated annealing and reduces to ordinary Metropolis annealing for symmetric \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Metropolis-Hastings Simulated Annealing

assumptions_latex: The proposal kernel \(Q(x,\cdot)\) is irreducible on the feasible state space \(X\).
The positive temperature sequence \((T_n)\) decreases toward zero according to a schedule satisfying an appropriate global-convergence condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under a valid cooling condition, the probability of occupying any fixed nonoptimal energy level tends to zero, and best-so-far values approach the global minimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metropolis simulated annealing; the precise sufficient cooling schedule depends on state-space assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(X_0\in X\) and temperatures \(T_n\downarrow0\). Given \(X_n=x\), propose \(Y_n\sim Q(x,\cdot)\) and accept it with probability \(\alpha_n(x,Y_n)=\min\{1,\exp(-(f(Y_n)-f(x))/T_n)\}\); otherwise set \(X_{n+1}=x\). Record the best state visited and stop according to a prescribed evaluation budget or convergence diagnostic. At fixed \(T\), the acceptance rule favors low objective values while allowing uphill moves. Global convergence requires sufficiently slow cooling relative to the energy barriers and irreducibility properties of the chosen state-space model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use Metropolis moves whose willingness to accept objective increases decreases with temperature; sufficiently slow cooling can concentrate the search on global minima.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulated Annealing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and an unspecified 'appropriate global-convergence condition' cannot support the stated concentration conclusion. Cooling theorems differ materially between finite, countable, and continuous state spaces; proposal irreducibility alone is insufficient. The algorithm kind fits, but the theorem component needs a precise sourced variant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Temperature-controlled neighborhood search for minimization, with unconditional acceptance of strict improvements and probabilistic acceptance otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(i:=i_{\mathrm{start}}\), \(k:=0\), \(c_k:=c_0\), and \(L_k:=L_0\). Repeat: for \(l=0,\ldots,L_k\), generate \(j\in S_i\); if \(f(j)<f(i)\), set \(i:=j\); otherwise, set \(i:=j\) with probability \(\exp((f(i)-f(j))/c_k)\). Set \(k:=k+1\), compute \((L_k,c_k)\), and stop when \(c_k\simeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an initial solution, simulated annealing repeatedly generates neighbors. It always accepts a strict improvement and otherwise accepts the neighbor with the stated temperature-dependent exponential probability. After each stage it updates the iteration count and temperature, stopping when the temperature is approximately zero.
assumptions_latex: c_k>0\text{ whenever the acceptance probability is evaluated}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i\text{ is updated by simulated-annealing transitions until }c_k\simeq0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-temperature limits of equilibrium objective statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains the mathematically consistent mean and variance limits. The entropy limits are excluded because they contradict the sign of the extracted definition of H_c.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varnothing\ne S be finite and let q_i(c)=\frac{e^{-f(i)/c}}{\sum_{j\in S}e^{-f(j)/c}}. Define \langle f\rangle_c=\sum_{i\in S}q_i(c)f(i) and \sigma_c^2=\sum_{i\in S}q_i(c)(f(i)-\langle f\rangle_c)^2. If f_{\mathrm{Opt}}=\min_{i\in S}f(i), then \lim_{c\to\infty}\langle f\rangle_c=\frac1{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}f(i), \lim_{c\to0^+}\langle f\rangle_c=f_{\mathrm{Opt}}, \lim_{c\to\infty}\sigma_c^2=\frac1{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}(f(i)-\langle f\rangle_\infty)^2, and \lim_{c\to0^+}\sigma_c^2=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At infinite temperature, the Gibbs distribution becomes uniform, so the objective mean and variance become their uniform-state values. At zero temperature, the mean reaches the global minimum and the variance vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}\lim_{c\to\infty}\langle f\rangle_c=\frac1{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}f(i),\qquad \lim_{c\to0^+}\langle f\rangle_c=f_{\mathrm{Opt}},\\\lim_{c\to\infty}\sigma_c^2=\frac1{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}(f(i)-\langle f\rangle_\infty)^2,\qquad \lim_{c\to0^+}\sigma_c^2=0.\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simulated annealing acceptance and cooling principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative method description; the extract does not provide hypotheses sufficient for a formal convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Simulated annealing samples a neighbor randomly. A neighbor with a better objective value replaces the incumbent with probability \(1\), whereas a worse neighbor is accepted with a probability strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). Slight deteriorations are accepted more readily than large deteriorations, and the probability of accepting worsening moves decreases over time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated annealing randomly samples a neighbor, always accepts an improvement, and may accept a worsening move. Smaller deteriorations are accepted more readily, while cooling makes worsening moves progressively less likely.
assumptions_latex: A solution space, objective value, and neighborhood relation are defined.
The acceptance mechanism assigns positive probability to worsening moves and reduces that probability over time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted worsening moves provide a mechanism for leaving local minima, while cooling increasingly favors nonworsening moves.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metropolis Acceptance Criterion for Simulated Annealing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance probability for a proposed transition in combinatorial simulated annealing; positivity of the temperature parameter is required for the stated probability rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S,f)\) be a combinatorial minimization problem, let \(i,j\in S\), and let \(c>0\). The criterion accepts a proposed move from \(i\) to \(j\) with probability \[\Pr\{\operatorname{accept}j\mid i\}=\begin{cases}1,&f(j)<f(i),\\ \exp\!\left(\dfrac{f(i)-f(j)}{c}\right),&f(j)\geq f(i).\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly improving proposal is always accepted. A nonimproving proposal is accepted with probability exp((f(i)-f(j))/c), where c is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\{\operatorname{accept}j\mid i\}=\begin{cases}1,&f(j)<f(i),\\ e^{(f(i)-f(j))/c},&f(j)\geq f(i).\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Temperature-dependent acceptance rule for minimization-form simulated annealing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a current solution $s$, candidate $s'\in\mathcal N(s)$, and temperature $T>0$, the Metropolis rule is \[p_{\mathrm{accept}}(s,s',T)=\begin{cases}1,&f(s')<f(s),\\ \exp\!\left(\dfrac{f(s)-f(s')}{T}\right),&f(s')\ge f(s).\end{cases}\] Thus improving candidates are accepted, equal-cost candidates are accepted with probability $1$, and strictly worse candidates have acceptance probability decreasing toward $0$ as $T$ decreases toward $0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, simulated annealing always accepts an improving or equal-cost neighbor. A strictly worse neighbor is accepted with probability exp((f(s)-f(s'))/T), which decreases as the positive temperature is lowered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{\mathrm{accept}}(s,s',T)=\begin{cases}1,&f(s')<f(s),\\ \exp((f(s)-f(s'))/T),&f(s')\ge f(s).\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current bitstring x_k, generate a candidate y_k by randomly flipping selected bits. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence in probability of simulated-annealing objective values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific convergence to the global maximum value under the proposal-density and cooling assumptions stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be generated by the stated simulated-annealing algorithm, and let \(f^*\) be the global maximum of \(f\) on \(S\). Suppose each proposal distribution \(R(x,\cdot)\) is absolutely continuous with density \(r(x,\cdot)\), the family of densities is uniformly bounded away from zero, and, for every starting point \(x_0\), the cooling schedule converges to zero in probability. Then, for every \(\epsilon>0\) and \(x_0\in S\), \[\Pr\!\left(f(X_n)<f^*-\epsilon\mid X_0=x_0\right)\longrightarrow 0.\] Thus \(f(X_n)\) converges in probability to \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the simulated-annealing proposal densities are uniformly bounded away from zero and the cooling schedule converges to zero in probability from every starting point, then the sampled objective values converge in probability to the global maximum value.
assumptions_latex: \{X_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\text{ is generated by the stated simulated-annealing algorithm on }S.
\forall x\in S,\;R(x,\cdot)\text{ is absolutely continuous with density }r(x,\cdot).
\text{The densities }r(x,\cdot)\text{ are uniformly bounded away from zero.
\forall x_0\in S,\quad T_n\xrightarrow{\Pr}0\text{ under the process initialized at }X_0=x_0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall \epsilon>0\;\forall x_0\in S,\quad \Pr\!\left(f(X_n)<f^*-\epsilon\mid X_0=x_0\right)\longrightarrow0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization form with a fixed number of trials per temperature and best-so-far output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial solution \(S\), an initial temperature \(T>0\), a reduction factor \(r\in(0,1)\), and a positive integer \(L\), repeat until the process is frozen: perform \(L\) trials in which a random neighbor \(S'\) is sampled and \(\Delta=f(S')-f(S)\) is computed; accept \(S'\) whenever \(\Delta\leq 0\), and when \(\Delta>0\), accept it with probability \(e^{-\Delta/T}\). After the trials, set \(T\leftarrow rT\). Return the best solution encountered.

Always accept a nonworsening neighbor and accept a worsening one with probability exp(-deterioration/temperature). Multiply the temperature by a factor between zero and one after each batch, stop when frozen, and return the best solution found.
assumptions_latex: A random-neighbor sampler and a freezing criterion are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The heuristic returns the best visited solution after Metropolis acceptance and geometric cooling \(T_{k+1}=rT_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i,j\in S\) at iteration \(k\), the simulated-annealing transition probabilities are \[P_{ij}(k)=P_{ij}(c_k)=\begin{cases}G_{ij}(c_k)A_{ij}(c_k),&i\ne j,\\1-\sum_{\ell\ne i}P_{i\ell}(c_k),&i=j,\end{cases}\] where \(G_{ij}(c_k)\) is the probability of generating \(j\) from \(i\), and \[A_{ij}(c_k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{(f(j)-f(i))^+}{c_k}\right),\qquad a^+=\begin{cases}a,&a>0,\\0,&a\le0.\end{cases}\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Metropolis-type acceptance rule, a standard additive proposal construction, the infinite-inverse-temperature boundary, and commonly used—but not required—kernel conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x_n\in A$, propose $z_n$ according to $Q_n(x_n,\cdot)$ and set $\Delta_n=f(z_n)-f(x_n)$. For finite $\beta_n\ge0$, accept $z_n$ with probability $p_n=\min\{1,\exp(-\beta_n\Delta_n)\}$: if $\Delta_n\le0$, then $p_n=1$, whereas if $\Delta_n>0$, then $p_n=\exp(-\beta_n\Delta_n)>0$. A standard construction sets $z_n=x_n+\xi_n$ and resamples $\xi_n$ until $z_n\in A$. In the limiting case $\beta_n=\infty$ for every $n$, strict uphill moves are rejected and the scheme becomes Markov monotonous search. Frequently used additional choices include symmetric transition densities and $q_n(x,z)\ge c>0$ for all $n$ and $x,z\in A$; for discrete $A$, the corresponding condition is $Q_n(x,z)\ge c>0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated annealing always accepts a non-worsening proposal and accepts a worsening proposal with probability equal to the exponential of minus the inverse-temperature parameter times the objective increase. Finite inverse temperature therefore gives worsening moves positive acceptance probability. A standard implementation adds a random perturbation and resamples when it is infeasible. Infinite inverse temperature gives monotone search. Symmetry and uniform positivity of the transition kernel are common additional choices, not defining requirements of the acceptance rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_n=\begin{cases}1,&\Delta_n\le0,\\e^{-\beta_n\Delta_n},&\Delta_n>0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary distribution under symmetric proposals and multiplicative acceptance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The stationary distribution is for the transition kernel frozen at the current positive temperature \(c_k\). OCR-corrupted indices in the hypotheses have been normalized without changing their mathematical direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each iteration \(k\) with \(c_k>0\), suppose: (G1) for all \(i,j\in S\), there are \(p\ge1\) and \(l_0=i,l_1,\ldots,l_p=j\) such that \(G_{l_r l_{r+1}}(c_k)>0\) for \(r=0,\ldots,p-1\); (G2) \(G_{ij}(c_k)=G_{ji}(c_k)\) for all \(i,j\in S\); (A1) \(A_{ij}(c_k)=1\) if \(f(i)\ge f(j)\), and \(0<A_{ij}(c_k)<1\) if \(f(i)<f(j)\); (A2) if \(f(i)\le f(j)\le f(h)\), then \(A_{ih}(c_k)=A_{ij}(c_k)A_{jh}(c_k)\); and (A3) if \(f(i)<f(j)\), then \(\lim_{c_k\to0^+}A_{ij}(c_k)=0\). Then the frozen kernel has a stationary distribution satisfying, for any \(i_{\mathrm{Opt}}\in S_{\mathrm{Opt}}\), \[q_i(c_k)=\frac{A_{i_{\mathrm{Opt}}i}(c_k)}{\sum_{j\in S}A_{i_{\mathrm{Opt}}j}(c_k)},\qquad i\in S.\] Moreover, \[\lim_{c_k\to0^+}q_i(c_k)=\frac{1}{|S_{\mathrm{Opt}}|}\kappa_{S_{\mathrm{Opt}}}(i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a connected symmetric proposal mechanism and an acceptance rule satisfying the stated acceptance, multiplicativity, and zero-temperature conditions, the transition kernel at each fixed temperature has a stationary distribution proportional to the acceptance probabilities from any optimal state. As temperature approaches zero, this distribution becomes uniform over the optimal states.
assumptions_latex: \forall i,j\in S\ \exists p\ge1,\ l_0=i,\ldots,l_p=j:\ G_{l_r l_{r+1}}(c_k)>0\ \forall r<p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i_{\mathrm{Opt}}\in S_{\mathrm{Opt}}:\quad q_i(c_k)=\frac{A_{i_{\mathrm{Opt}}i}(c_k)}{\sum_{j\in S}A_{i_{\mathrm{Opt}}j}(c_k)},\qquad \lim_{c_k\to0^+}q_i(c_k)=\frac{1}{|S_{\mathrm{Opt}}|}\kappa_{S_{\mathrm{Opt}}}(i).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generational Replacement Is Not Necessarily Elitist
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes synchronous replacement from elite preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under pure replacement \(P_{t+1}=O_t\), the current best value can increase because a best member of \(P_t\) need not occur in \(O_t\). Monotonicity of the current-population minimum therefore requires elitist survival or an external archive; it does not follow from generational organization alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whole-population replacement can lose the current best individual, so synchronous generations do not imply elitism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Current-population best values need not be nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.title: Generational Replacement Is Not Necessarily Elitist

assumptions_latex: The population size is a fixed integer \(N\ge1\).
Selection and variation define probability kernels on the population space \(X^N\).
Every generated individual is evaluated by the objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update defines a Markov chain on \(X^N\), and elitist survival makes the recorded best objective value nonincreasing across generations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous population replacement with optional elitism and a fixed evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(P_0\in X^N\) and evaluate all members. At generation \(t\), sample parents \(M_t\) from a selection kernel depending on the evaluated population, generate \(N\) offspring \(O_t\) through a variation kernel, and evaluate them. A generational replacement rule sets \(P_{t+1}=O_t\); an elitist rule instead applies a survivor kernel to \(P_t\cup O_t\) while retaining at least one current best individual. Stop after a prescribed number of generations or evaluations and output the best individual ever evaluated. Conditional on \(P_t\), the selection, variation, and replacement kernels determine the distribution of \(P_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select parents, generate and evaluate an entire offspring population, then replace the current generation; elitism preserves the best value found.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential greedy replacement for minimization using current and perturbed populations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(P\ge 1\), a current population \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\), and a perturbed population \(\mathbf Y=(\mathbf y_1,\ldots,\mathbf y_P)\), process \(p=1,\ldots,P\) sequentially. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population-based evolutionary search using fitness evaluation, selection, variation, replacement, and a quality- or resource-based stopping condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a quality function $f$ on a candidate domain $X$ to be maximized, an evolutionary algorithm begins with a randomly generated population of candidates and evaluates their fitness. It repeatedly selects parents using fitness, produces offspring through recombination of two or more parents and/or mutation of individual candidates, evaluates the offspring, and selects candidates from the new and possibly old populations for the next generation, potentially using age as well as fitness. It terminates when a candidate of sufficient quality is found or a prescribed computational limit is reached. Selection, recombination, and mutation are typically stochastic, so selection need not deterministically retain only the best candidates. Variation supplies diversity and selection tends to increase population quality, but improvement in every generation is not guaranteed.

It stops when sufficient quality or a computational limit is reached. Its selection and variation steps are typically stochastic, and population fitness is not guaranteed to improve in every generation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded description of the basic differential-evolution generation, its parameters, and its standard designation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_\mu\rangle\subset\mathbb{R}^n. For each i, randomly select a base vector b_i and two other population vectors y_i,z_i, and form v_i=b_i+F(y_i-z_i), where F>0. Form u_i by coordinatewise uniform crossover between v_i and x_i with crossover probability Cr\in[0,1], forcing at least one coordinate to be inherited from v_i. For minimization, set x_i^+=u_i when f(u_i)\leq f(x_i), and set x_i^+=x_i otherwise. This basic scheme is denoted \mathrm{DE/rand/1/bin}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each member of a real-vector population, basic differential evolution randomly selects a base vector and two other population vectors, adds a positively scaled difference of the latter two to the base, crosses the resulting mutant with the current member while forcing at least one coordinate to originate from the mutant, and retains the trial when it is no worse than the current member. Its parameters are the population size, scaling factor, and crossover probability, and the scheme is called DE/rand/1/bin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_i=b_i+F(y_i-z_i),\qquad x_i^+=\begin{cases}u_i,&f(u_i)\leq f(x_i),\\x_i,&f(u_i)>f(x_i),\end{cases}\quad\text{with at least one coordinate of }u_i\text{ inherited from }v_i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A differential-evolution population update for objective minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\in(0,2)\), \(CR\in(0,1)\), \(P\ge4\), and \(n\ge1\). For each target index \(i\), choose \(\bar i\) uniformly from \(\{1,ldots,n\}\) and choose distinct \(k_1,k_2,k_3\in\{1,ldots,P\}\setminus\{i\}\). Form \(\mathbf t=mathbf x_{k_1}+F(\mathbf x_{k_2}-mathbf x_{k_3})\). For each \(j\ne\bar i\), restore \(t^{(j)}=x_i^{(j)}\) when a draw from \(\mathcal U(0,1)\) exceeds \(CR\); coordinate \(\bar i\) remains from the donor vector. If \(f(\mathbf t)<f(\mathbf x_i)\), set \(\mathbf x_i\leftarrow\mathbf t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each target, create a donor from one population vector plus a scaled difference of two others. Coordinate crossover retains at least one donor coordinate, and the trial replaces the target only under strict objective improvement.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ge4\), permitting three distinct indices different from the target index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each target vector is replaced exactly when its differential-mutation and crossover trial has strictly smaller objective value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded real-vector initialization and the defining scaled-difference offspring mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For population size k\geq4 and dimension D, initialize x_{ij}=x_j^{lo}+R_j(x_j^{hi}-x_j^{lo}) for i\in\{1,\ldots,k\} and j\in\{1,\ldots,D\}, where each indicated R_j is uniformly distributed on [0,1]. Given parent i and selected population members r_1,r_2,r_3, use F\in[0,1] and CR\in[0,1]. For coordinate j, use x_{r_3j}+F(x_{r_1j}-x_{r_2j}) when the crossover draw is below CR or j=j_{\mathrm{rand}}; otherwise inherit x_{ij}. The forced coordinate j_{\mathrm{rand}} ensures that at least one coordinate uses the difference-based construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differential evolution uniformly initializes bounded real vectors. It constructs offspring coordinates from a base vector plus a scaled difference of two population vectors when crossover succeeds, while other coordinates inherit from the parent; one forced coordinate always uses the difference-based construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists j\in\{1,\ldots,D\}\text{ such that the offspring coordinate is generated by }x_{r_3j}+F(x_{r_1j}-x_{r_2j}).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization by individual space, evaluation map, variation operators, population update, selection rule, termination criterion, and population-size restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evolutionary algorithm \(EA=(I,\Phi,\Omega,\Psi,s,\iota,\mu,\lambda)\) is called an evolution strategy if and only if: (i) \(I=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^{n_\sigma}\times[-\pi,\pi]^{n_\alpha}\), where \(n_\sigma\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(n_\alpha\in\{0,(2n-n_\sigma)(n_\sigma-1)/2\}\); (ii) \(\Phi=f\); (iii) \(\Omega\) contains the specified mutation maps \(m_{\{\tau,\tau',\beta\}}:I^\lambda\to I^\lambda\) and recombination maps \(r_{r_xr_\sigma r_\alpha}:I^\mu\to I^\lambda\); (iv) \(\Psi(P)=s\bigl(Q\cup m(r(P))\bigr)\), with \(Q=\varnothing\) for \((\mu,\lambda)\)-selection and \(Q=P\) for \((\mu+\lambda)\)-selection; (v) \(s\in\{s_{(\mu+\lambda)},s_{(\mu,\lambda)}\}\); (vi) a termination criterion \(\iota\) is specified; and (vii) if \(s=s_{(\mu,\lambda)}\), then \(1\leq\mu\leq\lambda\), whereas plus selection imposes no special restriction on the relation between \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evolutionary algorithm is an evolution strategy exactly when its individuals combine real decision variables with positive mutation scales and an allowed number of rotation parameters, its evaluation is the objective function, its variation uses the specified recombination and mutation operators, and its update applies comma or plus selection with a termination criterion. Comma selection requires 1 ≤ mu ≤ lambda; plus selection imposes no special relation between the population sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: EA\text{ is an evolution strategy}\iff\text{conditions (i)--(vii) hold.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generational evolution strategy using strategy parameters and either comma or plus selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(t:=0\) and \(P(0)=\{a_1(0),\ldots,a_\mu(0)\}\in I^\mu\), where \(I=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^{n_\sigma}\times[-\pi,\pi]^{n_\alpha}\), and each individual contains decision variables \(x\), mutation scales \(\sigma\), and, when present, rotation parameters \(\alpha\). Evaluate each individual by \(\Phi(a_k)=f(x_k)\). While \(\iota(P(t))\ne\mathrm{true}\), generate \(\lambda\) recombinants \(\widetilde a'_k(t):=r'(P(t))\), mutate them as \(\widetilde a''_k(t):=m'_{\{\tau,\tau',\beta\}}(\widetilde a'_k(t))\), evaluate the resulting offspring population \(P''(t)\), and set \(P(t+1):=s_{(\mu,\lambda)}(P''(t))\) under comma selection or \(P(t+1):=s_{(\mu+\lambda)}(P(t)\cup P''(t))\) under plus selection; then set \(t:=t+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize and evaluate a population of mu individuals containing real decision variables, positive mutation scales, and optionally rotation parameters. Until the termination criterion holds, produce lambda recombined offspring, mutate and evaluate them, and form the next population either from offspring alone under comma selection or from parents and offspring under plus selection.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi(a)=f(x)\) for the decision component \(x\) of individual \(a\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(t+1)=\begin{cases}s_{(\mu,\lambda)}(P''(t)),&\text{under comma selection},\\s_{(\mu+\lambda)}(P(t)\cup P''(t)),&\text{under plus selection}.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Architecture and variants of evolution strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic architecture of single-parent and population evolution strategies, including self-adaptation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evolution strategies represent candidate solutions by vectors \(\bar{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and use Gaussian mutation with mean zero and mutation step size \(\sigma\). In a \((1+1)\)-ES, one offspring is generated from one parent and accepted if fitter; in a \((1,1)\)-ES, the offspring always replaces the parent. Multi-member variants use \(\mu\) population members and generate \(\lambda\) offspring per cycle, with \((\mu+\lambda)\) or \((\mu,\lambda)\) survivor selection. In a self-adaptive ES, chromosomes have the form \(\langle\bar{x},\bar{p}\rangle\), where \(\bar{p}\) contains strategy parameters that coevolve with the candidate solution; mutation step sizes, and sometimes rotation angles, are adapted this way.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evolution strategies operate on real-valued vectors using zero-mean Gaussian mutation. A one-plus-one strategy retains an offspring when it is fitter, whereas a one-comma-one strategy always replaces the parent. Population variants use mu members and lambda offspring with plus or comma replacement. Self-adaptive variants encode strategy parameters with the solution so that they coevolve, especially mutation step sizes and sometimes rotation angles.
assumptions_latex: \text{Mutation increments are independently drawn from zero-mean Gaussian distributions with step size }\sigma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{ES applies Gaussian variation and plus- or comma-style replacement, with self-adaptive variants coevolving }\bar{p}\text{ and }\bar{x}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the characteristic structure of evolutionary programming while distinguishing its historical and representative modern forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evolutionary programming (EP) is an evolutionary-search family without recombination. In its characteristic population scheme, each of the \(\mu\) parents produces exactly one offspring by mutation, so \(\lambda=\mu\); the \(\mu\) parents and \(\mu\) offspring are then merged and compete for survival through stochastic round-robin tournaments. Classical EP represented individuals by finite-state machines, whereas modern EP frequently uses real-valued vectors with Gaussian mutation and may self-adapt mutation step sizes. These modern choices are representative rather than mandatory: representation and mutation are selected according to the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evolutionary programming is an evolutionary-search family that uses mutation but no recombination. Each of mu parents produces one offspring, so lambda equals mu, and the combined parent-offspring population undergoes stochastic round-robin survivor selection. Classical EP used finite-state machines; modern EP often uses real vectors, Gaussian mutation, and sometimes self-adaptive step sizes, but these choices are representative rather than required.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each parent generates exactly one offspring by mutation, hence }\lambda=\mu.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{EP uses no recombination and selects survivors stochastically from the merged }(\mu+\mu)\text{ population; its representation and mutation operator are problem-dependent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the usual evolutionary-programming representation and generational procedure; individual implementations may adapt the operators to the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evolutionary programming searches over a population of candidate solutions while emphasizing phenotypic behavior rather than genotypic encoding. Typically, each selected parent produces a mutated child, the offspring count equals the parent count, and the best half of the combined parent--offspring population is retained. Self-adaptive variants also evolve mutation-strategy parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evolutionary programming is a population-based evolutionary paradigm centered on observable behavior. It typically selects parents by tournament, generates one mutated child per parent without relying on sexual recombination, ranks the combined parent and child population, retains the best half, and may evolve its own mutation-strategy parameters.
assumptions_latex: \text{A population of candidate solutions and a fitness-based ranking are available.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Search proceeds primarily through mutation and survivor selection in phenotype space, optionally with self-adaptation.}

assumptions_latex: \text{An environment or objective, fitness rule, random mutation rule, survivor-selection rule, and stopping condition are specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{t+1}=\operatorname{Select}\!\left(P_t\cup\operatorname{Mutate}(P_t)\right)\quad\text{after evaluation of the candidate pool.}

children.title: Population Diversity Control
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms preserving exploratory variation within a search population.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A checkable survivor operator enforcing minimum metric separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order a finite evaluated candidate pool by nondecreasing objective value with deterministic tie breaking. Scan in that order and accept \(x\) only if \(\rho(x,z)>r\) for every previously accepted survivor \(z\), stopping at the survivor capacity. The accepted set is pairwise more than \(r\) apart and contains the best-ranked candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy survivor selection retains the best candidate and rejects later candidates lying within a chosen radius of an accepted survivor.
assumptions_latex: The candidate pool is finite and totally ordered by fitness and tie breaking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted survivors are pairwise separated by more than \(r\), and the first-ranked candidate is retained.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Distance-Separated Survivor Selection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diversity Alone Does Not Ensure Global Exploration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates population spread from reachability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive within-population diversity statistic does not imply access to every region of \(X\). A transition can preserve pairwise separation while keeping all members in a strict suboptimal invariant subset \(S\subset X\). Hence diversity control alone implies neither irreducibility nor global convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A population can remain diverse inside a suboptimal invariant region, so diversity is not a substitute for global reachability.
assumptions_latex: A strict suboptimal subset \(S\) is closed under the population transition.
The diversity requirement is feasible within \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diversity requirement can hold indefinitely without reaching a global minimizer outside \(S\).
knowledge_statements.title: Diversity Alone Does Not Ensure Global Exploration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct metric-space summaries used by diversity controls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) in \((X,\rho)\), define \[\delta_{\min}(P)=\min_{i<j}\rho(x_i,x_j),\quad \Delta(P)=\frac{2}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i<j}\rho(x_i,x_j),\quad R(P)=\max_i\rho(x_i,c(P)).\] These statistics are generally inequivalent; for example, duplicate points and one distant outlier can give \(\delta_{\min}(P)=0\) while \(R(P)\) is large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum separation, mean pairwise distance, and radius measure different aspects of diversity and are not interchangeable.
assumptions_latex: The center rule \(c(P)\) is declared when radius is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed statistics are well-defined and generally inequivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Common Population-Diversity Statistics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Packing Feasibility of a Separation Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility test for a minimum-distance population constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a metric space (X,\rho) and r\ge0, define M_r(X)=\sup\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \rho(x,z)>r\text{ for all distinct }x,z\in S\}. A population of N members satisfying \delta_{\min}(P)>r exists if and only if N\le M_r(X). Consequently, no enforcement operator can guarantee such a population when N>M_r(X).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-separation threshold is feasible exactly when the domain's packing number at that radius is at least the requested population size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists P\in X^N:\delta_{\min}(P)>r\iff N\le M_r(X).

notation.meaning: maximum attainable cardinality of an r-separated subset

knowledge_statements.title: Packing Feasibility of a Separation Threshold

assumptions_latex: The population is \(P=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\in X^N\) in a metric space \((X,\rho)\).
A diversity statistic and admissible range are fixed before the update.
The control operator can reject, repair, or replace candidates without altering already recorded evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted population satisfies the prescribed diversity constraint, while any elitist implementation can simultaneously retain a best-so-far individual.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A checkable pairwise-distance diversity constraint with rejection or repair enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(N\ge2\), define the mean pairwise diversity \(\Delta(P)=\frac{2}{N(N-1)}\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\rho(x_i,x_j)\). At iteration \(t\), a population satisfies the diversity-control condition when \(\Delta(P_t)\ge\delta_t\), where \(\delta_t\) is a prescribed nonnegative threshold. Given a proposed population \(P'_t\), accept it only if the condition holds; otherwise apply a specified repair or replacement operator until the inequality holds or a declared failure limit is reached. An elitist repair must retain at least one member attaining the best objective value previously recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Require population mean pairwise distance to exceed a chosen threshold, repairing or rejecting populations that violate it while optionally preserving an elite.
knowledge_statements.title: Population Diversity Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. A prescribed threshold can be infeasible for the metric space and population size, so repair need not produce an accepted population; the conclusion needs an explicit feasibility or conditional-success hypothesis. The record also mixes a diversity condition with an enforcement algorithm, making the selected condition kind only partially aligned.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fine-grained spatial population structure with neighborhood-restricted reproduction and replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cellular evolutionary algorithm places one population member at each node of a spatial structure, commonly a toroidal grid, and defines a local deme or neighborhood for every node. In the outlined generational procedure, each deme selects two local parents, generates an offspring by recombination, mutates and evaluates it, and selects a resident of the deme for replacement. Restricting mating and survival competition to neighborhoods causes genetic information to spread gradually through the population. Implementations may vary in topology, synchronous or asynchronous updating, parent selection, local improvement, and replacement policy. Analyses cited in the extract found that local versions of selection schemes generally exerted less selection pressure than their global counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cellular evolutionary algorithm spatially places individuals and restricts parent selection and replacement to local neighborhoods. Each neighborhood produces, mutates, and evaluates offspring and replaces a local resident, so genetic information spreads gradually. Implementations may use different topologies and update rules.
assumptions_latex: \text{One individual occupies each node of a specified spatial topology.}
\text{Each node has a defined local deme.}
\text{Local parent-selection, recombination, mutation, evaluation, and replacement rules are specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Neighborhood-restricted reproduction and replacement produce gradual spatial diffusion through the population.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phenotype-, genotype-, or tag-based restrictions on reproductive opportunities in evolutionary populations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Automatic speciation distinguishes multiple species within a population and restricts recombination so that a selected parent may mate only with members of the same or a sufficiently similar species. Species may be determined from phenotype or genotype information, or from additional heritable genotype tags that encode species rather than solution components. Mate selection uses an appropriate pairwise distance, rejecting candidates beyond a prescribed threshold. In tag-based schemes, similar tags need not initially correspond to similar solutions, and different species need not contain different solutions. Phenotype-based restricted mating also does not by itself guarantee diversity maintenance, although either approach may be combined with fitness sharing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Automatic speciation restricts mating to the same or a sufficiently similar species, using phenotype or genotype distances or separate heritable species tags. Similar tags need not represent similar solutions, different species need not contain different solutions, and restricted mating alone does not guarantee diversity.
assumptions_latex: \text{A phenotype-, genotype-, or tag-based species descriptor and corresponding pairwise distance are available.}
\text{A mating-distance threshold or equivalent same-species rule is specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Mating is restricted by species similarity, but neither solution distinctness nor diversity preservation is guaranteed.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population replacement combining nearest-neighbor competition with a dissimilarity threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(P\ge1\), \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\), \(\mathbf Y=(\mathbf y_1,\ldots,\mathbf y_P)\), and \(D_{\mathrm{cut}}\ge0\), process \(p=1,ldots,P\) sequentially. Choose \(c\in\arg\min_{1\le i\le P}d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf y_p)\). If \(d(\mathbf x_c,\mathbf y_p)>D_{\mathrm{cut}}\), choose instead \(c\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le P}f(\mathbf x_i)\). Replace \(\mathbf x_c\) by \(\mathbf y_p\) if and only if \(f(\mathbf y_p)<f(\mathbf x_c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed point competes with its nearest population member when it lies within the threshold; otherwise it competes with a currently worst member. It replaces that member only under strict objective improvement.
assumptions_latex: The distance \(d\) and objective \(f\) are defined at all processed points, and \(f\) is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequentially modified \(\mathbf X\) is the threshold-dependent selection \(\operatorname{Select}(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Similarity-based parent-offspring competition for preserving niches in evolutionary search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Deterministic crowding randomly pairs parents \(p_1,p_2\), generates two offspring \(o_1,o_2\) by recombination, mutates and evaluates them, and computes the four parent-offspring distances. It chooses the two parent-offspring tournament pairings that minimize total intercompetition distance. Thus the direct pairing is selected when
\[
d(p_1,o_1)+d(p_2,o_2)<d(p_1,o_2)+d(p_2,o_1),
\]
while the crossed pairing is selected when its total distance is smaller; the extract does not prescribe a tie rule. Each offspring then competes for survival with its assigned parent. This similarity-based competition tends to preserve niche subpopulations, whose sizes, in the idealized account, are distributed evenly among available peaks rather than proportionally to peak fitness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic crowding pairs parents, produces and evaluates two offspring, and assigns offspring to parents by minimizing the total parent-offspring distance. Each offspring competes with its assigned similar parent, tending to preserve niches. The source does not specify how equal-distance ties are resolved.
assumptions_latex: p_1,p_2\text{ form a randomly selected parent pair}
o_1,o_2\text{ are their recombined, mutated, and evaluated offspring}
d\text{ is the chosen parent-offspring distance}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The tournament assignment minimizes total parent-offspring distance and thereby tends to preserve niche subpopulations.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of spaces and mechanisms used to preserve diversity in evolutionary populations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evolutionary algorithm may be viewed in three spaces: genotype space, consisting of representable solutions with distances induced by a metric or elementary move; phenotype space, consisting of realized solutions with solution-level distances, whose neighborhood structure may differ substantially from that of genotype space; and algorithmic space, describing the spatial organization of the population in working memory. Explicit diversity-maintenance approaches modify operators or selection distributions using genotype- or phenotype-space measures and include fitness sharing, crowding, and speciation. Implicit approaches structure algorithmic space and include island-model and cellular evolutionary algorithms; they permit but do not guarantee preservation of diverse solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evolutionary algorithms can be described using genotype, phenotype, and algorithmic spaces. Explicit diversity methods use genotype or phenotype relationships, whereas implicit methods spatially structure the population but do not guarantee preserved diversity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Diversity-maintenance approaches divide broadly into explicit genotype/phenotype-based mechanisms and implicit algorithmic-space structures, without a diversity guarantee for the latter.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dissimilarity-Based PBH Selection with Population Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-controlled population updating that can append sufficiently dissimilar improving candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current population \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\), candidates \(Y\), and \(D_{\mathrm{cut}}\ge0\), process each \(\mathbf y\in Y\) using the current value of \(P\). Choose \(c\in\arg\min_{1\le i\le P}d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf y)\). If \(d(\mathbf x_c,\mathbf y)>D_{\mathrm{cut}}\), choose \(c\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le P}f(\mathbf x_i)\); when \(f(\mathbf y)<f(\mathbf x_c)\), set \(P\leftarrow P+1\) and append \(\mathbf x_P=mathbf y\). Otherwise, if the nearest member is within the threshold and \(f(\mathbf y)<f(\mathbf x_c)\), replace \(\mathbf x_c\leftarrow\mathbf y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearby improving candidate replaces its nearest member. A candidate beyond the threshold is appended, rather than substituted, when it improves on the current worst objective value.
assumptions_latex: The initial population size satisfies \(P\ge1\) and may increase during processing.
The distance \(d\) and objective \(f\) are defined at all processed points, and \(f\) is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update combines local replacement with conditional population growth for sufficiently dissimilar candidates.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a pool containing locally optimized offspring and unchanged parents, order candidates by increasing energy. Traverse the ordered pool and admit a candidate to the next fixed-size generation when its geometry is sufficiently distinct from previously selected candidates, thereby opening a dynamic niche. A geometrically similar candidate may also be admitted while the niche remains below its capacity and its energy is sufficiently separated from existing niche members. Reserve a niche for mutants to maintain exploration, and continue until the population is full. Niches exist only during selection, may change between generations, and are determined by prescribed geometry-dependent widths and capacity limits rather than by a fixed number of niches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order the pool of locally optimized offspring and unchanged parents by increasing energy. Select candidates into the next fixed-size generation using geometry-based dynamic niches. A distinct candidate opens a niche; a similar candidate is accepted only while that niche has capacity and its energy is sufficiently separated from those already admitted. A reserved mutant niche maintains some exploration. The niches exist only during selection, their number can vary between generations, and their criteria depend on the cluster class.
assumptions_latex: \text{A finite candidate pool of locally optimized cluster geometries and their energies is available.}
\text{Geometric-similarity criteria, niche widths, niche capacities, and an energy-separation threshold are specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The selection mechanism produces a fixed-size population with explicit geometric-diversity controls, but it supplies neither a global-optimality guarantee nor a reliable stopping certificate.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based fitness adjustment for maintaining multiple niches in an evolutionary population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each population member \(i\), fitness sharing defines
\[
F'(i)=\frac{F(i)}{\sum_j \operatorname{sh}(d(i,j))},\qquad
\operatorname{sh}(d)=\begin{cases}1-(d/\sigma_{\mathrm{share}})^\alpha,&d\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{share}},\\0,&d>\sigma_{\mathrm{share}},\end{cases}
\]
where the sum includes \(j=i\), \(d\) is preferably a phenotypic distance and otherwise may be genotypic, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{share}}\) is the sharing radius, and \(\alpha\) controls the sharing-function shape. For \(\alpha=1\) the function is linear; for \(\alpha>1\), the fitness-reducing effect of similar individuals falls off more rapidly with distance. Under fitness-proportionate selection, if all solutions within niche \(k\) coincide and the niches have equal effective fitness, then \(F'_k=F_k/n_k\) and the stable niche sizes satisfy \(n_k\propto F_k\). Alternative selection methods need not form and preserve such stable niche subpopulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fitness sharing divides an individual's fitness by the total sharing weight of population members within a prescribed radius, including itself. Under fitness-proportionate selection and the stated idealized niche assumptions, stable niche size is proportional to niche fitness; this stability need not hold with other selection methods.
assumptions_latex: d(i,j)\text{ is a selected phenotype- or genotype-space distance}
\text{For the stable-distribution conclusion, selection is fitness-proportionate, members of each niche coincide, and niches have equal effective fitness.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(i)=\frac{F(i)}{\sum_j\operatorname{sh}(d(i,j))};\qquad \text{under the stated stability assumptions, }n_k\propto F_k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse-grained population structure with periodic migration among separately evolving subpopulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An island-model evolutionary algorithm evolves multiple subpopulations connected by a communication graph, whether concurrently or through a sequential implementation. After an epoch, selected individuals are exchanged with neighboring islands by moving or copying them; copied migrants require survivor selection if subpopulation sizes are to remain fixed. Epoch length, migrant count, migrant-selection policy, topology, and subpopulation size affect mixing. Communication that is too frequent can cause the subpopulations to converge to the same solution, whereas communication that is too infrequent can waste computation after an island has converged near a peak. Larger exchanges and fitness-based migrant selection can accelerate mixing or takeover. Islands may use different parameters or operators, but the model does not itself guarantee that different subpopulations explore different search regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An island-model evolutionary algorithm evolves several populations connected by a communication graph and periodically migrates selected individuals between neighboring islands. Migration choices control mixing and takeover, and separate exploration by the islands is not guaranteed. The model can also be run sequentially, without parallel speedup.
assumptions_latex: \text{The population is divided into multiple evolving subpopulations.}
\text{A communication graph, epoch rule, migration count, migrant-selection rule, and move-or-copy policy are specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Periodic migration couples the island populations, permitting but not guaranteeing exploration of different search regions.}

children.title: Selection-Pressure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior associated with weak, balanced, or aggressive population selection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Premature-convergence boundary when nonbest parents receive zero probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If selection assigns zero probability to every nonbest candidate and variation from current best candidates is confined to a strict reachable subset, then a global minimizer outside that subset has zero discovery probability. Increasing selection pressure is therefore not necessarily a monotone improvement in global-search reliability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting only current best candidates can eliminate material needed to reach better basins when variation lacks independent global support.
assumptions_latex: Nonbest candidates receive zero parent-selection probability.
Variation from current best candidates is confined to a strict reachable subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global minimizer outside that subset cannot be discovered.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Pressure Can Destroy Exploration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Pressure Is Invariant to Objective-Gap Magnitude
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes rank-based from magnitude-sensitive selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed ranks, tournament-selection probabilities are unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of objective values. Thus tournament pressure cannot distinguish populations with identical rankings but different objective gaps, whereas magnitude-based rules generally can.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tournament selection responds to ranks, not to the sizes of objective gaps.
assumptions_latex: The transformation preserves the candidates' total rank order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tournament-selection probabilities are unchanged when only objective-gap magnitudes change.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Pressure Is Invariant to Objective-Gap Magnitude

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-based pressure parameterization for tournaments sampled with replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rank \(N\) candidates from best to worst. Draw \(k\ge1\) ranks independently and uniformly with replacement and select the best sampled rank. Then \[p_r(k)=\left(\frac{N-r+1}{N}\right)^k-\left(\frac{N-r}{N}\right)^k.\] Thus \(k=1\) is uniform selection, while the best-rank probability \(1-(1-1/N)^k\) increases with \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tournament size parameterizes rank pressure: size one is uniform, and larger tournaments increasingly favor better ranks.
assumptions_latex: \(N\ge1\) candidates have a deterministic total rank order.
Tournament draws are independent, uniform, and with replacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formula gives the rank-selection probabilities, and the best-rank probability is nondecreasing in \(k\).
knowledge_statements.title: Tournament-Selection Pressure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent comparison of rank-based parent-selection pressure; informal regime labels still require a declared family or threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rank \(N\) candidates from best to worst, and let \(p_r^A\) and \(p_r^B\) be their parent-selection probabilities under rules \(A\) and \(B\). Rule \(A\) has at least as much rank-selection pressure as \(B\) when \[\sum_{r=1}^{m}p_r^A\geq\sum_{r=1}^{m}p_r^B\qquad(m=1,\ldots,N).\] Dominance is strict if at least one inequality is strict. Uniform rank selection is a neutral reference, deterministic selection of rank one is maximal in this order, and rules unrelated by these inequalities have incomparable rank-pressure profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-based rule exerts greater selection pressure when it assigns at least as much probability to every top-ranked prefix.
assumptions_latex: The population has \(N\geq1\) candidates with a deterministic total rank order.
Each rule defines a probability distribution over ranks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cumulative-prefix inequalities define a partial order of rank-selection pressure; best-only selection is maximal, while some rules are incomparable.

notation.meaning: Probability that rule A selects rank r

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Distribution Ordering of Selection Pressure

assumptions_latex: A population contains candidates with finite objective values \(f_1,ldots,f_N\).
Parent selection uses Boltzmann weights with inverse-selection parameter \(\beta\ge0\).
All candidates with finite objective values receive positive selection probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\beta=0\) selection is uniform; finite \(\beta>0\) gives soft selection; and \(\beta\to\infty\) concentrates probability on the current minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boltzmann selection provides a precise weak-to-strong pressure parameterization for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For objective values \(f_1,ldots,f_N\), define \(p_i(\beta)=\exp(-\beta f_i)/\sum_{j=1}^N\exp(-\beta f_j)\). The selection-pressure ratio between candidates \(i\) and \(j\) is \(p_i(\beta)/p_j(\beta)=\exp(\beta(f_j-f_i))\). The regime \(\beta=0\) is neutral selection, since \(p_i(0)=1/N\). Finite \(\beta>0\) is soft fitness-biased selection, with every candidate retaining positive probability. As \(\beta\to\infty\), total probability concentrates uniformly on the indices attaining \(\min_j f_j\), defining the limiting maximal-pressure regime. Thus increasing \(\beta\) monotonically amplifies every fixed favorable objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boltzmann selection ranges from uniform sampling at zero pressure to concentration on current best candidates as inverse temperature grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Pressure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for choosing Boltzmann selection as the representation of this regime leaf. Both the assumptions and statement contain malformed LaTeX, writing `ldots` instead of \(\ldots\). Because the record parameterizes and characterizes regimes rather than imposing a condition, representation or property is a better exact kind than condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Takeover Time as a Measure of Selection Pressure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines takeover time and records the two mechanism-specific expressions stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The takeover time \(\tau^*\) of a selection mechanism is the number of generations required for repeated application of selection to fill the population with copies of the best individual, starting with one copy. The stated expression involving \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\) is \(\tau^*=\frac{\ln\lambda}{\ln(\lambda/\mu)}\). For fitness-proportional selection in a genetic algorithm, the stated expression is \(\tau^*=\lambda\ln\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The takeover time of a selection mechanism is the number of generations needed for selection to fill the population with copies of the best individual when there is initially one copy. The extract gives ln(lambda) divided by ln(lambda/mu) for the mu-lambda setting and lambda times ln(lambda) for fitness-proportional selection in a genetic algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \text{Initially, the population contains one copy of the best individual.}
\text{The first expression concerns the stated }(\mu,\lambda)\text{ selection setting.}
\text{The second expression concerns fitness-proportional selection in a genetic algorithm.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau^*=\frac{\ln\lambda}{\ln(\lambda/\mu)}\quad\text{or, for the stated fitness-proportional case,}\quad\tau^*=\lambda\ln\lambda.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rank-based parent-selection rule used for large genetic-programming populations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rank a population of size N and partition it into the top x\% and the remaining (100-x)\%. Draw 80\% of parent selections from the top group and 20\% from the remaining group. Choose x empirically as a function of N so that the favored group remains in the low hundreds; under this rule, selection pressure increases markedly as N grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over-selection ranks the population, places the top x percent in one group and the rest in another, and takes 80 percent of parent selections from the top group and 20 percent from the other. The value of x is chosen empirically so the favored group remains in the low hundreds as population size grows, causing selection pressure to increase for larger populations.
assumptions_latex: x=x(N)\text{ is chosen empirically so that }xN/100\text{ remains in the low hundreds.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\text{parent from top }x\%)=0.8,\qquad \Pr(\text{parent from remainder})=0.2,\quad\text{with selection pressure increasing as }N\text{ grows under the stated choice of }x.

children.title: Particle Swarm Optimization
children.top_down_role: Particle-swarm algorithms using velocity updates driven by personal-best and swarm-best positions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extracted global-best PSO template for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Randomly initialize particle positions and velocities. For a minimization problem, repeatedly evaluate the particles and, for every particle \(i\), update \[v_i(t)=v_i(t-1)+\rho_1\bigl(p_i-x_i(t-1)\bigr)+\rho_2\bigl(p_g-x_i(t-1)\bigr),\qquad x_i(t)=x_i(t-1)+v_i(t),\] where \(p_i\) is particle \(i\)'s best recorded position and \(p_g\) is the swarm's best recorded position. Replace a personal-best or global-best record when the corresponding new objective value is smaller. Continue until the stopping criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly initialize particle positions and velocities. At each iteration, update every velocity using attraction toward the particle's personal-best position and the swarm's global-best position, move the particle, evaluate it, and replace best records when the objective decreases. Continue until the stopping criterion.
assumptions_latex: \rho_1,\rho_2\ \text{are the attraction coefficients appearing in the extracted update.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Particle positions are iteratively moved using personal-best and global-best information until termination.}
