source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

children.title: Feasible-Geometry Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for equality-dominated and ill-conditioned feasible geometry.

children.title: Thin Feasible Regions
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets occupying very small volume within the surrounding search domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Thin Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible sets whose ambient thickness is zero or uniformly small relative to the search scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). The feasible region is ambiently thin if \(C\) has empty interior in \(X\); equivalently, no relative open ball of positive radius is contained in \(C\). A quantitative \(\varepsilon\)-thin regime occurs when the inradius \(\rho(C;X)=\sup\{r\ge0:\exists x\in C,\ B(x,r)\cap X\subseteq C\}\) satisfies \(\rho(C;X)\le\varepsilon\). Empty-interior sets have \(\rho(C;X)=0\), while narrow full-dimensional corridors may have positive but small inradius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible region is thin when it contains no ambient open ball, or quantitatively when its largest contained ball is small relative to the search scale.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) carries the relative Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_X(C)=\varnothing\Longrightarrow\rho(C;X)=0\).

notation.meaning: Relative inradius of the feasible set.
Euclidean ball of center x and radius r.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological Thinness Does Not Imply Small Volume
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating empty interior from measure-zero or low-volume feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a compact set \(C\subset[0,1]\) with empty relative interior and positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, the Smith--Volterra--Cantor set satisfies \(\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]}(C)=\varnothing\) and \(\lambda_1(C)=\tfrac12\). Thus empty relative interior, equivalently zero relative inradius for this compact set, does not imply zero ambient measure or zero probability under every absolutely continuous sampling law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible set may have empty interior and zero inradius while retaining positive volume; the Smith–Volterra–Cantor set is a standard example.
assumptions_latex: Thinness is interpreted as empty relative interior in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]}(C)=\varnothing\not\Longrightarrow\lambda_1(C)=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Thinness Does Not Imply Small Volume

children.title: Degenerate Feasible Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-set geometry lacking robust local dimension or conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Feasible Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local constraint geometry with dependent active gradients and failure of the linear independence constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m;\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), where all constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in C\). Let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The feasible geometry is LICQ-degenerate at \(\bar x\) when the family \(\{\nabla g_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\cup\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):j=1,\ldots,p\}\) is linearly dependent. This includes redundant active constraints and vanishing active gradients. In this regime, LICQ-based existence or uniqueness guarantees for local multiplier representations are unavailable, although a particular problem may still have unique multipliers for other reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible geometry is LICQ-degenerate when the gradients of active inequalities and equalities are linearly dependent at a feasible point; consequently, LICQ-based multiplier guarantees do not apply.
assumptions_latex: All constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}\{\nabla g_i(\bar x),\nabla h_j(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x),\ 1\le j\le p\}<|I(\bar x)|+p\).

notation.meaning: Index set of active inequality constraints.
Feasible set defined by smooth equalities and inequalities.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weaker smooth constraint-qualification boundary and its abnormal-multiplier alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point \( ar x\), MFCQ holds when the equality gradients are linearly independent and there exists \(d\) satisfying \(
abla h_j( ar x)^Td=0\) for every equality and \(
abla g_i( ar x)^Td<0\) for every active inequality. LICQ implies MFCQ, but not conversely. MFCQ fails if and only if there is a nonzero pair \((\lambda,\mu)\), with \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for active inequalities, such that \(\sum_{i\in I( ar x)}\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_j\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ fails exactly when the active constraint gradients admit a nonzero abnormal dependence with nonnegative inequality coefficients.
assumptions_latex: All constraints are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
eg\mathrm{MFCQ}( ar x)\iff\exists(\lambda,\mu)
e0:\ \lambda\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I( ar x)}\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_j\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0.

notation.meaning: A strict feasible direction for the active linearized inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Mangasarian–Fromovitz Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent descriptions of one feasible set can have different active-gradient degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) is represented both by \(h_1(x)=x=0\), whose gradient at zero is nonzero, and by \(h_2(x)=x^2=0\), whose gradient at zero vanishes. Thus LICQ degeneracy is a property of the chosen constraint representation at the point, not solely of the underlying feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent equality descriptions of the same feasible set can differ in whether their active gradients are degenerate.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence of Gradient Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Failure under a Vanishing Active Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example showing failure of KKT necessity under degenerate constraint geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(x^2\le0\). The sole feasible point \(x=0\) is the global minimizer, but the active constraint gradient is zero. The KKT stationarity equation \(1+\lambda(2x)=0\) therefore reduces to \(1=0\) at \(x=0\), so no multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimizer can fail the KKT equations when its active constraint has a vanishing gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*=0\text{ is globally optimal, but no }\lambda\ge0\text{ satisfies KKT stationarity.}
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Failure under a Vanishing Active Gradient

children.title: Equality-Dominated Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Models whose feasible sets are largely determined by equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Dominated Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility confined locally to lower-dimensional equality sets in the ambient search space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) be continuously differentiable, let \(g:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and define \(C=\{x\in X:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Feasibility is equality-dominated near \(\bar x\in C\) if \(p\ge1\) and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=p\) throughout a neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Then \(h^{-1}(0)\) is locally an \((n-p)\)-dimensional embedded manifold, and \(C\), being locally contained in this manifold, has zero \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure near \(\bar x\). Thus exact feasible points occupy no positive-volume subset of a sufficiently small ambient neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally independent equality constraints confine nearby feasible points to a lower-dimensional manifold, so exact feasibility has zero ambient volume near the point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) is continuously differentiable.
\(p\ge1\), \(\bar x\in C\), and \(Dh\) has full row rank \(p\) near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is locally contained in an }(n-p)\text{-dimensional manifold and has local }n\text{-dimensional measure }0\).

notation.meaning: Number of locally independent equality constraints.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Probability of Exact Equality Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling consequence of regular equality-defined feasibility having zero ambient measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(h\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^p)\) with \(p\ge1\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=p\) for every \(x\in h^{-1}(0)\). If the law of a random vector \(Z\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure, then \(\mathbb P(Z\in C)=0\) for every measurable \(C\subseteq h^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambient sample with an absolutely continuous distribution hits a regular positive-codimension equality-feasible set with probability zero.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(h\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^p)\).
\(p\ge1\) and \(Dh\) has full row rank on \(h^{-1}(0)\).
\(C\subseteq h^{-1}(0)\) is measurable and the law of \(Z\) is absolutely continuous with respect to ambient Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(Z\in C)=0\).

notation.meaning: Random point sampled in the ambient space.
Measurable feasible set contained in the equality zero set.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Probability of Exact Equality Feasibility

children.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of apparent feasibility on numerical acceptance tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric and sampling sensitivity caused by replacing an exact equality with a residual-tolerance band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=[-1,1]^n\), let \(h:X\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(h(x)=x_1\), and define \(C_\tau=\{x\in X:|h(x)|\le\tau\}\) for \(\tau\ge0\). Then \(C_0=\{x\in X:x_1=0\}\) has zero \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure. For \(0<\tau\le1\), one has \(C_\tau=[-\tau,\tau]\times[-1,1]^{n-1}\) and \(\lambda_n(C_\tau)=2^n\tau\). Thus every positive tolerance changes the exact zero-volume set into a positive-volume band. Under uniform sampling on \(X\), the probability of tolerance-feasibility is \(\lambda_n(C_\tau)/\lambda_n(X)=\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In this equality example, any positive residual tolerance turns a zero-volume feasible set into a band whose volume, and whose acceptance probability under uniform sampling, grows linearly with the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility uses the absolute residual tolerance \(\tau\).
The acceptance-probability statement uses uniform sampling on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_n(C_0)=0\), while \(\lambda_n(C_\tau)=2^n\tau>0\) and \(\mathbb P(X_{\mathrm{unif}}\in C_\tau)=\tau\) for \(0<\tau\le1\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set under residual tolerance tau.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Solvability of the Global Optimization Problem p. 4

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.2 Solvability of the Global Optimization Problem p. 4

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set and optimal-value limits for residual tolerances on a compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a compact metric space, let \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) be continuous, and define \(C_\tau=\{x\in X:\|h(x)\|\le\tau\}\). Then \(C_{\tau_1}\subseteq C_{\tau_2}\) for \(0\le\tau_1\le\tau_2\), and \(C_0=\bigcap_{\tau>0}C_\tau\). If \(\tau_k\downarrow0\) and \(x_k\in C_{\tau_k}\), every cluster point of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(C_0\). If additionally \(C_0\ne\varnothing\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, then \(v(\tau)=\min_{x\in C_\tau}f(x)\) increases to \(v(0)\) as \(\tau\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain with continuous residuals, tolerance-feasible sets shrink to the exact feasible set, and their minimum values converge monotonically to the exact constrained value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a compact metric space and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) is continuous.
For the value statement, \(C_0\ne\varnothing\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_0=\bigcap_{\tau>0}C_\tau,\quad x_k\in C_{\tau_k},\ \tau_k\downarrow0\Longrightarrow \operatorname{cluster}(x_k)\subseteq C_0,\quad \lim_{\tau\downarrow0}v(\tau)=v(0).

notation.meaning: Feasible set under residual tolerance tau.
Minimum objective value over the tolerance-feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Tolerance Set and Value Convergence

children.title: Unknown or Misspecified Modulus Information
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for missing, nonconservative, or excessively conservative variation estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown or Misspecified Modulus Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure modes caused by absent, underestimated, or excessively conservative variation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L_*\|x-y\|\) on \(X\), with true minimal Lipschitz modulus \(L_*\). A global method using an estimate \(\widehat L\) has three regimes: if no finite \(\widehat L\) is available, Lipschitz lower bounds cannot be instantiated; if \(\widehat L<L_*\), the bound \(f(x)\ge f(y)-\widehat L\|x-y\|\) need not hold and pruning may discard a global minimizer; if \(\widehat L\ge L_*\), bounds are valid, but excessive overestimation weakens them and can severely enlarge the required partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Missing modulus information prevents Lipschitz bounds; underestimation makes pruning unsound; overestimation remains valid but can make global search inefficient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f\) has finite true Lipschitz modulus \(L_*\).
The method constructs lower bounds using \(\widehat L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat L<L_*\) may invalidate bounds, whereas \(\widehat L\ge L_*\) preserves validity but may reduce sharpness.

notation.meaning: Minimal valid Lipschitz modulus of the objective.
Modulus estimate used by the optimization method.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Estimation of Lipschitzian Problem Characteristics in Global Optimization p. 155

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Estimation of Lipschitzian Problem Characteristics in Global Optimization p. 155

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Values Cannot Certify an Unrestricted Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary for obtaining a global Lipschitz upper bound from finitely many values alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) contain a nonempty open ball and let \(S\subset X\) be finite. For every \(M>0\), there exist globally Lipschitz functions \(f_0,f_1:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), smooth on \(\mathbb R^n\), such that \(f_0(s)=f_1(s)\) for all \(s\in S\), \(\operatorname{Lip}(f_0)=0\), and \(\operatorname{Lip}(f_1|_X)>M\). Consequently, finitely many exact function values cannot certify a finite upper bound on an unknown global Lipschitz modulus without additional structural or derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over an unrestricted smooth function class, finitely many function values cannot certify a global Lipschitz upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) contains a nonempty open ball.
\(S\subset X\) is finite and the available information consists only of exact values on \(S\).
The admissible class permits smooth compactly supported perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup\{\operatorname{Lip}(f|_X): f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n),\ f|_S=y\}=+\infty\) for compatible constant sample data \(y\).

notation.meaning: Minimal global Lipschitz modulus of the restriction of f to X.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Values Cannot Certify an Unrestricted Modulus

children.title: Landscape-Dimension Search Failures
children.top_down_role: Landscape structures that impede reliable global exploration.

children.title: Proliferation of Local Minima
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for highly multiextremal landscapes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines proliferation using genuine relative strict local minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), let \(L(f;D)\) contain every \(x\in D\) for which some \(r>0\) satisfies \(f(x)<f(y)\) whenever \(y\in D\) and \(0<\|y-x\|<r\). A family \((f_d,D_d)\) exhibits proliferation of strict local minima if, for every fixed \(q>0\), \(|L(f_d;D_d)|/d^q\to\infty\), with infinite cardinality also qualifying.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proliferation means that the number of genuine strict local minima grows faster than every polynomial in dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall q>0,\quad |L(f_d;D_d)|/d^q\to\infty.

notation.meaning: set of strict local minimizers relative to D

review_flags: The asymptotic problem family and dimension convention must be declared.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Local-Minimum Proliferation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Minimality Does Not Rank Wells Globally
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the informational failure intrinsic to multiextremal landscapes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(m\ge2\), there exists a smooth function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) having at least \(m\) strict local minimizers with pairwise distinct objective values. Therefore strict local minimality, even together with a count of other local minima, neither implies global minimality nor determines the attained value's global rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerous locally valid wells may have different depths, so local optimality cannot identify the global well.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Strict local minimality does not imply or rank global minimality.}
knowledge_statements.title: Local Minimality Does Not Rank Wells Globally

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides a canonical family with exponentially many strict local minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\prod_{i=1}^dD_i\) and \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^dq_i(x_i)\). If each \(q_i\) has two distinct strict local minimizers \(a_i,b_i\) relative to \(D_i\), then every point in \(\prod_{i=1}^d\{a_i,b_i\}\) is a strict local minimizer of \(f\) relative to \(D\). Consequently, \(|L(f;D)|\ge2^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two strict coordinate wells produce at least two-to-the-d strict local minima in a separable objective.
assumptions_latex: Each \(q_i\) has distinct strict local minimizers \(a_i,b_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |L(f;D)|\ge2^d.

notation.meaning: two strict local minimizers of the ith coordinate function

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Proliferation in Separable Landscapes
Proliferation of Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies multiextremality by separated strict local minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) continuous. For \(r,\gamma>0\), define \(M_{r,\gamma}(f)\) as the largest cardinality of a set \(S\subset D\) such that distinct points of \(S\) are at least \(2r\) apart and every \(x\in S\) satisfies \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\gamma\) whenever \(y\in D\) and \(\lVert y-x\rVert=r\). A family \((f_d)\) exhibits proliferation of local minima when \(M_{r_d,\gamma_d}(f_d)\) grows superpolynomially in \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime contains superpolynomially many well-separated strict local minima, each protected by a positive objective barrier on a surrounding sphere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{r_d,\gamma_d}(f_d)\) grows superpolynomially with dimension.

notation.meaning: maximum number of separated local minima having radius-r barrier at least gamma

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Local, Global, epsilon-Global Minima p. 57

review_flags: quantitative proliferation criterion is a local formalization

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Local, Global, epsilon-Global Minima p. 57

The cited section covers local and global minima but does not directly support the constructed superpolynomial proliferation criterion, so the intended mathematical definition requires a dedicated source and corrected hypotheses.

children.title: Narrow Global Basins
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for globally best regions with small sampling or attraction volume.

assumptions_latex: \(D\) is equipped with a probability measure \(\mu\).
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is measurable and attains its minimum.
The \(N\) samples are independent with common distribution \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(p_d=\mu_d(B_{\varepsilon_d})\in(0,1)\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), success probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \(N\ge \log(\delta)/\log(1-p_d)\).

notation.meaning: measurable epsilon-sublevel set around the global optimum value
sampling probability of the epsilon-global basin in dimension d

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures narrowness using sampling probability rather than geometric width alone.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.3 Convergence of Global Random Search Algorithms p. 34

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) carry a probability measure \(\mu\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be measurable and attain \(f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x)\), and, for \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define \(B_\varepsilon=\{x\in D:f(x)\le f^*+\varepsilon\}\). For \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) independent samples from \(\mu\), the probability of never entering \(B_\varepsilon\) is \((1-\mu(B_\varepsilon))^N\). A family has narrow global basins when \(p_d=\mu_d(B_{\varepsilon_d})\to0\). For \(p_d\in(0,1)\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), attaining success probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \(N\ge \log(\delta)/\log(1-p_d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global basin is narrow when its sampling mass vanishes. Independent random search then requires on the order of the reciprocal basin mass to hit it with a fixed positive reliability.

children.title: Plateau-Ridge Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for weak directional information and slow regional discrimination.

children.title: Flat Plateau Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regions with weak variation across multiple search directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Plateau Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes exact or approximately flat positive-volume regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(P\subset D\) be measurable with positive volume, and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). An exact flat plateau is a set satisfying \(f(x)=c\) for every \(x\in P\). Given \(\eta\ge0\), an approximate plateau satisfies \(\sup_{x,y\in P}|f(x)-f(y)|\le\eta\). If \(f\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(P\), a first-order flat plateau additionally satisfies \(\sup_{x\in P}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert\le\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A plateau is a positive-volume region on which objective variation, and optionally gradient magnitude, is uniformly negligible.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset D\) is measurable and has positive volume.
For the gradient clause, \(f\) is differentiable near \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{osc}_P f\le\eta\), and optionally \(\sup_{x\in P}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert\le\eta\).

notation.meaning: supremum of absolute objective differences over P

review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports this plateau formalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed exact and approximate plateau criteria are plausible local formalizations, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container, but no inspectable source locator is supplied for the positive-volume, oscillation, or gradient-threshold formulation.

children.title: Ridge-Dominated Regimes
children.top_down_role: Landscapes concentrated near elongated high-curvature or low-curvature structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies thin-ridge discovery in an explicit product-domain model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[0,1]^k\times[-1,1]^{d-k}\), \(R=[0,1]^k\times\{0\}^{d-k}\), and \(T_\rho=\{(u,v)\in D:\|v\|_\infty\le\rho\}\), where \(0<\rho\le1\). A uniform sample from \(D\) lies in \(T_\rho\) with probability \(\rho^{d-k}\). For \(N\) independent samples the hit probability is \(1-(1-\rho^{d-k})^N\), so reliability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \(N\ge\log(\delta)/\log(1-\rho^{d-k})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform exploration incurs an exponential-in-codimension penalty for hitting a thin ridge tube.
assumptions_latex: Samples are independent and uniform on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P\{\text{at least one hit of }T_\rho\}=1-(1-\rho^{d-k})^N.
knowledge_statements.title: Codimension Penalty for Isotropic Sampling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ridge domination by uniform deterioration normal to a lower-dimensional manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^d\), let \(R\subset D\) be a \(k\)-dimensional \(C^1\) embedded manifold with \(k<d\), and fix \(\alpha,\rho>0\). The landscape is transversely \((\alpha,\rho)\)-ridge-dominated along \(R\) if \(f(x+v)\ge f(x)+\alpha\|v\|^2\) for every \(x\in R\) and every \(v\in N_xR\) satisfying \(0<\|v\|\le\rho\) and \(x+v\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional ridge is favored against nearby normal displacements by uniform quadratic growth.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a lower-dimensional C1 embedded manifold.
\(f\) is defined on the stated normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x+v)-f(x)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2\quad\text{for admissible }v\in N_xR.

notation.meaning: normal space of R at x

review_flags: Quantitative ridge taxonomy definition; it makes no sampling claim without a sampling law.
knowledge_statements.title: Transversely Quadratic Ridge Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates along-ridge variation from uniformly curved normal directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^{d-k}\) and \(f(u,v)=g(u)+\tfrac12v^THv\), where \(g\in C^2\) and \(H\succ0\). Then \(R=\{(u,0)\}\) satisfies \(f(u,v)-f(u,0)\ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(H)\|v\|^2\), and \(\nabla^2f(u,0)=\operatorname{diag}(\nabla^2g(u),H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical quadratic model separates tangent behavior from positive normal curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(u,v)-f(u,0)\ge\frac{\lambda_{\min}(H)}2\|v\|^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Normal Quadratic Ridge Model
Ridge-Dominated Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes low-dimensional favorable manifolds with strong transverse deterioration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) and let \(R\subset D\) be a \(k\)-dimensional embedded manifold with \(k<d\). A minimization landscape is \((\alpha,\rho)\)-ridge-dominated along \(R\) if, for every \(x\in R\) and every normal vector \(v\) with \(\lVert v\rVert\le\rho\) and \(x+v\in D\), \(f(x+v)\ge f(x)+\alpha\lVert v\rVert^2\). When useful descent or near-optimal points are confined to a thin tubular neighborhood of such an \(R\), isotropic exploration spends most evaluations away from the ridge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Good points lie near a lower-dimensional manifold, while moving normally away from it causes uniform quadratic deterioration.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a lower-dimensional embedded manifold in \(D\).
\(f\) is defined on the radius-\(\rho\) normal neighborhood of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x+v)-f(x)\ge\alpha\lVert v\rVert^2\) for admissible normal displacements.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports the ridge criterion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic transverse-growth condition is a plausible ridge model, but it is locally constructed and uncited. The assertion that isotropic exploration spends most evaluations away from the ridge also requires a specified sampling law, tube width, and quantitative bound.

children.title: Plateau-to-Ridge Transitions
children.top_down_role: Search regions where broadly flat geometry gives way to directional structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a determinate transition definition using explicit gradient and curvature tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^d\) be open, \(f\in C^2(D)\), and \(x:[0,1]\to D\) be continuous. Fix \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(0\le\tau_0<\tau_1\). A plateau-to-ridge transition occurs along \(x\) if there are ordered nonempty intervals \(I_0,I_1\subset[0,1]\) and an integer \(k\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}\) such that \(\|\nabla f(x(t))\|\le\varepsilon\) throughout \(I_0\cup I_1\), every Hessian eigenvalue has magnitude at most \(\tau_0\) on \(I_0\), and on \(I_1\) exactly \(k\) eigenvalues have magnitude at least \(\tau_1\) while all remaining eigenvalues have magnitude at most \(\tau_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a low-gradient path, uniformly weak curvature gives way to a tolerance-separated mixture of curved and flat directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The path changes from a }\tau_0\text{-flat regime to a }(k,\tau_0,\tau_1)\text{-anisotropic regime.}
review_flags: Quantitative taxonomy definition; tolerances must be declared for each application.
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Separated Plateau-to-Ridge Transition

For \(c

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locates changes of thresholded Hessian rank along the transition path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the preceding smoothness assumptions, let \(\lambda_1(t)\le\cdots\le\lambda_d(t)\) be the eigenvalues of \(\nabla^2f(x(t))\) and let \(r_\tau(t)=\#\{i:|\lambda_i(t)|>\tau\}\). Each \(\lambda_i\) is continuous, so \(r_\tau\) is locally constant wherever \(|\lambda_i(t)|\ne\tau\) for every \(i\). Consequently, every boundary at which \(r_\tau\) changes contains a point satisfying \(|\lambda_i(t)|=\tau\) for some \(i\).

Plateau-to-Ridge Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Captures rank changes in local directional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(D)\) and let \(x(t)\), \(t\in[0,1]\), be a continuous path in \(D\). For a threshold \(\tau>0\), define \(r_\tau(t)\) as the number of eigenvalues of \(\nabla^2 f(x(t))\) whose absolute values exceed \(\tau\). A plateau-to-ridge transition occurs when \(r_\tau(t)\) changes from \(0\) on an initial interval to a value in \(\{1,\ldots,d-1\}\) on a later interval, while \(\lVert\nabla f(x(t))\rVert\) remains small along the path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a path, an almost curvature-free plateau becomes anisotropic: some curvature directions emerge while other directions remain flat.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\tau\) changes from \(0\) to an intermediate rank while the gradient remains small.

notation.meaning: number of Hessian eigenvalues above the curvature threshold in magnitude

children.title: Directional Information Failure
children.top_down_role: Consequences of insufficient local discrimination for global search.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indistinguishable Inexact Gradients with Opposite Descent Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact two-instance witness for failure to infer a uniformly valid descent direction from a bounded-error gradient observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\eta>0\), a nonzero vector \(u\in\mathbb R^d\) with \(\lVert u\rVert\le\eta\), and the observed gradient \(g=0\). The observation is compatible both with \(\nabla f_+(x)=u\), using error \(e_+=-u\), and with \(\nabla f_-(x)=-u\), using error \(e_-=u\); both errors satisfy \(\lVert e_\pm\rVert\le\eta\). For every direction \(d\), the two true directional derivatives are \(u^\top d\) and \(-u^\top d\), which cannot both be strictly negative. Therefore no decision rule using only this observation can guarantee a strict true descent direction uniformly over all gradients and errors compatible with the bounded-error oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same zero inexact-gradient observation can hide two opposite true gradients, so no observation-only rule can guarantee descent for every compatible instance.
assumptions_latex: A proposed direction depends only on the observed gradient \(g=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists d=d(g)\text{ such that }v^\top d<0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^d\text{ with }\lVert v-g\rVert\le\eta.\)

notation.meaning: nonzero candidate true gradient hidden by the observation

knowledge_statements.title: Indistinguishable Inexact Gradients with Opposite Descent Directions
Directional Information Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when local first-order data cannot identify productive directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be differentiable at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and suppose the available gradient is corrupted by an unknown error \(e\) satisfying \(\lVert eVert\le\eta\), so the oracle returns \(g=
abla f(x)+e\). If \(\lVert
abla f(x)Vert\le\eta\), then \(g=0\) is compatible with the oracle model, and the exact direction \(-
abla f(x)/\lVert
abla f(x)Vert\) cannot be inferred uniformly. Hence no rule using only \(g\) can guarantee a strictly negative true directional derivative over all admissible errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When gradient signal is no larger than oracle error, first-order observations cannot uniformly certify a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert\le\eta\), no observation-only rule uniformly guarantees true descent.
review_flags: no supplied locator covers inexact-gradient indistinguishability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indistinguishability idea is mathematically plausible, but the conclusion must clearly quantify over observations, decision rules, true gradients, and admissible errors. No source locator is supplied for this inexact-oracle failure statement.

children.title: Symmetry-Induced Basin Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for redundant search caused by equivalent solutions.

children.title: Landscape Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Transformations that preserve objective or feasibility structure across the search domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an equivalent transformation-group formulation of landscape invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), define \(\operatorname{Sym}(D,f)=\{h:D\to D:h\text{ is bijective and }f(hx)=f(x)\ \forall x\in D\}\). Under composition this is a group. A group \(G\) is a symmetry group of the landscape when it acts on \(D\) through a homomorphism into \(\operatorname{Sym}(D,f)\). Every orbit then has constant objective value, and every orbit of a global minimizer lies in the global solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Landscape symmetries are feasible-set bijections that preserve every objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\in\operatorname{Sym}(D,f)\Rightarrow f(hx)=f(x),\quad \operatorname{Sym}(D,f)\text{ is a group}.

notation.meaning: group of objective-preserving bijections of D

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Landscape Symmetry Group

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient and Hessian Equivariance under Orthogonal Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the differential structure imposed by a smooth orthogonal symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open, \(f\in C^2(D)\), and let \(Q\) be orthogonal with \(QD=D\) and \(f(Qx)=f(x)\). Then \(
abla f(Qx)=Q
abla f(x)\) and \(
abla^2f(Qx)=Q
abla^2f(x)Q^T\). Hence stationarity, Hessian eigenvalues, and second-order stationary-point type are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal symmetry transports gradients and conjugates Hessians.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
abla f(Qx)=Q
abla f(x),\qquad 
abla^2f(Qx)=Q
abla^2f(x)Q^T.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient and Hessian Equivariance under Orthogonal Symmetry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a symmetric problem on a set meeting every orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on \(D\), let \(f(gx)=f(x)\), and let \(F\subseteq D\) meet every orbit. Then \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). If an optimum is attained on either side, a symmetry maps an optimizer to an equal-valued optimizer on the other side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric objective may be optimized over any set containing a representative of every orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_Df=\inf_Ff.
review_flags: Symmetry and orbit coverage do not imply attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Orbit Representatives
Landscape Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a group action preserving both feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a feasible set \(D\). The optimization landscape \((D,f)\) is \(G\)-symmetric if \(g\cdot x\in D\) and \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in D\). The orbit \(Gx=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}\) therefore consists entirely of points having the same objective value. In particular, the orbit of any global minimizer is contained in the global solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A landscape is symmetric when a group maps feasible points to feasible points without changing their objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: orbit of x under the group action

review_flags: standard group-invariance definition but no symmetry source was supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard definition of objective invariance under a group action, and definition is the correct knowledge kind for the leaf, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Duplicate Global Basins
children.top_down_role: Separated basins representing equivalent globally optimal solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines separated attraction basins associated with symmetry-equivalent global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:D\to D\) be an iteration map and \(B(z)=\{x\in D:T^n(x)\to z\}\). Two basins \(B(z_1)\) and \(B(z_2)\) are duplicate global basins when \(z_1\ne z_2\) are global minimizers and a declared landscape symmetry maps \(z_1\) to \(z_2\) and \(B(z_1)\) to \(B(z_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate global basins are distinct attraction regions for symmetry-equivalent global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(T:D\to D\) has the stated attraction basins.
A declared symmetry acts on the points and basins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(z_2)=gB(z_1)\text{ for some symmetry }g\text{ with }z_2=gz_1.

notation.meaning: attraction basin of z under T

knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate Global Basins

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregate Sampling Mass of Duplicate Basins
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies discovery probability for disjoint equal-mass global basin copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) be pairwise disjoint duplicate global basins under a probability measure \(\mu\), with \(\mu(B_i)=p\) for every \(i\). Then \(\mu(\bigcup_iB_i)=mp\). For \(N\) independent samples, the probability of entering at least one duplicate global basin is \(1-(1-mp)^N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple disjoint copies increase the chance of finding some equivalent global basin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P\{\text{some }B_i\text{ is hit by time }N\}=1-(1-mp)^N.

notation.meaning: sampling mass of each duplicate basin

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Sampling Mass of Duplicate Basins

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States sufficient topological hypotheses for symmetry to transport attraction limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on \(D\) by homeomorphisms, and let \(T:D\to D\) satisfy \(T(gx)=gT(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in D\). For \(B(z)=\{x:T^n(x)\to z\}\), one has \(B(gz)=gB(z)\) for every \(g\in G\). If \(z\) is a global minimizer of a \(G\)-invariant objective, then every \(gz\) is also globally minimizing; basins of distinct limits are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous symmetry actions and equivariant dynamics carry each global basin to the basin of the symmetry-related global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The objective is G-invariant for the global-minimizer conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(gz)=gB(z)\quad\forall g\in G.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivariant Transport of Attraction Basins

children.title: Basin Equivalence Classes
children.top_down_role: Grouping of search regions according to solution equivalence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines basin classes once a symmetry action on the basin collection is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a basin collection \(\mathcal B\). Define \(B_1\sim_GB_2\) if \(B_2=gB_1\) for some \(g\in G\). This is an equivalence relation, and its classes are precisely the orbits \(G\cdot B=\{gB:g\in G\}\). The quotient \(\mathcal B/G\) is the set of these basin orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basins are equivalent exactly when they lie in the same orbit of the induced symmetry action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B/G=\{G\cdot B:B\in\mathcal B\}\text{ partitions }\mathcal B.
review_flags: Existence of the action on basins must be established separately, for example by equivariant continuous dynamics.
knowledge_statements.title: Basin-Orbit Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariant Basin Statistics Descend to the Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes basin quantities that are well defined classwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B/G\) be the orbit projection and let \(s:\mathcal B\to S\). There is a unique \(\bar s:\mathcal B/G\to S\) satisfying \(s=\bar s\circ\pi\) if and only if \(s(gB)=s(B)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(B\in\mathcal B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basin statistic is well defined on classes exactly when it is constant on each orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\text{ factors uniquely through }\mathcal B/G\iff s(gB)=s(B)\ \forall g,B.
knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Basin Statistics Descend to the Quotient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orbit-Stabilizer Size of a Basin Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts equivalent basins under a finite symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on \(\mathcal B\), and let \(G_B=\{g\in G:gB=B\}\). Then the basin class containing \(B\) has cardinality \(|G\cdot B|=[G:G_B]=|G|/|G_B|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of equivalent copies equals the group size divided by the basin stabilizer size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |G\cdot B|=\frac{|G|}{|G_B|}.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbit-Stabilizer Size of a Basin Class
Basin Equivalence Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines basin equivalence through the landscape symmetry action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a collection of attraction basins for a \(G\)-equivariant search map on a \(G\)-symmetric landscape. Define \(B_1\sim_G B_2\) if there exists \(g\in G\) such that \(B_2=g\cdot B_1\). Because the group action contains an identity and is closed under inverses and composition, \(\sim_G\) is an equivalence relation. The quotient \(\mathcal{B}/G\) is the set of basin equivalence classes; each class may be represented by any one of its member basins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two attraction basins are equivalent when a landscape symmetry maps one onto the other; symmetry orbits partition the basin collection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{B}/G=\{[B]_G:B\in\mathcal{B}\}\) partitions \(\mathcal{B}\).

notation.meaning: equivalence under the induced group action on basins

review_flags: standard orbit equivalence construction but no symmetry source was supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Given an actual group action on the basin collection, the orbit relation and quotient construction are correct, and definition fits the leaf. However, the record has no citation or explicit standard-field rationale supporting the induced basin action.

children.title: Redundant Search Burden
children.top_down_role: Computational effort spent revisiting equivalent regions or solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Search Burden
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies repeated discovery of equivalent basins under symmetric sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(m\) disjoint, symmetry-equivalent basins have equal sampling probability \(p>0\), and independent restarts enter each basin with that probability. After \(N\) restarts, the expected number of distinct basins discovered is \(m(1-(1-p)^N)\), while the expected number of basin hits is \(Nmp\). Thus the expected redundant hits equal \(Nmp-m(1-(1-p)^N)\). If only basin equivalence classes matter, these repeated hits consume evaluations without increasing the number of distinct classes represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent restarts repeatedly hit symmetry-equivalent basins; the excess of total hits over distinct basins measures redundant search.
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) disjoint basins, each sampled with probability \(p\).
Restarts are independent and identically distributed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[R_N]=Nmp-m(1-(1-p)^N)\).

notation.meaning: number of basin hits beyond first discoveries after N restarts

source_refs.locator: 2 Global Random Search: Fundamentals and Statistical Inference p. 29

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Global Random Search: Fundamentals and Statistical Inference p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupon-Collector Cost of Discovering All Equivalent Basins
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complements the accepted redundant-hit expectation with full basin-discovery time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(m\) disjoint basins each have probability \(p>0\) per independent restart, with \(mp\le1\). If \(T_{\mathrm{all}}\) is the first restart by which every basin has been hit, then \(\mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{all}}]=H_m/p\), where \(H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m1/j\). When \(p=1/m\), \(\mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{all}}]=mH_m=\Theta(m\log m)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discovering every equivalent basin has coupon-collector cost, reaching order m log m under exhaustive equal-probability sampling.
assumptions_latex: Each basin has probability \(p>0\) per restart.
Restarts are independent and identically distributed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{all}}]=\frac{H_m}{p}.

notation.meaning: restart count required to hit every basin

knowledge_statements.title: Coupon-Collector Cost of Discovering All Equivalent Basins

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicity Alone Does Not Imply Redundant Runtime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates structural duplication from policy-dependent computational overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The existence of multiple symmetry-equivalent basins does not itself imply a proportional runtime penalty. If every query is restricted to a representative set meeting each relevant basin orbit at most once, no query can revisit a second basin from an already represented orbit. Redundant burden therefore requires a search policy capable of revisiting equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate basins cause redundant work only when the search policy can revisit their equivalence class.
assumptions_latex: The search queries a representative set meeting each relevant basin orbit at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Repeated visits to an already represented basin orbit equal }0.
review_flags: The cost of constructing or enforcing representatives is outside this claim.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity Alone Does Not Imply Redundant Runtime

children.title: High-Dimensional Coverage Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of practical domain coverage as dimension increases.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Dimensional Coverage Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the covering-number obstruction for uniform-resolution exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[0,1]^d\) with Euclidean distance, and require evaluated points to form an \(r\)-net of \(D\), where \(0<r<1/2\). If \(N_r(D)\) is the minimum number of closed radius-\(r\) balls covering \(D\), then volume comparison gives \(N_r(D)\ge 1/(v_d r^d)\), where \(v_d\) is the volume of the unit Euclidean ball. Consequently, any method guaranteeing coverage at resolution \(r\) by point evaluations requires at least \(1/(v_d r^d)\) evaluated centers in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly covering a unit cube at fixed resolution requires exponentially many evaluation points as dimension increases.
assumptions_latex: Coverage means every point of \(D\) lies within distance \(r\) of an evaluated center.

notation.meaning: volume of the Euclidean unit ball in d dimensions

review_flags: standard volume bound but no covering-number source was supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The volume comparison gives the stated Euclidean covering-number lower bound, and complexity_bound is the correct role for the leaf. Nevertheless, no source or standard-field rationale is supplied, so the nontrivial bound lacks admissible evidence.

children.title: Dimension-Driven Basin Sparsity
children.top_down_role: Diminishing probability of encountering narrow useful basins in high-dimensional domains.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed \(q\in(0,1)\), the set \(B_d\) lies inside a product of intervals, each having length at most \(q\).
The \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) samples are independent and uniformly distributed on \(D_d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), \(\Pr\{\text{at least one sample hits }B_d\}\le Nq^d\); consequently, this probability tends to \(0\) for every polynomially bounded sequence \(N=N(d)\).

notation.meaning: uniform probability measure on the d-dimensional unit cube

review_flags: product-width sparsity model is a local specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models basin mass decay through coordinatewise geometric contraction.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Basic Ideas of Global Random Search p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_d=[0,1]^d\) carry the uniform probability measure \(\mu_d\), and suppose \(B_d\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^d I_i\), where each interval \(I_i\subseteq[0,1]\) has length at most a fixed \(q\in(0,1)\). Then \(\mu_d(B_d)\le q^d\). For \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) independent uniform samples, the probability of hitting \(B_d\) is at most \(1-(1-q^d)^N\le Nq^d\). Hence, if \(N=N(d)\) is bounded by a polynomial in \(d\), the success probability tends to \(0\) as \(d\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a basin contracts by a fixed factor in every coordinate, its mass decays exponentially, and the probability that polynomially many independent uniform samples hit it tends to zero as dimension grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Driven Basin Sparsity

children.top_down_role: Navigation container for extreme-value inference under misspecified tails.

knowledge_statements.title: Incorrect Tail Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Misspecified lower-tail index in endpoint inference from independent objective observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be independent with lower endpoint \(f_*\), and suppose \(F(f_*+t)=c t^{\alpha}+o(t^{\alpha})\) as \(t\downarrow0\), where \(c,\alpha>0\). Then the sample minimum \(M_n=\min_iY_i\) has error of order \(n^{-1/\alpha}\). A certification rule constructed with an incorrect index \(\beta\) generally has invalid coverage. In particular, if \(\beta<\alpha\), then for every \(q>0\), \[\Pr\!\left(M_n-f_*\le qn^{-1/\beta}\right)\longrightarrow0.\] Thus a nominal endpoint bound using the faster scale \(n^{-1/\beta}\) can exclude the true optimum with probability tending to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the assumed lower-tail index is too small, the claimed endpoint-error scale is too optimistic and its coverage can converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(M_n-f_*\le qn^{-1/\beta})\to0\) for every \(q>0\).

notation.meaning: lower endpoint, interpreted as the global optimum value
minimum of the first n observations

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Using an Incorrect Value of the Tail Index p. 77

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.2 Using an Incorrect Value of the Tail Index p. 77

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Opposite misspecification direction for lower-endpoint confidence scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F(f_*+t)=ct^\alpha+o(t^\alpha)\) as \(t\downarrow0\), and let \(M_n=\min_{1\le i\le n}Y_i\). If an assumed index \(\beta>\alpha\) is used, then for every \(q>0\), \[\Pr\!\left(M_n-f_*\le qn^{-1/\beta}\right)\longrightarrow1.\] The radius \(n^{-1/\beta}\) is asymptotically larger than the true \(n^{-1/\alpha}\) scale, producing overconservative rather than nominally calibrated coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming a tail index larger than the true index gives an overly slow error scale whose coverage tends to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(M_n-f_*\le qn^{-1/\beta})\to1\) for every \(q>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Overconservative Tail-Index Misspecification

children.title: Noise-Induced False Incumbents
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for apparent optima produced by observation error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise ordering certificate from validated observation-error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Y(x)=f(x)+e_x\) with validated bounds \(|e_x|\le\delta_x\). For evaluated points \(a,b\), \[Y(a)+\delta_a<Y(b)-\delta_b\] implies \(f(a)<f(b)\). If the two validated value intervals overlap, they do not certify either strict ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated validated observation intervals certify which point is better; overlapping intervals leave the strict ordering unresolved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(a)+\delta_a<Y(b)-\delta_b\Rightarrow f(a)<f(b)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Error Incumbent Comparison

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise false selection caused by one noisy observation at each feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(a)=0\) and \(f(b)=1\), and observe \(Y(x)=f(x)+e_x\), where \(e_a,e_b\) are independent uniform random variables on \([-1,1]\). Although \(a\) is strictly better, selecting the smallest single observation chooses \(b\) whenever \(e_a-e_b>1\), which has probability \(1/8\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With independent uniform observation errors, an inferior point is selected from two points with probability 1/8.
assumptions_latex: \(e_a,e_b\) are independent and uniformly distributed on \([-1,1]\).
The incumbent is the point with the smaller single observation.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Noise False Incumbent
Noise-Induced False Incumbents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: False selection caused by unbounded additive observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two feasible points satisfy \(f(a)<f(b)\), but let their observed values be \(Y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon_x\), with independent \(N(0,\sigma^2)\) errors and \(\sigma>0\). Selecting the smallest single observation declares \(b\) incumbent whenever \(Y(b)<Y(a)\), an event having probability \[\Pr(Y(b)<Y(a))=\Phi\!\left(-\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{\sqrt{2}\sigma}\right)>0.\] Hence an observed incumbent need not be a true incumbent. With many independently evaluated inferior points, extreme negative errors can further increase false selection unless replication, uncertainty bounds, or noise-aware comparisons are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under unbounded observation noise, an inferior point has positive probability of producing the best observed value and being selected as incumbent.

notation.meaning: noisy observation of the objective at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian comparison formula is mathematically correct and the failure_boundary kind fits, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Premature Probabilistic Stopping
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for unjustified confidence in incomplete exploration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage failure when a probabilistic stopping rule overstates the chance of an epsilon-optimal draw.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let independent samples hit the \(\varepsilon\)-optimal set with true probability \(p\in[0,1]\). After \(n\) samples, the probability of missing that set is exactly \((1-p)^n\). If a stopping rule assumes \(p_0>p\) and calibrates \(n\) using \((1-p_0)^n\le\alpha\), its advertised failure bound is unjustified: the actual miss probability is \((1-p)^n>(1-p_0)^n\) and can exceed \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sample count calibrated with an overstated probability of hitting the near-optimal set can stop with failure probability above its advertised level.
assumptions_latex: Each sample hits the declared \(\varepsilon\)-optimal set with probability \(p\).
The stopping rule uses an asserted lower bound \(p_0>p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\text{no \(\varepsilon\)-optimal sample})=(1-p)^n\), so calibration using \(p_0\) is invalid.

notation.meaning: True probability mass of the epsilon-optimal set.
Assumed lower bound on that probability.

knowledge_statements.title: Misspecified Near-Optimal Sampling Mass

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated Unadjusted Confidence Checks Inflate Stopping Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Premature stopping caused by repeatedly applying a fixed per-look false-certification threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that under a nonoptimal state, \(T\) independent interim checks each issue a false global-success declaration with probability \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and the search stops at the first declaration. Then \[\Pr(\text{premature stop by look }T)=1-(1-\alpha)^T>\alpha\quad(T>1),\] and this probability tends to one as \(T\to\infty\). Thus a fixed-level certificate valid for one prespecified look is not an anytime-valid stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly checking at an unadjusted fixed confidence level can make premature stopping much more likely than the advertised per-look error.
assumptions_latex: Under the nonoptimal state, interim false-declaration events are independent and each has probability \(\alpha\).
The procedure stops at the first positive declaration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\tau\le T)=1-(1-\alpha)^T,\qquad \Pr(\tau<\infty)=1.

notation.meaning: first interim look producing a false success declaration

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Unadjusted Confidence Checks Inflate Stopping Error

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous confidence guarantees evaluated at a data-dependent stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\mathcal F_n) be the search filtration and let C_n be the event that the claimed global-accuracy statement at look n is correct. If \Pr(\bigcap_{n\ge1}C_n)\ge1-\alpha, then every almost surely finite (\mathcal F_n)-stopping time \tau satisfies \Pr(C_\tau)\ge1-\alpha. One sufficient construction uses numbers \alpha_n\ge0 with \sum_n\alpha_n\le\alpha and marginal guarantees \Pr(C_n^c)\le\alpha_n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A data-dependent stopping rule inherits confidence from a simultaneous or anytime-valid guarantee; summable per-look error spending is one sufficient construction.
assumptions_latex: \tau is an almost surely finite stopping time.
The events C_n satisfy the stated simultaneous guarantee, or the stated summable marginal error bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(C_\tau)\ge1-\alpha.

notation.meaning: event that the global-accuracy claim at look n is correct
error budget assigned to look n

knowledge_statements.title: Anytime-Valid Probabilistic Stopping Certificate
Premature Probabilistic Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exploration cannot support distribution-free confidence without assumptions controlling unsampled regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) contain an open ball and let an algorithm observe a continuous objective at only finitely many points \(S\subset X\) before stopping. If an open ball \(B\subset X\) is disjoint from \(S\), there exist continuous functions \(f_0,f_1\) agreeing on every point of \(S\) such that \(f_1\) has a value in \(B\) strictly below \(\min_{x\in S}f_0(x)\). The finite observations therefore cannot distinguish the two objectives. Any positive-confidence global-optimality claim based only on those observations is unjustified uniformly over all continuous objectives unless additional regularity, sampling, or probabilistic-model assumptions are validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite samples cannot certify global optimality over all continuous objectives because an unseen region may contain an indistinguishable deeper minimum.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many objective values on \(S\subset X\) have been observed.
No validated regularity or prior-model restriction controls unobserved values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No nontrivial distribution-free global-optimality confidence statement is identifiable from the finite observations alone.

children.title: Certification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where useful solutions may be available without finite global proof.

children.title: Heuristic Solutions without Global Certificates
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for incumbents lacking valid global bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic Solutions without Global Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An incumbent alone supplies an upper bound, not a certified global optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem \(f_*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\), a feasible heuristic incumbent \(\hat x\in X\) establishes only \(f_*\le f(\hat x)\). A finite \(\varepsilon\)-global certificate additionally requires a valid lower bound \(L\le f_*\) satisfying \(f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\). If the method supplies no such globally valid \(L\), then feasibility and objective quality of \(\hat x\), even relative to all sampled points or local solutions, do not certify \(f(\hat x)-f_*\le\varepsilon\). The missing lower bound is the precise certification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A good feasible incumbent is not a global certificate; certification also requires a valid lower bound closing the optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(\hat x\in X\) is produced by a heuristic method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(L\le f_*\) and \(f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\)-global optimality is not certified.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

children.title: Asymptotic Convergence without Finite Certification
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for convergent methods lacking finite proof of target accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Convergence without Finite Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic objective convergence does not itself provide a finite accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a global optimization method generate feasible points \((x_n)\) satisfying \(f(x_n)\to f_*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). This asymptotic statement alone neither identifies a computable index \(N(\varepsilon)\) such that \(f(x_n)-f_*\le\varepsilon\) for every \(n\ge N(\varepsilon)\), nor provides finite lower bounds \(L_n\le f_*\) with \(f(x_n)-L_n\le\varepsilon\). Consequently, convergence of the iterates or their values does not by itself yield a finitely checkable \(\varepsilon\)-global certificate; a rate, valid bound, or other verifiable stopping certificate is additionally required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence in the limit does not reveal when a requested global accuracy has been reached unless a computable finite certificate is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Asymptotic convergence alone does not furnish a finitely verifiable \(\varepsilon\)-global stopping rule.

notation.meaning: finite iteration threshold for accuracy epsilon
valid lower bound available at iteration n

children.title: Polynomial Optimization Certificate Hierarchy

children.title: Polynomial Positivity Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for positivity questions tied specifically to polynomial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Positivity Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary identifying positivity over semialgebraic sets as the algebraic certificate subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) and \(K:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\). The polynomial-positivity subproblem is to decide or certify \(p(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in K\), equivalently \(\inf_{x\in K}p(x)\ge0\). Within the ownership boundary, deriving algebraic representations of membership in, or approximation by, the cone of polynomials nonnegative on \(K\) belongs to polynomial positivity and certificate theory. The surrounding continuous-global-optimization problem owns the selection of the optimization model and use of the resulting bound, not the internal positivity calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial positivity owns algebraic certification that a polynomial is nonnegative on a semialgebraic set; global optimization consumes the resulting bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The predicate is \(p\ge0\) on \(K\), equivalently \(\inf_{x\in K}p(x)\ge0\).

notation.meaning: real polynomial ring in n variables

children.title: Moment Hierarchy Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for moment-based relaxation hierarchies.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment Hierarchy Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated-moment semidefinite relaxations for polynomial optimization over a basic semialgebraic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\{x:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) and polynomial objective \(p\), the order-\(d\) moment relaxation is \[\rho_d=\inf_y\{L_y(p):y_0=1,\ M_d(y)\succeq0,\ M_{d-r_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\ \text{for all }j\},\] where \(r_j=\lceil\deg(g_j)/2\rceil\) and \(d\) is large enough to contain all displayed moments. Construction, convergence, and rank analysis of this hierarchy belong to moment-certificate theory. The relaxation supplies the continuous global problem with a lower bound \(\rho_d\le\inf_{x\in K}p(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moment-hierarchy theory owns the semidefinite relaxations and their convergence; each relaxation provides a lower bound for the polynomial global problem.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation order \(d\) is sufficient for all objective and localizing moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_d\le\inf_{x\in K}p(x)\).

notation.meaning: linear functional induced by the truncated moment sequence y
localizing matrix for constraint polynomial g_j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the exact moment and localizing-matrix indexing depends on convention and has no authoritative citation. The relaxation order must also cover the objective degree.

children.title: Sum-of-Squares Certificate Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for algebraic certificates based on sum-of-squares structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite construction of a quadratic-module lower-bound certificate at fixed degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix degree bounds and monomial vectors \(z_j\) for multipliers in \(p-\gamma=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_jg_j\). Substituting \(\sigma_j=z_j^\top Q_jz_j\), imposing \(Q_j\succeq0\), and matching coefficients gives a semidefinite program that maximizes \(\gamma\). Every feasible solution yields an algebraically checkable identity and hence \(p(x)\ge\gamma\) for all \(x\in K:=\{x:g_j(x)\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed degrees, SOS lower-bound certificates are constructed by an SDP over positive-semidefinite Gram matrices and coefficient equations.
assumptions_latex: Finite multiplier degree bounds and compatible monomial vectors are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{SDP feasibility at }\gamma\Longrightarrow \gamma\le\inf_{x\in K}p(x).

notation.meaning: Gram matrix for the j-th SOS multiplier

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Truncated SOS Certificate Search

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical limitation of a failed degree-truncated SOS search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the degree-truncated SOS semidefinite system for a proposed bound \(\gamma\) is infeasible, this establishes only that no certificate exists in the selected truncated quadratic module. Without a completeness theorem applicable to the instance, it does not imply that \(p(x)\ge\gamma\) fails on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure to find an SOS certificate at one degree is not a counterexample to the proposed lower bound.
assumptions_latex: A finite multiplier-degree truncation has been fixed.
The corresponding exact SDP feasibility system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{truncated infeasibility}\not\Longrightarrow \exists x\in K:\ p(x)<\gamma.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Degree Infeasibility Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gram-Matrix Representation of an SOS Polynomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite representation used to construct and verify bounded-degree SOS multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R[x]\) satisfy \(\deg q\le2d\), and let \(z_d(x)\) contain all monomials of degree at most \(d\). Then \[q\in\Sigma[x]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists Q\succeq0:\ q(x)=z_d(x)^\top Qz_d(x).\] Thus bounded-degree SOS membership is an affine coefficient-matching feasibility problem over the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree polynomial is SOS exactly when it has a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(z_d\) contains every monomial of degree at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\in\Sigma[x]\iff\exists Q\succeq0\text{ such that }q=z_d^\top Qz_d.
knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Matrix Representation of an SOS Polynomial
Sum-of-Squares Certificate Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraically verifiable lower-bound certificates for polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\). A sum-of-squares certificate for the lower bound \(\gamma\) is an identity \[p-\gamma=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_jg_j,\] where every \(\sigma_j\) is a sum-of-squares polynomial and any prescribed degree limits are satisfied. Evaluating the identity at \(x\in K\) gives \(p(x)-\gamma\ge0\), so \(\gamma\le\inf_{x\in K}p(x)\). Producing and verifying this algebraic identity belongs to sum-of-squares certificate theory; the continuous global problem uses it as a globally valid bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS identity expresses the objective minus a bound using nonnegative polynomial terms, thereby certifying that bound globally on the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\sigma_j\) is a sum of squares.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(x)\ge\gamma\) for every \(x\in K\), hence \(\gamma\le\inf_{x\in K}p(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed SOS identity is a valid sufficient lower-bound certificate and certificate is the correct content kind. A dedicated source with a theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Solution Extraction Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for recovering candidate solutions from algebraic relaxation output.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way logical boundary for moment-based solution extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an optimal truncated moment sequence fails the applicable flat-rank condition at the current relaxation order, one may not conclude that the relaxation value is inexact, that global minimizers do not exist, or that the minimizer set is infinite. Nonflatness means only that this particular finite-atomic extraction certificate has not been obtained at that order; a higher order, a different optimal moment solution, or another recovery method may still succeed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonflat moment matrix means only that the standard finite-atomic extraction certificate is unavailable at that order.
assumptions_latex: A finite-order optimal moment solution has been computed.
The applicable flat-rank equality is not satisfied.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Flatness Is Inconclusive

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assigns positive extraction theorems and recovery procedures to their canonical polynomial moment/SOS homes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Recovering optimizers from a polynomial moment relaxation requires a theorem-specific extraction certificate whose hypotheses verify a feasible representing measure and whose objective condition makes its support optimal. The flat-extension or flat-truncation theorem, rank convention, support construction, and atom or weight recovery algorithm belong to polynomial moment/SOS extraction theory. This boundary leaf records that handoff and does not supply an independent generic-search extraction rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizer recovery from moment data is justified only by the applicable polynomial moment/SOS extraction theorem; generic continuous search supplies no substitute extraction rule.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial optimization relaxation has produced candidate truncated moment data.
Any claimed recovery is intended to be certified rather than heuristic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Certified extraction must be justified at the applicable polynomial moment/SOS extraction node.}
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Extraction Ownership Boundary
Solution Extraction Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flat moment matrices certify finite atomic representations from which global minimizers can be recovered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an optimal feasible truncated moment sequence \(y^*\) for a polynomial moment relaxation over \(K\). Let \(r:=\max_j\lceil\deg(g_j)/2\rceil\). Under the applicable truncated-moment extension hypotheses, the flatness condition \[\operatorname{rank}M_d(y^*)=\operatorname{rank}M_{d-r}(y^*)=:s\] certifies an \(s\)-atomic representing measure supported on \(K\). Its support points can be recovered by moment-matrix linear algebra; when the relaxation value equals the polynomial optimum, those support points are global minimizers. Verifying flatness and extracting atoms belong to moment/SOS solution-extraction theory, rather than to generic continuous search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat optimal moment matrix certifies a finite atomic measure; its recovered support points are global minimizers when the relaxation is exact.
assumptions_latex: \(y^*\) is an optimal feasible truncated moment sequence.
The required truncated-moment extension and support hypotheses hold.
The moment relaxation is exact for the original polynomial problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flatness yields an \(s\)-atomic representing measure whose extracted support points are global minimizers.

notation.meaning: optimal moment matrix of order d
maximum half-degree index of the constraint polynomials
rank and number of extracted atoms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits, but 'applicable truncated-moment extension hypotheses' is not explicit enough to validate the flatness implication, and the rank index depends on the precise constrained flat-extension theorem. An authoritative theorem citation is required.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Nonconvex Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for models whose defining feature is discrete decision structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Nonconvex Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between purely continuous global models and models with essential integral decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer nonconvex optimization problem has the form \[\inf\{f(x,z):(x,z)\in C,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ z\in\mathbb{Z}^q\},\] where \(q\ge1\) and either the objective, the continuous feasible slices, or their coupling is nonconvex. The model lies beyond the purely continuous global-problem class when integrality of \(z\) is an essential feasibility condition rather than an encoding removable without changing feasible solutions or objective values. Fixing \(z\) may produce continuous global subproblems, but enumeration, branching, or other discrete-search logic belongs to mixed-integer nonconvex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model crosses the mixed-integer boundary when essential integer variables require discrete search, even if each fixed-integer subproblem is continuous.
assumptions_latex: Integrality cannot be removed without changing the optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is mixed-integer nonconvex rather than a purely continuous global optimization problem.
