children.title: Bilevel Model Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for optimization models with nested decision levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilevel Model Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical optimistic bilevel optimization with a lower-level optimal-response constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(y,v\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(U,L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\). An optimistic bilevel problem is \[\inf_{x,y}\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in U,\ y\in S(x)\},\qquad S(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in\mathbb{R}^m}\{f(x,v):(x,v)\in L\}.\] The upper-level decision \(x\) is feasible only together with a lower-level optimal response \(y\). If \(S(x)\) contains multiple points, the optimistic convention permits selection of the response best for the upper-level objective. Modeling and analyzing the set-valued optimal-response constraint belong to bilevel optimization; treating a fixed or reformulated instance as a continuous nonconvex problem does not remove that hierarchical origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilevel model constrains the upper-level decision by a lower-level optimizer; the optimistic convention selects the upper-level-preferred lower solution.
assumptions_latex: The lower-level solution set \(S(x)\) is nonempty for every upper-level point under consideration.
The optimistic convention is used when \(S(x)\) is not a singleton.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \((x,y)\in U\) and \(y\in S(x)\).

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Bilevel Linear Programming Problem p. 175

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Bilevel Linear Programming Problem p. 175

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adversarial selection among multiple lower-level optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in L(x)}f(x,v)\). Under the pessimistic convention, the leader evaluates \(x\) by \(\Psi(x)=\sup_{y\in S(x)}F(x,y)\) and minimizes \(\Psi\), subject to the declared interpretation of upper constraints for all relevant follower responses. This differs from the optimistic value \(\Phi(x)=\inf_{y\in S(x)}F(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pessimistic bilevel model evaluates each leader decision at its worst lower-level optimum instead of selecting the leader-preferred optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(S(x)\) is nonempty for every leader decision under consideration.
The extended-real and upper-constraint conventions are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Psi(x)=\sup_{y\in S(x)}F(x,y),\qquad \Phi(x)=\inf_{y\in S(x)}F(x,y).
knowledge_statements.title: Pessimistic Bilevel Convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation retaining global follower optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\varphi(x)=\inf\{f(x,v):(x,v)\in L\}\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-union geometry induced by componentwise complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b\in\mathbb R^q\), \(0\le a\perp b\ge0\) holds exactly when, for every \(i\), either \(a_i=0,\ b_i\ge0\) or \(a_i\ge0,\ b_i=0\). Equivalently, \[\{(a,b):0\le a\perp b\ge0\}=\bigcup_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}}\{a_I=0,\ b_I\ge0,\ a_{I^c}\ge0,\ b_{I^c}=0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementarity set is a finite union of orthants indexed by which member of each pair is fixed to zero.
assumptions_latex: Vector inequalities and complementarity are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{0\le a\perp b\ge0\}=\bigcup_{I\subseteq[q]}\{a_I=0,b_I\ge0,a_{I^c}\ge0,b_{I^c}=0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity Problems and Their Linear and Nonlinear Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the general complementarity problem for a mapping on Euclidean space and classifies it according to whether the mapping is affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the complementarity problem is to find \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(z\ge 0\), \(f(z)\ge 0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}f(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i f_i(z)=0\). If \(f(z)=Mz+q\), where \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the problem is a linear complementarity problem. If \(f\) is not affine, it is a nonlinear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementarity problem seeks a nonnegative vector z whose image f(z) is nonnegative and orthogonal to z. It is linear when f has the affine form Mz+q and nonlinear when f is not affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\ge 0,\quad f(z)\ge 0,\quad z^{\mathsf T}f(z)=0;\qquad f(z)=Mz+q\Rightarrow\mathrm{LCP},\quad f\text{ nonaffine}\Rightarrow\mathrm{NCP}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wardrop-type equilibrium conditions for feasible multimodal path flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible link-load pattern \(f^*\) is a multimodal traffic-network equilibrium if, for every mode \(i\), origin-destination pair \(w\), and path \(p\in P_w\), there exists an equilibrium travel disutility \(\lambda_w^i\) such that
\[
C_p^i=\lambda_w^i\quad\text{if }x_p^{i*}>0,
\qquad
C_p^i\geq\lambda_w^i\quad\text{if }x_p^{i*}=0.
\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equilibrium conditions for allocating multiple population classes among locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume migrants are rational and migration continues while a unilateral move can increase utility. A feasible multiclass population vector \(p^*\in K\) is a migration equilibrium if, for every class \(k=1,\ldots,J\), there exists \(\lambda^k\) such that, for every location \(i\),
\[
u_i^k=\lambda^k\quad\text{if }p_i^{k*}>0,
\qquad
u_i^k\leq\lambda^k\quad\text{if }p_i^{k*}=0.
\]
Thus each class occupies only locations of maximal utility, with utility equalized across its occupied locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under rational unilateral migration, a feasible multiclass population allocation is an equilibrium when each class occupies only maximum-utility locations, has equal utility at occupied locations, and cannot obtain greater utility at an unoccupied location.

children.title: Robust Optimization Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for models defined through protection against uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies models by pointwise protection over a prescribed uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(U\ne\varnothing\) be an uncertainty set, let \(f:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and let \(g_i:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\). A static robust problem has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{u\in U}f(x,u)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x,u)\le0\quad\forall u\in U,\ i=1,\ldots,p.\] Its ownership is determined by pointwise worst-case quantification over \(U\), not by whether the resulting deterministic counterpart is convex or globally difficult.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust optimization chooses a decision protected against every realization in a prescribed uncertainty set, commonly with a worst-case objective.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty decision set and \(U\) is a nonempty uncertainty set.
\(p\in\mathbb N\), and \(f\) and \(g_i\) are defined on \(X\times U\).
One static decision \(x\) is selected before the uncertain realization is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is robustly feasible}\iff x\in X\text{ and }g_i(x,u)\le0\ \forall u\in U,\ i=1,\ldots,p.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Optimization Ownership Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and the uncertainty set \(U\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded deterministic-equivalent representation for the stated two-stage production-and-recourse model with finitely many scenarios and known probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let first-stage production decisions \(x_j\) be chosen before demand is observed. Suppose demand has finitely many scenarios \(r=1,\ldots,m\) with known probabilities \(p_r\), and let \(y_j^{(r)}\) and \(z_j^{(r)}\) denote scenario-dependent excess-production and shortfall decisions. The model is the linear program
\[
\min\ \sum_j c_jx_j+\sum_{r=1}^m p_r\left(\sum_j e_jy_j^{(r)}+\sum_j f_jz_j^{(r)}\right)
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\le b_i\quad\text{for every production constraint }i,
\]
\[
x_j-y_j^{(r)}+z_j^{(r)}=d_j^{(r)},\qquad x_j,y_j^{(r)},z_j^{(r)}\ge0\quad\text{for all }j,r.
\]
The first-stage variables are common to all scenarios, whereas the second-stage variables are scenario indexed; after demand is observed, only the second-stage decisions corresponding to the realized scenario are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finitely many demand scenarios of known probability, production is chosen before demand is observed and separate excess-production and shortfall variables are introduced for each scenario. The probability-weighted expected-cost formulation, together with common production constraints and scenario-specific balance constraints, is a linear program. Only the recourse decisions for the realized scenario are ultimately used.
assumptions_latex: r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\text{ indexes finitely many demand scenarios}
x\text{ is selected before demand is observed}
\text{The displayed objective and constraints are linear}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated finite-scenario two-stage expected-cost model has a deterministic linear-programming representation with common first-stage and scenario-indexed second-stage variables.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a two-stage recourse model, $x_1$ is selected before observing $\xi_1$, and an admissible second-stage policy $x_2=x_2(x_1,\xi_1)$ is applied after observation. The illustrated formulation is
\[\min_{x_1,x_2(\cdot)} C_1(x_1)+E\!\left[C_2\bigl(x_2(x_1,\xi_1)\bigr)\right]\]
subject to
\[P\{U_1(x_1,\xi_1)\ge U_{\min}^{(1)}\}\ge p,\qquad E[U_2(x_1,\xi_1,x_2(x_1,\xi_1))]\ge U_{\min}^{(2)}.\]
Here $C_1$ is deterministic, while the second-stage cost is random through $\xi_1$ and the recourse policy. In the extract's complete-recourse illustration, an admissible second-stage decision can satisfy the terminal condition for each relevant realization $\bar\xi_1$, represented by
\[U_2(x_1,\bar\xi_1,x_2)=U_{\min}^{(2)}.\]
A common numerical approach discretizes the probability space and solves the resulting finite-scenario approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-stage recourse model chooses a first-stage decision before uncertainty is observed and then applies a second-stage decision depending on that observation. The illustrated model minimizes first-stage cost plus expected recourse cost under a chance constraint and an expected-utility requirement. In the source's complete-recourse illustration, a suitable second-stage action satisfies the terminal condition for every relevant realization. Probability-space discretization yields a common scenario approximation.
assumptions_latex: x_2=x_2(x_1,\xi_1)\text{ is a measurable admissible policy applied after observing }\xi_1
C_1(x_1)\text{ is deterministic and the displayed expectations exist}
\text{the illustrated complete-recourse condition requires an admissible }x_2\text{ for every relevant realization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x_1,x_2(\cdot)}\;C_1(x_1)+E[C_2(x_2(x_1,\xi_1))]\quad\text{subject to the stated chance and expected-utility constraints}

children.title: Distributional Uncertainty Ownership
children.top_down_role: Routing for uncertainty models positioned between robust protection and stochastic representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies models whose optimization quantifies over an ambiguity set of probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty set of probability measures on a measurable uncertainty space \(\Xi\), and suppose \(\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\) is well-defined for every relevant \((x,P)\). A distributionally robust objective has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)].\] Its defining feature is optimization over probability laws. If \(\mathcal P=\{P_0\}\), it reduces to a fixed-law stochastic objective; if \(\mathcal P\) consists of all Dirac laws \(\delta_u\) for \(u\in U\), it reduces to \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributional uncertainty is modeled by worst-case optimization over an ambiguity set of probability laws, specializing to fixed-law stochastic or pointwise robust objectives in limiting cases.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable uncertainty space.
\(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty set of probability measures on \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\).
For every relevant \(x\) and \(P\), \(\ell(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and its expectation is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P=\{P_0\}\Longrightarrow\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell]=\mathbb E_{P_0}[\ell],\qquad \mathcal P=\{\delta_u:u\in U\}\Longrightarrow\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell]=\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u).

notation.meaning: Dirac probability law concentrated at u

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Uncertainty Ownership Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty set of probability measures on \(\Xi\).
For every feasible \(x\), the loss \(\ell(x,\cdot)\) is measurable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distributional uncertainty is represented by optimization over \(P\in\mathcal P\), rather than by one fixed probability law.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the distributionally robust formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes ambiguity about probability laws from pointwise uncertainty and from a single known distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distributionally robust optimization problem is \[\inf_{x\in X}\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\] possibly subject to distributionally robust constraints such as \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\bigl(g(x,\xi)\le 0\bigr)\ge 1-\varepsilon.\] Its defining object is the ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\) of probability laws. When \(\mathcal P=\{P_0\}\), the worst-distribution objective reduces to an ordinary stochastic expectation; when uncertainty is quantified pointwise over realizations without probability laws, the model instead has robust-optimization form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributionally robust optimization minimizes worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of probability distributions, lying between fixed-law stochastic programming and pointwise robust optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Uncertainty Ownership

children.title: Randomized Search Distinction
children.top_down_role: Separation of stochastic solution procedures from optimization models defined by uncertainty.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) defines a deterministic optimization model.
\((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) supports random variables \(R_k:\Omega\to\mathcal R\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the randomization space.
For each \(k\ge 0\), the update map \(A_k:X^{k+1}\times\mathcal R\to X\) is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Randomness in \((R_k)_{k\ge 0}\) does not make the deterministic model \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) a stochastic program.
review_flags: The locator addresses random search, while explicit support for the ownership distinction remains provisional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates randomness in a solver from uncertainty encoded in the optimization model.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.2 'Globalized' Local Optimization Strategies, Combined with Grid Search or Random Search p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the deterministic problem \(v^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). A randomized search may generate \(x_{k+1}=A_k(x_0,\ldots,x_k,R_k)\), while every objective evaluation returns the deterministic value \(f(x_k)\). The random variables \((R_k)_{k\ge 0}\) can change the distribution of the iterates and the probability of satisfying a specified solution criterion, but they do not change \(v^*\), \(X\), or \(f\). Thus randomized search is not stochastic programming unless random quantities also occur in the optimization model or its information structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random sampling by a solver does not make a deterministic optimization model stochastic; model uncertainty and algorithmic randomness belong to different classifications.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Search Distinction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Divergence Criterion for Infinitely Many Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General probability lemma used in stochastic-search convergence analysis; the conditioning event is retained exactly as extracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{A_k\}_{k\ge 0}\) be events. If, for every \(k,n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) with \(k\ge n\), \[P\!\left(A_k\mid\bigcap_{j=n}^{k-1}\overline A_{k-j}\right)\ge p_k,\qquad 0\le p_k\le1,\] and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p_k=\infty\), then \[P\!\left(\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}\bigcup_{k=n}^{\infty}A_k\right)=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the stated conditional probabilities have nonsummable lower bounds, then infinitely many of the events occur almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \forall k,n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ k\ge n:\quad P\!\left(A_k\mid\bigcap_{j=n}^{k-1}\overline A_{k-j}\right)\ge p_k,\quad 0\le p_k\le1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\!\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}A_k\right)=P\!\left(\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}\bigcup_{k=n}^{\infty}A_k\right)=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Summability Criterion for Finitely Many Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General probability lemma used in stochastic-search convergence analysis; the conditioning event is retained exactly as extracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{A_k\}_{k\ge 0}\) be events. If, for every \(k,n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) with \(k\ge n\), \[P\!\left(A_k\mid\bigcap_{j=n}^{k-1}\overline A_{k-j}\right)\le p_k,\qquad 0\le p_k\le1,\] and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p_k<\infty\), then \[P\!\left(\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}\bigcup_{k=n}^{\infty}A_k\right)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the stated conditional probabilities have summable upper bounds, then only finitely many of the events occur almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \forall k,n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ k\ge n:\quad P\!\left(A_k\mid\bigcap_{j=n}^{k-1}\overline A_{k-j}\right)\le p_k,\quad 0\le p_k\le1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\!\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}A_k\right)=P\!\left(\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}\bigcup_{k=n}^{\infty}A_k\right)=0.

children.title: Local Optimization Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for local solution concepts, stationarity, and neighborhood-based analysis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local ownership concerns improvement near \(x^*\); global ownership compares \(x^*\) with every point of \(X\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean open ball of radius r about x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies optimization by the neighborhood-based guarantee of its solution concept.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Global versus Local Optimization p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x^*\in X\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(X\) if there exists \(r>0\) such that \[f(x^*)\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in X\cap B_r(x^*).\] It is a strict local minimizer if the inequality is strict for every \(x\in X\cap B_r(x^*)\) with \(x\ne x^*\). Local optimization owns methods and guarantees whose terminal claim is neighborhood minimality or stationarity, without a certificate comparing the returned point against all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local optimization seeks neighborhood-based minimality or stationarity. Unlike global optimization, its guarantee need not compare the returned point with every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Optimization Ownership

children.title: Nonsmooth Optimization Ownership
children.top_down_role: Ownership boundary for generalized derivative structures and nonsmooth calculus.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies models requiring calculus beyond classical derivatives without asserting a particular stationarity formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous optimization model has nonsmooth-optimization ownership when its objective or constraints fail to possess the classical derivatives required by the proposed smooth analysis or method, so generalized derivatives, derivative-free models, or other nonsmooth tools are required. Nonsmoothness is independent of globality and convexity: a nonsmooth problem may be local or global and convex or nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth ownership is triggered by unavailable required classical derivatives, not by nonconvexity, globality, or randomized search.
assumptions_latex: A continuous optimization model and the derivative requirements of the proposed analysis or method are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{required classical derivative unavailable}\Longrightarrow\text{smooth calculus is insufficient for that analysis}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Optimization Ownership Boundary

assumptions_latex: The objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is not assumed differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonsmooth ownership requires generalized first-order objects whenever \(\nabla f(x)\) is unavailable.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the generalized-gradient formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses locally Lipschitz objectives and Clarke stationarity as the representative nonsmooth local calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous optimization problem \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) has nonsmooth-optimization ownership when its analysis or method must accommodate points at which the classical gradient of \(f\) does not exist, or analogous nonsmooth constraints. For a locally Lipschitz objective and a closed feasible set, a representative generalized first-order condition is \[0\in\partial^{\circ}f(x^*)+N_X^{\circ}(x^*).\] This condition is local and generally necessary rather than globally sufficient. Nonsmoothness alone does not imply global-optimization ownership, and nonconvexity alone does not imply nonsmoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth optimization treats objectives or constraints lacking classical derivatives, using generalized derivatives and stationarity conditions that are usually local rather than globally sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Optimization Ownership

children.title: Nonsmooth Local Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Routing for local optimization problems dominated by nonsmooth structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Routes nonsmooth methods by their local terminal guarantee rather than by a particular algorithm family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method is in a nonsmooth local-search regime when it is designed for a model lacking the required classical derivatives and its terminal guarantee is only local minimality or a specified generalized-stationarity condition. In the unconstrained locally Lipschitz case, Clarke stationarity \(0\in\partial^\circ f(x)\) is one such terminal condition. This condition does not imply global optimality or a bound on \(f(x)-\inf f\) without an independent global argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth method is locally classified when its guarantee is local minimality or generalized stationarity; that guarantee alone is not global certification.
assumptions_latex: The modeled objective or constraints lack classical derivatives required by the method's smooth calculus.
Any stated generalized-stationarity condition uses a derivative notion whose hypotheses hold.
For the displayed Clarke condition, \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\) and the problem is unconstrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial^\circ f(x)\not\Longrightarrow f(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^n}f(y)\quad\text{in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Local-Search Classification

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near the iterates.
A computable generalized first-order model is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search is local when its stopping claim is approximate generalized stationarity, not global objective dominance.

notation.meaning: trial step or local search direction

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the nonsmooth local-search boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes nonsmooth searches by local models and generalized-stationarity termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonsmooth method operates in a local-search regime when each accepted step \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\) is selected from information localized near \(x_k\), and its declared success criterion is \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(0,\partial^{\circ}f(x_k)\bigr)\le\varepsilon\] in the unconstrained locally Lipschitz case, or the corresponding constrained generalized-stationarity residual. Such a criterion certifies approximate local stationarity only. Without an independent global lower bound or exhaustive valid enclosure, it does not certify \(f(x_k)-\inf_x f(x)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth search is local when it uses nearby generalized first-order information and terminates at approximate generalized stationarity without a global objective-gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Local Search Regimes

A source-backed, explicitly delimited class of methods is required.

children.title: Global-to-Local Handoff
children.top_down_role: Interface where global exploration transfers candidate regions to local refinement.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is bounded below.
A global phase supplies a feasible incumbent \(x^G\in X\) and a valid lower bound \(L\le f^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).
A local solver returns \(x^L\in X\) satisfying \(f(x^L)\le f(x^G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local phase improves the incumbent, while the valid bound \(L\) remains responsible for the global certificate \(L\le f^*\le f(x^L)\).

notation.meaning: feasible incumbent supplied to local search
valid lower bound on the global optimum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates local incumbent refinement from the lower-bound mechanism responsible for global certification.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a global method has a feasible incumbent \(x^G\in X\) and a valid lower bound \(L\le f^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). A local refinement returns \(x^L\in X\) with \(f(x^L)\le f(x^G)\). Replacing the incumbent by \(x^L\) gives the certified bounds \[L\le f^*\le f(x^L).\] Global validity is retained because \(L\) remains valid; local optimality or stationarity of \(x^L\) alone supplies no global certificate. For a tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), an \(\varepsilon\)-global termination claim is justified whenever \(f(x^L)-L\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global search may hand an incumbent to local refinement, but the retained global lower bound, not local stationarity, certifies the final objective gap.

children.title: Nonlinear Equation-Enclosure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for complete root enclosure as a neighboring validated-computation subject.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Minimization Decides Root Existence on a Compact Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact but limited interface between scalar global minimization and nonlinear root enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact and let \(F:D\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuous. For \(r(x)=\|F(x)\|^2\), the minimum of \(r\) is attained and \[\min_{x\in D}r(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists x\in D:\ F(x)=0.\] A certified exact residual minimum can therefore decide whether at least one root exists, but it neither enumerates all roots nor certifies root-free subregions or uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain, exact residual minimization decides whether any root exists, but it does not provide complete root enclosure.
assumptions_latex: The residual and its global minimum are certified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_D\|F\|^2=0\iff F^{-1}(0)\cap D\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Minimization Decides Root Existence on a Compact Domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite output specification permitting unresolved boxes at a declared spatial resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a compact initial box, let \(F:D\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuous, and fix \(\delta>0\). A resolution-complete enclosure consists of finite box families \(\mathcal E,\mathcal C,\mathcal U\) covering \(D\). Every \(B\in\mathcal E\) has a validated root-exclusion certificate; every \(B\in\mathcal C\) has a validated existence certificate and may additionally have a uniqueness certificate; and every unresolved \(B\in\mathcal U\) satisfies \(\operatorname{diam}B\le\delta\). Completeness requires \[F^{-1}(0)\cap D\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal C\cup\mathcal U}B.\] A box having only an at-most-one-root certificate, without existence, remains unresolved for this classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite enclosure at resolution delta may retain small unresolved boxes, but every discarded box must be certified root-free and every positively classified box must have an existence certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every asserted certificate is validated under its own theorem-specific hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal C\cup\mathcal U}B,\qquad \max_{B\in\mathcal U}\operatorname{diam}B\le\delta.

notation.meaning: boxes certified to contain no root
boxes carrying a validated root-existence certificate
unresolved boxes retained at the declared resolution

knowledge_statements.title: Resolution-Complete Root-Enclosure Output

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation of the principal validated-equation certificate roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a box \(B\), an exclusion certificate proves \(F^{-1}(0)\cap B=\varnothing\); an existence certificate proves \(F^{-1}(0)\cap B\ne\varnothing\); and an at-most-one-root certificate proves \(|F^{-1}(0)\cap B|\le1\). A unique-root conclusion requires both existence and at-most-one-root claims, unless one validated theorem supplies both. None of exclusion, existence, or at-most-one-root alone implies either of the other claims. The analytic tests establishing them belong to validated nonlinear equation solving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root exclusion, existence, and at-most-one-root claims are different; uniqueness requires both existence and at-most-one-root certification.
assumptions_latex: Each certificate is interpreted only through its validated theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{unique root in }B\Longleftrightarrow\bigl(\text{existence in }B\bigr)\land\bigl(\text{at most one root in }B\bigr).
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Claims Are Logically Noninterchangeable

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete root enclosure seeks verified boxes covering \(Z=\{x\in D:F(x)=0\}\), not minimizers of a scalar objective.

notation.meaning: root set in the search domain
finite family of verified enclosing boxes

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses validated nonlinear equation solving or complete root enclosure.
A source is needed for the existence, uniqueness, and exclusion certificate taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks complete validated root enclosure as adjacent to, but distinct from, scalar global optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonlinear system \(F(x)=0\) on \(D\), complete root enclosure asks for a finite family of boxes \(\mathcal B\) such that \[Z:=\{x\in D:F(x)=0\}\subseteq\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal B}B,\] together with validated tests that exclude roots from the discarded part of \(D\); boxes may additionally carry existence or uniqueness certificates. The task is not, by itself, the scalar minimization of \(\lVert F(x)\rVert\): minimizing a residual can locate candidates, but without validated exclusion and existence tests it does not certify that all roots have been enclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete nonlinear root enclosure must cover every root and validate excluded regions. Merely globally minimizing a residual does not provide those existence and completeness certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Equation-Enclosure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal container, but no source supports complete validated root enclosure or the existence, uniqueness, and exclusion certificate taxonomy. Continuity on an arbitrary prescribed domain also does not ensure that a finite box enclosure of all roots is available, so the intended task class needs source-backed domain and finiteness qualifications.
